  It is recorded as applied in this database without running it; empty databases are created from it.
Saved the entity schema as the baseline snapshot: .migrax/snapshot.json

0001_baseline.sql describes the table as it is:

-- Generated by Migrax 0.17.1 for postgresql
-- Baseline: the tables the database already had before its first migration.
-- That database records it as applied without running it; empty databases are created from it.

CREATE TABLE customers (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(255) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customers_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customers_email UNIQUE (email));

This database won't run it, because the table is already there. A new laptop, a test database or migrax verify starts empty and builds the table from it. "No changes detected" means the entities and the database agree, so nothing is lost by switching. If update had already left old columns behind, they would show up here as changes to review.

Commit the migration folder and .migrax/snapshot.json.

docs.title: 3. Make the change again
docs.text:
Now the same three changes to Customer. This time generate writes them down instead of running them:

$ migrax generate --rename customers.name=full_name
warning: Adding NOT NULL column 'customers.country' without a default fails if the table has rows. Add a default in the SQL, or add it as nullable, backfill, then make it NOT NULL.
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql:
  - rename column customers.name to full_name
  - add column customers.country
  - alter column customers.email
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
src/main/resources/db/migration/0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql, statement 1: warning MX008
  ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name
  Application instances still running the old code use the old name and will fail.
  ...
src/main/resources/db/migration/0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql, statement 2: warning MX002
  ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN country varchar(2) NOT NULL
  Adding a NOT NULL column without a default fails when customers has rows.
  Fix: Add a DEFAULT, or add the column as nullable, backfill it, then make it NOT NULL.
...
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

Without --rename, Migrax notices that a column went away while another appeared and asks whether it was a rename; in CI it refuses to guess and stops. Renaming columns and tables without losing data shows both.

The warning MX002 is the failure from the update run, found before anything ran. The migration is a plain SQL file, so fix it the way the warning says: add the column, fill it, then make it required.

-- Generated by Migrax 0.17.1 for postgresql

ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN country varchar(2);
UPDATE customers SET country = 'GB';
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN country SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN email TYPE varchar(320);

Next to it, rollback/0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql undoes the change:

ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN country;
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN email TYPE varchar(255);
ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN full_name TO name;

docs.title: 4. Apply it
docs.text:
$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 2 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.

The application starts with validate, the next customer signs up, and the existing ones kept their names:

 id |       email       |  full_name   | country
----+-------------------+--------------+---------
  1 | ada@example.com   | Ada Lovelace | GB
  2 | alan@example.com  | Alan Turing  | GB
  3 | grace@example.com | Grace Hopper | GB

docs.title: The other environments
docs.text:
Production, staging and every teammate's database have the same table but no migration history. Each one needs to be told once that the baseline is already there:

$ migrax status
Migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop_prod
  [ ] 0001_baseline.sql                        pending
  [ ] 0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql  pending
2 pending.

$ migrax baseline 0001 --yes
Recording 1 migration(s) as applied without running them:
  0001_baseline.sql
Recorded. Run 'migrax migrate' to apply the migrations after 0001_baseline.sql.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 2 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.

(Point each command at that database with --url, or the environment variables your deployment already uses.)

Forgetting baseline is safe. migrate tries to create the table, the database refuses, and nothing is recorded or changed:

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_baseline.sql'...
error: Failed executing migration '0001_baseline.sql': ERROR: relation "customers" already exists
error[MXE102]: Migration '0001_baseline.sql' failed and was not recorded as applied. ...

baseline then refuses too, because the failed attempt counts as history. Record the baseline with repair instead, and carry on:

$ migrax repair 0001_baseline.sql --action applied --yes
Repaired history for 0001_baseline.sql (action: applied). Keep a record of this repair.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_rename_customers_name_and_more.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 2 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.

docs.title: Other frameworks
docs.text:
The setting has a different name outside Spring Boot, and migrax doctor finds each of them:

Framework Setting Change to Spring Boot spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto validate or none Quarkus quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy validate or none Micronaut jpa.default.properties.hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto validate or none Plain Hibernate, Jakarta EE hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto validate or none

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ddl-auto=update only adds. It turns a rename into a second, empty column, can't add a required column to a table with rows, and lets the application start when a statement fails.
  • Switch between releases: set validate, run migrax generate once to record the existing tables as 0001_baseline.sql, and run migrax baseline 0001 --yes once on every other database.
  • From then on every change is a SQL file you review, with lint warnings for the statements that fail on real data, and a rollback script.

More in the guides: Quick start and Production safety.

docs.title: Frameworks and build tools
docs.text:
Migrax doesn't depend on any framework, or on Java. It works in two ways:

  • Any language: you write SQL migrations, Migrax applies them with history, checksums, locking and rollbacks. Python, Node.js, Go, .NET, PHP, Ruby or anything else: see Any language. The container image needs only Docker.
  • Java with JPA entities: Migrax also writes the migrations for you from your entities, with the frameworks below.

For Java applications, Migrax comes in two parts, and most projects use both: a tool for your terminal (the Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin or the migrax command-line tool) that writes and checks the migrations, and a startup library for your framework that applies them when the application starts. Each framework page begins with what to add.

Migrax reads your entities and talks to the database over JDBC, so the command line works the same everywhere. What differs per framework is:

  • where the database settings are, which Migrax reads for you;
  • how Hibernate names tables and columns, which Migrax must match exactly;
  • how migrations can run at startup, through a small integration library.

Migrax recognizes the framework from your build file and configuration. migrax doctor shows what it detected.

Framework Database settings Naming Startup integration Spring Boot spring.datasource.* spring migrax-spring-boot-starter Quarkus quarkus.datasource.* jpa migrax-quarkus Micronaut datasources.default.* micronaut with Micronaut Data, else jpa migrax-micronaut Helidon javax.sql.DataSource.<name>.*, db.connection.* (SE) jpa migrax-helidon (MP) Jakarta EE, plain Hibernate persistence.xml jpa migrax-jakarta-ee Any language MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL and the other MIGRAX_* variables (no entities) the container image, before the application starts

Build tools: Maven plugin and Gradle plugin.

Getting the integration libraries

The libraries and both build plugins are on Maven Central from Migrax 0.14.0 on: add the dependency or plugin shown on each page, and Maven or Gradle downloads it. For 0.13.0 and older, install them from the source instead (mvn install, then mvn install -f integrations/pom.xml, in a clone of the repository).

Upgrading from 0.3 or older

Since 0.4.0, Migrax is published as org.migrax instead of io.migrax: the groupId, the Gradle plugin ID (id("org.migrax")), the Java packages (org.migrax.api.JavaMigration) and the logger name. Replace io.migrax with org.migrax in your build files, Java migrations and logging configuration. During the upgrade, let only one instance run migrations against a database at a time: 0.3 and 0.4 use differently named migration locks.

docs.title: Any language
docs.text:
Migrax isn't only for Java. Any application that keeps its database changes as SQL files can use it to apply them: Python, Node.js, Go, .NET, PHP, Ruby or anything else. You write the migrations; Migrax runs them once and in order, records them, and refuses to run a file that changed after it was applied. You don't need a second migration tool next to your framework.

What you get Numbered migrations, applied once and in order 0001_create_customer.sql, 0002_add_email.sql Repeatable migrations for views and functions R__customer_view.sql, run again when they change A history table, checksums and a lock Safe with several instances starting at the same time Rollback scripts rollback/0002_add_email.sql, run by migrax rollback Checks before anything runs migrax lint finds statements that lock tables or lose data A status overview migrax status, also as JSON for scripts

The commands that compare the database with Java entities (generate, check, drift and verify) have nothing to read in such a project; everything else works the same.

docs.title: Two ways to run it
docs.text: Needs Best for Container image Docker Docker Compose, Kubernetes, CI. Drivers for PostgreSQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite and H2 included Command line Java 17 or newer Running it on your machine like any other development tool

docs.title: In three steps
docs.text:
1. Put your SQL files in a folder, for example db/migrations:

    db/migrations/0001_create_customer.sql
    CREATE TABLE customer (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL);

  2. Tell Migrax the database, as a JDBC URL:

    export MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret
export MIGRAX_LOCATIONS=filesystem:db/migrations

  3. Apply the migrations:

    Container imageCommand line 
    docker run --rm --network host \
  -v "$PWD/db/migrations:/migrations:ro" \
  -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL \
  -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER \
  -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD \
  ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1 migrate

    The image reads the migrations from /migrations, so MIGRAX_LOCATIONS isn't needed there.

    $ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_create_customer.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_create_customer.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 1 total in db/migrations.

    The command line also needs the database's JDBC driver: see Drivers.

docs.title: Before your application starts
docs.text:
With Docker Compose, run Migrax as a service of its own and start the application only after it finished:

compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
      POSTGRES_USER: shop
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U shop -d shop"]
      interval: 2s
      retries: 30

  migrate:
    image: ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1
    command: migrate --lock-timeout 2m
    volumes:
      - ./db/migrations:/migrations:ro
    environment:
      MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop
      MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER: shop
      MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD: secret
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  app:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

When a migration fails, migrate exits with code 1 and the application doesn't start. In Kubernetes, the same image runs as an init container or a Job: see Containers and Kubernetes.

docs.title: From your project's scripts
docs.text:
Call Migrax from the task runner your project already has, so everyone runs the same command:

Node.jsPHPPython, Go, Ruby, .NET package.json
{
  "scripts": {
    "db:migrate": "migrax migrate",
    "db:status": "migrax status",
    "db:new": "migrax new"
  }
}

npm run db:new -- add_email creates the next numbered file.

composer.json
{
  "scripts": {
    "db:migrate": "migrax migrate",
    "db:status": "migrax status"
  }
}
Makefile
db-migrate:
    migrax migrate

db-status:
    migrax status

Settings in environment variables (or a .env file your shell loads) keep these scripts free of passwords. Every setting is listed in Configuration.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
Check the migrations on every pull request, before they reach a database:

migrax lint --strict
migrax migrate --dry-run

lint needs no database; migrate --dry-run connects and shows what would run. More in Continuous integration.

Tasks

docs.text: Property Meaning packageName Entity package url, user, password Database connection (default: application config) locations Migration folders, comma-separated, e.g. classpath:db/migration naming spring, jpa, jpa-snake or micronaut dialect postgresql, mysql, mariadb, sqlserver, oracle or h2 args Extra arguments for every task, e.g. --verbose version Migrax version used to run the tasks

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Migrax comes in two parts, and most projects use both:

Part What it's for How you get it A tool for your terminal Writing migrations from your entities (generate) and looking after them: status, lint, verify, rollback and the other commands The Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin or the migrax command-line tool The startup library migrax-helidon Applying the pending migrations each time the application starts, before JPA A dependency: see Migrate at startup

The tool for your terminal, pick one:

Maven pluginGradle pluginCommand line tool pom.xml
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
      <artifactId>migrax</artifactId>
      <version>0.17.1</version>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

Then run mvn migrax:generate, mvn migrax:status and so on in the project folder. See Maven plugin.

build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("org.migrax") version "0.17.1"
}

Then run ./gradlew migraxGenerate, ./gradlew migraxStatus and so on. See Gradle plugin.

Install migrax once per machine (Installation), then run migrax generate, migrax status and so on in the project folder. It works with any build, and nothing is added to the project.

Only one of the two?

  • Without the startup library the application doesn't migrate by itself: run migrate yourself or in the deployment pipeline (mvn migrax:migrate, ./gradlew migraxMigrate, migrax migrate or the container image).
  • Without a tool for your terminal there's no generate: write the migration files yourself, and the startup library still applies them.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Migrax reads META-INF/microprofile-config.properties (and the mp.config.profile) together with META-INF/persistence.xml:

META-INF/microprofile-config.properties
javax.sql.DataSource.shop.dataSourceClassName=org.postgresql.ds.PGSimpleDataSource
javax.sql.DataSource.shop.dataSource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
javax.sql.DataSource.shop.dataSource.user=shop
javax.sql.DataSource.shop.dataSource.password=secret
META-INF/persistence.xml
<persistence-unit name="shop" transaction-type="JTA">
  <jta-data-source>shop</jta-data-source>
  <properties>
    <property name="hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto" value="none"/>
  </properties>
</persistence-unit>

When several data sources are configured, Migrax uses the one persistence.xml names. The jdbcUrl, username and password keys of other connection pools work too, and so do the MicroProfile environment variables, such as JAVAX_SQL_DATASOURCE_SHOP_DATASOURCE_URL. hibernate.* properties from persistence.xml are passed to Hibernate.

Naming: Helidon keeps Hibernate's default naming (jpa).

docs.title: Migrate at startup
docs.text:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-helidon</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
</dependency>

Migrations run when the application starts, before your own beans and before JPA is first used, so hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=validate works. Settings go in microprofile-config.properties:

Setting Default Meaning migrax.enabled true Apply migrations at startup migrax.migrate-at-startup true false: start without migrating, when a pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations; the health check and the pending gauge still report them (details) migrax.drift.check off warn or fail: compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when the application starts; the build must put .migrax/snapshot.json into the application (details) migrax.datasource the one persistence.xml names, or the only one Data source to migrate migrax.locations db/migration Migration folders on the classpath, comma-separated migrax.java-package db.migration Package of JavaMigration classes migrax.env Environment: migrations marked -- migrax:env <name> run only there migrax.resume false Re-run a failed migration marked -- migrax:resume-safe migrax.lock-timeout 0 How long to wait while another instance migrates, for example 2m when several start together migrax.placeholders.<name> Values for ${name} placeholders migrax.metrics.enabled true Micrometer metrics of the migrations, when the application has a MeterRegistry (Metrics and tracing) migrax.tracing.enabled true OpenTelemetry spans of the migrations, when the application has an OpenTelemetry migrax.schemas Schemas to migrate one after another

docs.title: Readiness check
docs.text: With helidon-microprofile-health in the application, Migrax adds a migrax readiness check: UP when every migration is applied and none failed, was edited or is missing, DOWN otherwise, with the counts as data (/health/ready).

docs.title: Helidon SE
docs.text:
Helidon SE uses its database client rather than JPA, so there are no entities to generate migrations from. Write migrations with migrax new and apply them with migrax migrate in your deployment (SQL migrations for any language explains this setup). Migrax reads the connection from application.yaml:

db:
  connection:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
    username: shop
    password: secret

docs.title: Jakarta EE and plain Hibernate
docs.text: Any project with JPA entities works, with or without an application framework.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Migrax comes in two parts, and most projects use both:

Part What it's for How you get it A tool for your terminal Writing migrations from your entities (generate) and looking after them: status, lint, verify, rollback and the other commands The Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin or the migrax command-line tool The startup library migrax-jakarta-ee Applying the pending migrations each time the application is deployed, before JPA A dependency: see Migrate at startup

The tool for your terminal, pick one:

Maven pluginGradle pluginCommand line tool pom.xml
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
      <artifactId>migrax</artifactId>
      <version>0.17.1</version>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

Then run mvn migrax:generate, mvn migrax:status and so on in the project folder. See Maven plugin.

build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("org.migrax") version "0.17.1"
}

Then run ./gradlew migraxGenerate, ./gradlew migraxStatus and so on. See Gradle plugin.

Install migrax once per machine (Installation), then run migrax generate, migrax status and so on in the project folder. It works with any build, and nothing is added to the project.

Only one of the two?

  • Without the startup library the application doesn't migrate by itself: run migrate yourself or in the deployment pipeline (mvn migrax:migrate, ./gradlew migraxMigrate, migrax migrate or the container image).
  • Without a tool for your terminal there's no generate: write the migration files yourself, and the startup library still applies them.

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
Migrax reads the first persistence unit in src/main/resources/META-INF/persistence.xml:

<persistence-unit name="shop">
  <properties>
    <property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url" value="jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop"/>
    <property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.user" value="shop"/>
    <property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.password" value="secret"/>
    <property name="hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto" value="none"/>
  </properties>
</persistence-unit>

javax.persistence.jdbc.* and hibernate.connection.* work too. On an application server, the data source is usually defined in the server's own configuration, which the migrax command can't read: give it the connection with environment variables or options, or let the startup integration migrate inside the server.

export MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret
migrax migrate

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: Plain Hibernate keeps names as written (jpa naming). A physical or implicit naming strategy in persistence.xml (hibernate.physical_naming_strategy) is used when Migrax reads the mapping.

docs.title: Running migrations
docs.text: Run migrax migrate as a step of your deployment, before the new version starts, or let the application migrate when it starts on the server.

docs.title: Migrate at startup
docs.text:
Add the integration to your WAR or EAR:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-jakarta-ee</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
</dependency>

When the application starts, Migrax applies the migrations from db/migration to the data source your persistence.xml names, as the server provides it. You don't repeat the connection settings. It is tested on WildFly and Payara and uses only standard Jakarta EE (CDI and JNDI), so it works on other servers too.

<persistence-unit name="shop">
  <jta-data-source>java:app/jdbc/shop</jta-data-source>
  <properties>
    <property name="jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action" value="none"/>
  </properties>
</persistence-unit>

Keep the schema generation at none. The server starts JPA while it deploys the application, before any application code runs, so Hibernate's validate would check the schema before the migrations. Validate in CI with migrax verify instead.

Setting Default Meaning migrax.enabled true Apply migrations at startup migrax.migrate-at-startup true false: start without migrating, when a pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations; the health check and the pending gauge still report them (details) migrax.drift.check off warn or fail: compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when the application starts; the build must put .migrax/snapshot.json into the application (details) migrax.datasource the data source persistence.xml names JNDI name of the data source to migrate migrax.locations db/migration Migration folders on the classpath, comma-separated migrax.java-package db.migration Package of JavaMigration classes migrax.env Environment: migrations marked -- migrax:env <name> run only there migrax.resume false Re-run a failed migration marked -- migrax:resume-safe migrax.lock-timeout 0 How long to wait while another instance migrates, for example 2m migrax.placeholders.<name> Values for ${name} placeholders migrax.metrics.enabled true Micrometer metrics of the migrations, when the application has a MeterRegistry (Metrics and tracing) migrax.tracing.enabled true OpenTelemetry spans of the migrations, when the application has an OpenTelemetry migrax.schemas Schemas to migrate one after another

Jakarta EE has no standard place for application settings, so Migrax reads them from migrax.properties in the application (src/main/resources), from MicroProfile Config where the server has it, from environment variables (MIGRAX_DATASOURCE, MIGRAX_LOCATIONS, MIGRAX_PLACEHOLDERS_<NAME>, ...) and from system properties. Each one overrides the one before.

JPA providers

Migrax reads the mapping through the server's JPA provider: Hibernate (WildFly), EclipseLink (Payara, GlassFish) or OpenJPA (TomEE). With another JPA provider it scans the annotations and applies Hibernate's naming rules; check the generated names, and use migrax drift --entities to compare.

docs.title: Maven plugin
docs.text: Everything the command line does is also available as Maven goals, which is handy in CI or when you prefer not to install the CLI.

docs.title: Setup
Goals
docs.text:
mvn migrax:generate
mvn migrax:migrate
mvn migrax:status
Goal Same as migrax:generate migrax generate migrax:migrate migrax migrate migrax:status migrax status migrax:plan migrax plan migrax:check migrax check migrax:lint migrax lint migrax:verify migrax verify migrax:drift migrax drift migrax:diff migrax diff (-Dmigrax.source=<url>) migrax:report migrax report migrax:rollback migrax rollback migrax:repair migrax repair migrax:baseline migrax baseline (-Dmigrax.version=<migration>) migrax:clean migrax clean migrax:backups migrax backups (-Dmigrax.drop=true, -Dmigrax.migration=<number>) migrax:new migrax new migrax:squash migrax squash migrax:merge migrax merge migrax:import migrax import (-Dmigrax.from=flyway or liquibase) migrax:package-snapshot No command: copies .migrax/snapshot.json into the application for drift at startup

docs.text:
Options are -Dmigrax.* properties (or <configuration> elements of the same name):

Property CLI option Goals migrax.allowDestructive=true --allow-destructive generate migrax.keepData=true --keep-data generate migrax.renames=customers.email=contact_email --rename generate migrax.renameTables=client=customer --rename-table generate migrax.name=split_name --name generate, new migrax.safe=true --safe generate migrax.zeroDowntime=true --zero-downtime generate migrax.contract=true --contract generate migrax.dryRun=true --dry-run migrate, rollback, clean, baseline migrax.resume=true --resume migrate migrax.sql=true --sql migrate migrax.lockTimeout=2m --lock-timeout migrate, rollback, repair, clean, generate migrax.steps=2, migrax.to=<migration> --steps, --to rollback (to also migrate) migrax.confirm=true --yes rollback, repair, clean, baseline, backups migrax.action=applied --action repair migrax.impact=true --impact plan migrax.all=true, migrax.strict=true --all, --strict lint migrax.verifyUrl=<jdbc-url>, migrax.skipRollbacks=true --url, --skip-rollbacks verify migrax.entities=true --entities drift migrax.html=target/migrax-report.html --html report migrax.java=true --java new migrax.url, migrax.user, migrax.password --url, --user, --password all migrax.database=billing --database all migrax.package, migrax.naming, migrax.dialect, migrax.locations, migrax.schemas same names all

Hints in the output use Maven syntax, for example:

$ mvn migrax:generate
[ERROR] Review them, then run 'mvn migrax:generate -Dmigrax.allowDestructive=true'.

docs.title: Micronaut
docs.text: Micronaut 4 and 5 are supported.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Migrax comes in two parts, and most projects use both:

Part What it's for How you get it A tool for your terminal Writing migrations from your entities (generate) and looking after them: status, lint, verify, rollback and the other commands The Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin or the migrax command-line tool The startup library migrax-micronaut Applying the pending migrations each time the application starts, before JPA A dependency: see Migrate at startup

The tool for your terminal, pick one:

Maven pluginGradle pluginCommand line tool pom.xml
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
      <artifactId>migrax</artifactId>
      <version>0.17.1</version>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

Then run mvn migrax:generate, mvn migrax:status and so on in the project folder. See Maven plugin.

build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("org.migrax") version "0.17.1"
}

Then run ./gradlew migraxGenerate, ./gradlew migraxStatus and so on. See Gradle plugin.

Install migrax once per machine (Installation), then run migrax generate, migrax status and so on in the project folder. It works with any build, and nothing is added to the project.

Only one of the two?

  • Without the startup library the application doesn't migrate by itself: run migrate yourself or in the deployment pipeline (mvn migrax:migrate, ./gradlew migraxMigrate, migrax migrate or the container image).
  • Without a tool for your terminal there's no generate: write the migration files yourself, and the startup library still applies them.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Migrax reads application.yml / application.properties and the environments in MICRONAUT_ENVIRONMENTS:

datasources:
  default:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
    username: shop
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
jpa:
  default:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        hbm2ddl:
          auto: none

DATASOURCES_DEFAULT_URL, DATASOURCES_DEFAULT_USERNAME and DATASOURCES_DEFAULT_PASSWORD work too. Without a default data source, Migrax uses the first one. Hibernate settings under jpa.default.properties.* are passed to Hibernate.

Change the starter's update

Projects created from the Micronaut starter set hbm2ddl.auto: update. Set it to none or validate; migrax doctor shows the exact line.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Project uses Naming Example: homepageURL Micronaut Data (micronaut-data-hibernate-jpa) micronaut homepage_url Micronaut Hibernate JPA without Micronaut Data jpa homepageURL

Micronaut Data converts names to snake_case with its own rule, which differs from other snake_case rules for names like myURL (my_url) or productSKU (product_sku). It also uses one shared hibernate_sequence for generated ids. Migrax matches both, and when Micronaut Data is on the classpath it uses Micronaut's own naming class.

docs.title: Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.17.0.

With Micronaut Data JDBC or R2DBC (@MappedEntity entities instead of JPA's @Entity), Migrax reads the mapping Micronaut's annotation processor compiled into your classes: tables, columns, relations, join tables, embedded values and generated ids, named the way your Micronaut Data version names them. Nothing to configure: build the project as usual (the processor micronaut-data-processor must run), and migrax doctor shows Micronaut Data <version>.

Micronaut 5 is compiled for Java 25, so run Migrax with Java 25 for a Micronaut 5 project (JAVA_HOME); Migrax says so when the Java is too old.

Details and what isn't read: Entity readers.

docs.title: Migrate at startup
docs.text:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-micronaut</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
</dependency>

Migrations run as soon as Micronaut creates the data source, before Hibernate starts, so hbm2ddl.auto: validate checks the migrated schema.

Setting Default Meaning migrax.enabled true Apply migrations at startup migrax.migrate-at-startup true false: start without migrating, when a pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations; the health check and the pending gauge still report them (details) migrax.drift.check off warn or fail: compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when the application starts; the build must put .migrax/snapshot.json into the application (details) migrax.datasource default Data source to migrate migrax.locations db/migration Migration folders on the classpath, comma-separated migrax.java-package db.migration Package of JavaMigration classes migrax.env Environment: migrations marked -- migrax:env <name> run only there migrax.resume false Re-run a failed migration marked -- migrax:resume-safe migrax.lock-timeout 0 How long to wait while another instance migrates, for example 2m when several start together migrax.placeholders.<name> Values for ${name} placeholders migrax.metrics.enabled true Micrometer metrics of the migrations, when the application has a MeterRegistry (Metrics and tracing) migrax.tracing.enabled true OpenTelemetry spans of the migrations, when the application has an OpenTelemetry migrax.schemas Schemas to migrate one after another

docs.title: Health check
docs.text: With micronaut-management in the application, Migrax adds a migrax health indicator: UP when every migration is applied and none failed, was edited or is missing, DOWN otherwise, with the counts as details (/health).

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Migrax reads application.properties / application.yaml with the active profile:

quarkus.datasource.db-kind=postgresql
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
quarkus.datasource.username=shop
quarkus.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

QUARKUS_DATASOURCE_JDBC_URL and the other Quarkus environment variables work too.

Naming: Quarkus keeps Hibernate's default naming, so columns are named exactly like fields (createdAt). Migrax uses jpa naming, or the strategy in quarkus.hibernate-orm.physical-naming-strategy.

Tell Hibernate not to change the schema itself. validate checks it against your entities when the application starts; none leaves it alone:

quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=validate

Not update

With update, Hibernate changes tables itself when the application starts, outside your migrations, and the next migration can fail with "already exists". migrax doctor warns about it.

docs.title: Migrate at startup
docs.text:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-quarkus</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
</dependency>

migrax-quarkus is a Quarkus extension. When the application starts, it applies the migrations from db/migration before Hibernate starts, so strategy=validate checks the migrated schema. It works in JVM mode and in native executables.

Setting Default Meaning migrax.enabled true Apply migrations at startup migrax.migrate-at-startup true false: start without migrating, when a pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations; the health check and the pending gauge still report them (details) migrax.drift.check off warn or fail: compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when the application starts; the extension packages .migrax/snapshot.json itself (details) migrax.locations db/migration Migration folders on the classpath, comma-separated migrax.java-package db.migration Package of JavaMigration classes migrax.env Environment: migrations marked -- migrax:env <name> run only there migrax.resume false Re-run a failed migration marked -- migrax:resume-safe migrax.lock-timeout 0 How long to wait while another instance migrates, for example 2m when several start together migrax.placeholders.<name> Values for ${name} placeholders migrax.metrics.enabled true Micrometer metrics of the migrations, when the application has a MeterRegistry (Metrics and tracing) migrax.tracing.enabled true OpenTelemetry spans of the migrations, when the application has an OpenTelemetry migrax.schemas Schemas to migrate one after another

Native executables

Quarkus lists the migrations while it builds the application, because a native executable can't look through its own files. Set migrax.locations and migrax.java-package before the build: in a native executable, a different value at runtime finds no new migrations. Migrations outside your application, in a library jar, are found only when that jar has a Jandex index.

docs.title: Readiness check
docs.text:
With quarkus-smallrye-health in the application, Migrax adds a migrax readiness check: UP when every migration is applied and none failed, was edited or is missing, DOWN otherwise, with the counts as data (/q/health/ready).

Without the health extension there is no readiness check, and nothing to configure.

<build>

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Nothing to configure. Migrax reads the database settings from application.properties or application.yml, including the active profile:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL, SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME and SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD environment variables work too, and so does spring.datasource.hikari.jdbc-url.

Naming: Spring Boot converts names to snake_case (fullName → full_name) and names join tables <owner table>_<attribute>. Migrax uses the same rules (spring naming), or a custom naming strategy from spring.jpa.hibernate.naming.*.

Hibernate settings: anything under spring.jpa.properties.* is passed to Hibernate when Migrax reads the mapping.

Set Hibernate so it doesn't change the schema itself:

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

docs.title: Without JPA: Spring Data JDBC
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.17.0.

When your application uses Spring Data JDBC instead of JPA, Migrax reads Spring Data JDBC's own mapping: your aggregates (classes with @Table, and the types of your repositories), their child tables with the back-reference and key columns, embedded values and ids. Nothing to configure: migrax doctor shows Spring Data JDBC <version>, and generate, check, verify and drift work as for JPA entities. Remove schema.sql once Migrax writes the tables, or set spring.sql.init.mode=never, so Spring Boot doesn't create them a second time.

Details and what isn't read: Entity readers.

docs.title: Migrate at startup
docs.text:
Add the starter:

MavenGradle 
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
</dependency>

implementation("org.migrax:migrax-spring-boot-starter:0.17.1")

Migrations are applied when the application starts, before JPA starts, so ddl-auto=validate checks the migrated schema. JavaMigration beans are picked up. The starter works with Spring Boot 3 and 4 (on Spring Boot 4 from Migrax 0.17.0 on).

Setting Default Meaning migrax.enabled true Apply migrations at startup migrax.migrate-at-startup true false: start without migrating, when a pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations; the health check and the pending gauge still report them (details) migrax.drift.check off warn or fail: compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when the application starts; the build must put .migrax/snapshot.json into the application (details) migrax.locations classpath:db/migration Migration folders, comma-separated migrax.java-package db.migration Package of JavaMigration classes migrax.env Environment: migrations marked -- migrax:env <name> run only there migrax.resume false Re-run a failed migration marked -- migrax:resume-safe migrax.lock-timeout 0 How long to wait while another instance migrates, for example 2m when several start together migrax.placeholders.<name> Values for ${name} placeholders migrax.metrics.enabled true Micrometer metrics of the migrations, when the application has a MeterRegistry (Metrics and tracing) migrax.tracing.enabled true OpenTelemetry spans of the migrations, when the application has an OpenTelemetry migrax.schemas Schemas to migrate one after another

docs.title: Development mode
docs.text:
application-dev.properties
migrax.dev.generate=true

With migrax.dev.generate=true, the application generates a migration for changed entities on every restart, then applies it. Drops still need migrax.dev.allow-destructive=true. Use it only in development, and review what it wrote before you commit.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text:
With Spring Boot Actuator in the application, Migrax adds a migrax health component: UP when every migration is applied and none failed, was edited or is missing, DOWN otherwise, with the counts as details:

"migrax": {"status": "UP", "details": {"applied": 3, "pending": 0, "problems": 0}}

Turn it off with management.health.migrax.enabled=false.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Migrax is a command line tool. It needs Java 17 or newer; nothing else has to be installed, and no administrator rights are needed.

docs.title: With a package manager
docs.text:
The quickest way, if you use one of these:

Homebrew (macOS and Linux)Scoop (Windows) 
brew install fsmutimeer/migrax/migrax

Homebrew installs Java with it. When JAVA_HOME is set, Migrax uses that Java instead.

scoop bucket add migrax https://github.com/fsmutimeer/scoop-migrax
scoop install migrax

Migrax needs Java 17 or newer. If you don't have it, install one with Scoop too: scoop bucket add java, then scoop install java/temurin21-jdk.

Then check it with migrax version and continue with the Quick start. The package managers get every stable release on the day it is published.

Without a package manager, install Migrax from its ZIP in three steps:

docs.title: 1. Get Migrax
docs.text:
From a releaseFrom source
  1. Open the Download page and click Download migrax-<version>.zip.
  2. Extract it (on Windows: right-click the file, Extract All…). You get a folder migrax-<version> containing install.ps1, install.sh, bin and lib.

Download the .zip, not a .jar

The Download page also lists .jar files. Those are libraries for build tools and frameworks (the Maven plugin, the Gradle plugin, the startup integrations); they don't contain the command line tool or the installer. Only the ZIP does.

git clone https://github.com/fsmutimeer/migrax.git
cd migrax
mvn clean install

This also installs the Maven plugin and the libraries the integrations use into your local Maven repository.

docs.title: 2. Run the installer
docs.text:
Open a terminal in the extracted folder (or the source folder) and run the installer:

WindowsmacOS and Linux

In Command Prompt or PowerShell, for example with the folder extracted to D:\:

cd /d D:\migrax-0.17.1
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1

(In PowerShell, use cd D:\migrax-0.17.1.) The installer copies Migrax to %LOCALAPPDATA%\migrax and adds its bin folder to your user PATH. After that you can delete the extracted folder and the ZIP.

sh install.sh

Installs to ~/.local/share/migrax and links ~/.local/bin/migrax. Set MIGRAX_INSTALL_DIR and MIGRAX_BIN_DIR to choose other folders.

docs.title: 3. Check it
docs.text:
Close the terminal and open a new one, then:

$ migrax version
migrax 0.17.1

migrax is not recognized?

A terminal reads PATH once, when it starts, so a window that was open while the installer ran doesn't see the new entry: open a new terminal. Terminals inside an editor (VS Code, IntelliJ IDEA) copy the editor's PATH from when the editor started, so close every editor window and open it again.

To keep using the current window instead:

Command PromptPowerShell 
set "PATH=%PATH%;%LOCALAPPDATA%\migrax\bin"

$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine') + ';' + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User')

The D:\> prompt is Command Prompt; PS D:\> is PowerShell. Their commands differ.

docs.title: In a container
docs.text: To run migrations in Kubernetes or a CI job without installing anything, use the container image ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax (from Migrax 0.3.0); see Containers and Kubernetes.

docs.title: Which Java does Migrax use?
docs.text:
Migrax uses JAVA_HOME when it is set, otherwise the java on your PATH. To run it with a different Java for one terminal session, set JAVA_HOME there:

Windows (PowerShell)macOS and Linux 
$env:JAVA_HOME = "C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-25.0.4.101-hotspot"

export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk-25

Extra JVM options go in MIGRAX_JAVA_OPTS.

docs.title: Updating and uninstalling
docs.text:
With Homebrew: brew upgrade migrax and brew uninstall migrax. With Scoop: scoop update migrax and scoop uninstall migrax.

Otherwise, run the installer of the new version again to update. To uninstall, delete the install folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\migrax on Windows, ~/.local/share/migrax and the ~/.local/bin/migrax link on macOS and Linux) and remove its bin folder from your user PATH.

Next: Quick start.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This takes about five minutes. You need a service with JPA entities, a pom.xml or build.gradle, and a database it can reach.

Run everything from the service folder, the one with pom.xml or build.gradle.

docs.title: 1. Let Migrax look at your project
docs.text:
$ migrax init

init creates the migration folder and shows what Migrax detected: entity package, framework, naming, database and dialect. It changes nothing else and is safe to run again.

docs.title: 2. Check everything is ready
docs.text:
$ migrax doctor
  [ok]    Java 21.0.5
  [ok]    Build tool: maven
  [ok]    Entity package: com.example.shop
  [info]  Framework: Spring Boot
  [info]  Naming: spring (must match Hibernate; ...)
  [ok]    Project compiled and dependencies resolved
  [ok]    Hibernate 6.6.13.Final: entities are read from Hibernate's own mapping
  [ok]    Entities: 4 table(s) under com.example.shop (Hibernate 6.6.13.Final mapping)
  [ok]    Database URL: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ok]    Connected: PostgreSQL 16.4
All checks passed.

Anything that fails comes with the fix. Warnings explain settings worth changing, for example when Hibernate is allowed to create tables itself.

Let Migrax own the schema

If your configuration lets Hibernate create or update tables at startup (spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update, quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=update and similar), set it to none or validate. doctor shows the exact line to change.

docs.title: 3. Generate the first migration
docs.text:
$ migrax generate
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customers
  - create table orders
  ...
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

The first generate compares your entities with the current database:

  • an empty database gets 0001_initial.sql with every table;
  • a database that already has tables gets 0001_baseline.sql with the tables it has, recorded as applied there without running it, and a second migration with only the differences. An empty database (a new environment, or migrax verify) is built from both.

Open the file and read it. Migrations are plain SQL, and you can edit them before they run.

docs.title: 4. Apply it
docs.text:
$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.

$ migrax status
  [X] 0001_initial.sql   applied 2026-10-08 11:02:05
1 applied.

docs.title: 5. Commit
docs.text:
Commit these with your code:

  • the migration files and the rollback/ folder in src/main/resources/db/migration;
  • .migrax/snapshot.json and .migrax/history/.

Everything else in .migrax/ is a local cache, and Migrax tells git to ignore it.

docs.title: From now on
docs.text:
Every time you change an entity:

$ migrax generate     # writes 0002_..., with a rollback script, linted
$ migrax migrate

Next, learn how Migrax works, or set up your framework: Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut or Helidon.

docs.title: Java migrations
docs.text:
Some data changes are easier in Java than in SQL. Create one with:

$ migrax new backfill_full_names --java
src/main/java/db/migration/V0006__BackfillFullNames.java
package db.migration;

import org.migrax.api.JavaMigration;
import java.sql.Connection;

public class V0006__BackfillFullNames implements JavaMigration {
    @Override
    public void migrate(Connection connection) throws Exception {
        try (var statement = connection.createStatement()) {
            statement.executeUpdate(
                "UPDATE customer SET full_name = first_name || ' ' || last_name");
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void rollback(Connection connection) throws Exception {
        // optional; without it, 'migrax rollback' refuses to roll this migration back
    }
}
  • The class name gives the version and order, like a file name: V0006__BackfillFullNames runs after 0005_....sql.
  • Classes live in the db.migration package (change it with migrax.java-package).
  • The migration runs in the same transaction as its history record. Don't commit or close the connection.
  • Add org.migrax:migrax as a provided (Maven) or compileOnly (Gradle) dependency so the class compiles. With the Spring Boot starter, JavaMigration beans are picked up too.

docs.title: Moving data between columns
docs.text:
Migrax writes the changes to the structure. When values have to change shape, for example when full_name becomes first_name and last_name, only you know the rule. Write that step yourself, between two generated migrations.

1. Add the new columns and keep the old one. Add first_name and last_name to the entity as nullable fields, leave full_name in place, and generate:

$ migrax generate
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0002_add_customer_first_name_add_customer_last_name.sql:
  - add column customer.first_name
  - add column customer.last_name
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

2. Move the values. Create a Java migration and write the rule in Java:

$ migrax new split_full_name --java
Created src/main/java/db/migration/V0003__SplitFullName.java.
src/main/java/db/migration/V0003__SplitFullName.java
package db.migration;

import org.migrax.api.JavaMigration;
import java.sql.Connection;

public class V0003__SplitFullName implements JavaMigration {
    @Override
    public void migrate(Connection connection) throws Exception {
        try (var select = connection.prepareStatement(
                 "SELECT id, full_name FROM customer WHERE first_name IS NULL");
             var update = connection.prepareStatement(
                 "UPDATE customer SET first_name = ?, last_name = ? WHERE id = ?");
             var rows = select.executeQuery()) {
            while (rows.next()) {
                String name = rows.getString("full_name").trim();
                int space = name.lastIndexOf(' ');
                update.setString(1, space < 0 ? name : name.substring(0, space));
                update.setString(2, space < 0 ? "" : name.substring(space + 1));
                update.setLong(3, rows.getLong("id"));
                update.addBatch();
            }
            update.executeBatch();
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void rollback(Connection connection) throws Exception {
        try (var statement = connection.createStatement()) {
            statement.executeUpdate("UPDATE customer SET first_name = NULL, last_name = NULL");
        }
    }
}

A SQL migration (migrax new split_full_name) works too, with your database's string functions.

3. Remove the old column. Delete full_name from the entity, make the new fields required, and generate again:

$ migrax generate --allow-destructive
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0004_alter_customer_first_name_and_more.sql:
  - alter column customer.first_name
  - alter column customer.last_name
  - drop column customer.full_name
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
src/main/resources/db/migration/0004_alter_customer_first_name_and_more.sql, statement 3: warning MX007
  ALTER TABLE customer DROP COLUMN full_name
  This deletes data, and running application instances that still use it will fail.
  Fix: Deploy code that no longer uses it first, then drop it in a later release (expand/contract: 'migrax generate --zero-downtime' does this).
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

migrax migrate runs the three in order:

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0002_add_customer_first_name_add_customer_last_name.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_add_customer_first_name_add_customer_last_name.sql'.
Applying migration 'V0003__SplitFullName'...
Successfully applied migration 'V0003__SplitFullName'.
Applying migration '0004_alter_customer_first_name_and_more.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0004_alter_customer_first_name_and_more.sql'.
Applied 3 migration(s); 4 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.
  • The column is dropped last. If making first_name required fails because a row has no value, the migration stops with full_name still there.
  • During a rolling deployment the old version keeps writing full_name only. Release step 3 later, with a second copy of the Java migration (its WHERE first_name IS NULL only touches the rows that are left), or let zero-downtime changes split the release.
  • Rolling back step 3 brings full_name back empty. Generate it with --keep-data to restore its values: see Keeping dropped data.
  • With Migrax 0.17.1 and older, generate can give its file the number of a Java migration that has the highest number. If it does, rename the file and its rollback script to the next free number before you migrate.

docs.title: Repeatable migrations
docs.text:
Files named R__<name>.sql run after the versioned migrations, and again whenever their content changes. Use them for views, functions, stored procedures and grants:

R__active_customers_view.sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW active_customers AS
SELECT id, email FROM customers WHERE active = true;

docs.title: Callbacks
docs.text:
SQL files with these names run around migrations:

File Runs beforeMigrate.sql once, before any migration beforeEachMigrate.sql before each migration afterEachMigrate.sql after each migration afterMigrate.sql once, after all migrations

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
${name} in a migration is replaced at run time:

GRANT SELECT ON customers TO ${reporting_role};

Set values in application config (migrax.placeholders.reporting_role=analyst), as a system property (-Dmigrax.placeholders.reporting_role=analyst) or an environment variable (MIGRAX_PLACEHOLDERS_REPORTING_ROLE=analyst).

${migrax.schema} is built in: it is the schema the migration runs in. With several schemas it changes from one schema to the next.

docs.title: Directives
docs.text:
Directives are comment lines in a migration:

Directive Effect -- migrax:no-transaction Run without a transaction, for statements like CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY -- migrax:resume-safe Allow migrate --resume to re-run it after a failure -- migrax:lint-ignore MX001 Silence a lint rule for the next statement -- migrax:no-split Send the whole file to the database as one statement -- migrax:require table-exists customer Run only when the condition holds; see Preconditions

docs.title: Procedures, functions and triggers
docs.text:
Write procedures, functions, triggers, Oracle packages and anonymous blocks (BEGIN ... END;, DECLARE ... BEGIN ... END;) as you would anywhere else. Migrax runs a migration statement by statement, and it knows that a semicolon inside a body doesn't end the statement: the body ends with the END that closes its first BEGIN. A package ends with its own last END.

CREATE TABLE note_log (id INT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(100));

CREATE PROCEDURE add_note(IN p_note VARCHAR(100))
BEGIN
  DECLARE next_id INT;
  SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 INTO next_id FROM note_log;
  INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) VALUES (next_id, p_note);
END;

On SQL Server, a procedure written without BEGIN and END runs to the end of the file, as it does in SQL Server's own tools. migrax lint warns (MX016) when a body seems to take in the statements after it.

You can also mark where a body ends the way your database's own tools do. Scripts copied from those tools work unchanged:

SQL ServerMySQL and MariaDBOraclePostgreSQLSQLite

A line with only GO ends a batch. Each batch is sent whole. GO 5 runs the batch five times.

CREATE TABLE note_log (id INT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(100));
GO
CREATE PROCEDURE add_note @note VARCHAR(100) AS
BEGIN
  SET NOCOUNT ON;
  INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1, @note FROM note_log;
END;
GO

DELIMITER changes what ends a statement, until the next DELIMITER line.

CREATE TABLE note_log (id INT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(100));
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE add_note(IN p_note VARCHAR(100))
BEGIN
  DECLARE next_id INT;
  SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 INTO next_id FROM note_log;
  INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) VALUES (next_id, p_note);
END$$
DELIMITER ;

A line with only / ends a PL/SQL block: CREATE PROCEDURE, FUNCTION, PACKAGE, TRIGGER, TYPE, or an anonymous BEGIN or DECLARE block. Other statements still end at their semicolon.

CREATE TABLE note_log (id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR2(100));
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE add_note(p_note IN VARCHAR2) AS
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT NVL(MAX(id), 0) + 1, p_note FROM note_log;
END;
/

Function bodies in dollar quotes ($$ ... $$) need nothing extra.

CREATE FUNCTION add_note(p_note VARCHAR) RETURNS void AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1, p_note FROM note_log;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

End a trigger with a line holding only /, as for Oracle.

CREATE TRIGGER add_note AFTER INSERT ON note_source
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO note_log (id, note) SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1, NEW.note FROM note_log;
END;
/

Anything else can go in a file of its own with -- migrax:no-split: Migrax then sends the whole file as one statement. lint and verify split files the same way.

docs.title: Several migration folders
docs.text:
Migrations can come from more than one folder, for example shared migrations from a library module next to the application's own, or test data that only some environments load:

migrax.locations=classpath:db/migration,filesystem:db/dev-data

(or --locations and MIGRAX_LOCATIONS with the same value). Migrax reads every folder and runs the files in version order across all of them. File names must be unique across the folders: two folders with the same file name is an error. A rollback script lives in the rollback folder next to its migration.

new, generate, squash, merge and import write to the first folder; new files are numbered after the highest number in any folder.

docs.title: Migrations for some environments only
docs.text:
Test data, demo accounts or development helpers can live in migrations that run only in some environments. Mark them with an env line:

0002_demo_customers.sql
-- migrax:env dev, test
INSERT INTO customer (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Demo customer');

and name the environment where Migrax runs: --env dev, MIGRAX_ENV=dev, or migrax.env=dev in the application configuration (also for the startup integrations). Migrations without an env line run everywhere. A marked migration runs only where its environment is set, and elsewhere status shows it as skipped:

$ migrax status
Migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [X] 0001_create_customer.sql  applied 2026-10-12 13:53:55
  [-] 0002_demo_customers.sql   only for dev, test
1 applied, 1 skipped.

$ migrax migrate --env dev
Applying migration '0002_demo_customers.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_demo_customers.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 2 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.

Skipped migrations are not pending: health checks stay up. A folder per environment (several migration folders) works too.

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.13.0.

A migration can check the database before it runs. Add require lines anywhere in the file:

0002_add_email.sql
-- migrax:require table-exists customer
-- migrax:require column-missing customer.email
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(200);
Check Holds when table-exists <table> the table exists (table or schema.table) table-missing <table> the table does not exist column-exists <table>.<column> the column exists column-missing <table>.<column> the column does not exist sql <query> the query returns a row whose first value is not NULL, false or 0

Names are found whatever case the database stores them in. A query may use ${placeholders}.

When a condition does not hold, migrate stops before that migration, runs nothing of it and fails with MXE114. Fix the database and run migrate again:

$ migrax migrate
error[MXE114]: Migration '0004_email_required.sql' requires sql select count(*) = 0 from customer where email is null, which is not met here. Nothing of it ran. Fix the database, or add 'else skip' to the line to record the migration without running it.
Run again with --verbose for details.

End the line with else skip when the migration is not needed where the condition does not hold. Migrax then records the migration as applied without running it, and doesn't check it again:

0003_move_legacy_customers.sql
-- migrax:require table-exists legacy_customer else skip
INSERT INTO customer (id, name) SELECT id, name FROM legacy_customer;
DROP TABLE legacy_customer;

status and migrate --dry-run show the conditions of pending migrations:

$ migrax status
Migrations in db/migrations for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ ] 0001_create_customer.sql        pending
  [ ] 0002_add_email.sql              pending: requires table-exists customer; requires column-missing customer.email
  [ ] 0003_move_legacy_customers.sql  pending: requires table-exists legacy_customer, else skipped
3 pending.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_create_customer.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_create_customer.sql'.
Applying migration '0002_add_email.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_add_email.sql'.
Skipped migration '0003_move_legacy_customers.sql': table-exists legacy_customer is not met; recorded as applied without running it.
Applied 2 migration(s); 3 total in db/migrations.

Each condition is checked right before its migration, so it sees what the migrations before it did. migrate --sql can only check the database as it is now: it checks the conditions of the first pending migration and stops before a later migration that has conditions. Run the script, then write the next one with migrate --sql.

docs.title: Several schemas (multi-tenant)
docs.text:
Run the same migrations once per schema:

$ migrax migrate --schemas tenant_a,tenant_b,tenant_c

Or set migrax.schemas=tenant_a,tenant_b in application config. status, rollback, migrate --sql and clean accept the same option, and the startup integrations read migrax.schemas. Each schema keeps its own migrax_history, so a schema added later gets every migration on the next run.

Create the schemas before the first run; Migrax creates the tables in them, not the schemas.

docs.title: SQL Server
docs.text:
SQL Server can't switch a connection to another schema: a table name without a schema always means the login's default schema, usually dbo. So in a project that sets migrax.schemas, generate puts ${migrax.schema}. in front of every table, and Migrax fills in each schema when it runs the migration:

CREATE TABLE ${migrax.schema}.book (id bigint NOT NULL, title varchar(255), ...);
CREATE INDEX ix_book_title ON ${migrax.schema}.book (title);

Write your own migrations the same way. migrax lint warns about a table without its schema (MX017), because that statement would change the table in the default schema, once for every tenant. Migrax's own history tables are named the same way ([tenant_a].migrax_history).

docs.title: Using Migrax with AI assistants
docs.text: AI coding assistants can use Migrax directly: they read what changed, preview the SQL with its risks, and explain it to you, while you stay the one who changes the database.

docs.title: The MCP server
docs.text:
migrax mcp is a Model Context Protocol server. Assistants that support MCP, such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Cursor, start it and call Migrax's commands as tools, getting their JSON results.

Tool What it does status Which migrations are applied, pending, failed or changed check Whether entities changed without a migration plan The SQL generate would write, with lint findings and table sizes lint Locking and risky statements in migrations drift Manual changes in the database environments Every environment's applied and pending migrations and drift doctor Setup problems and how to fix them verify Migrations applied to a throwaway database and validated (slow) show_migration One migration file's SQL, or its rollback script generate Writes a migration; only with migrax mcp --allow-generate

The server never changes a database: migrate, rollback, repair and clean are not offered, so an assistant can't apply or undo migrations on its own. With --allow-generate it can write migration files, which you review in version control before running migrax migrate yourself.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Run this in your service folder:

$ claude mcp add migrax -- migrax mcp

On Windows, migrax is a .cmd script, so start it through cmd:

> claude mcp add migrax -- cmd /c migrax mcp

To share it with your team, add --scope project: Claude Code then writes the setting to .mcp.json in the project, which you commit. To let the assistant write migrations, end the command with migrax mcp --allow-generate.

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
Run this in your service folder:

$ codex mcp add migrax -- migrax mcp

Codex writes the server to ~/.codex/config.toml, so it is available in every folder you start Codex in. To set it up for one project only, put the same lines in .codex/config.toml in the project (Codex reads it in projects you trust):

[mcp_servers.migrax]
command = "migrax"
args = ["mcp"]

Codex finds migrax.cmd on Windows by itself, so the command is the same there.

docs.title: Gemini CLI
docs.text:
Run this in your service folder:

$ gemini mcp add migrax migrax mcp

Gemini writes the server to .gemini/settings.json in the project; add --scope user to use it in every folder. gemini mcp list shows whether it connects. Gemini starts MCP servers only in folders you trust, so trust the folder when it asks. Like Codex, it finds migrax.cmd on Windows by itself.

docs.title: GitHub Copilot in VS Code
docs.text:
Create .vscode/mcp.json in your project:

{
  "servers": {
    "migrax": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "migrax",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

VS Code starts the server in the workspace folder. Note that the top-level key is servers here, not mcpServers as in the other clients.

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
Create .cursor/mcp.json in your project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json to use Migrax in every project:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "migrax": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "migrax",
      "args": ["mcp", "--dir", "${workspaceFolder}"]
    }
  }
}

${workspaceFolder} is the folder you opened in Cursor, so the server always reads that service.

docs.title: Other MCP clients
docs.text:
Most other clients (Claude Desktop, Windsurf, Cline, ...) read the same JSON as Cursor:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "migrax": {
      "command": "migrax",
      "args": ["mcp", "--dir", "/path/to/service"]
    }
  }
}

The server runs in the folder the client starts it in; --dir points it at your service instead. It uses the same database settings as the command line (application config, MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL, ...).

docs.title: Windows: start Migrax through cmd
docs.text:
On Windows, migrax is a .cmd script. Some clients start programs directly and can't run scripts, so they report that migrax was not found even though it works in a terminal. In JSON files, start it through cmd instead:

"command": "cmd",
"args": ["/c", "migrax", "mcp"]

This works in every client. Codex CLI and Gemini CLI don't need it.

docs.title: ChatGPT
docs.text: The ChatGPT app connects only to MCP servers on the internet, and migrax mcp runs on your own machine next to your code and database. To use Migrax with OpenAI's models, use Codex CLI (above).

docs.title: Instructions for your project's assistant
docs.text:
Assistants follow the instructions in files such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md. This block tells them how to work with Migrax; copy it into yours:

## Database migrations (Migrax)

- The schema is managed by Migrax. Never change the database by hand or with Hibernate's
  schema generation (`ddl-auto`, `schema-management.strategy`): change the entities, then run
  `migrax plan` to preview and `migrax generate` to write the migration.
- Read the plan's lint findings before generating. Explain locking statements, NOT NULL
  columns on existing tables and anything marked [DESTRUCTIVE].
- A renamed field or table must be passed as a rename (`--rename table.old=new`,
  `--rename-table old=new`); otherwise its data is dropped. Ask when unsure.
- Never edit a migration that is already applied anywhere; write a new one.
- Do not run `migrax migrate`, `rollback`, `repair` or `clean` against shared or production
  databases. Tell the person what to run.
- Use `--json` for machine-readable output; errors have stable codes (MXE...).

docs.title: Documentation for assistants
docs.text:
The documentation is also published as plain text for AI assistants:

  • llms.txt: an index of every page, with a one-line summary each;
  • llms-full.txt: every page in one file.

Point an assistant at llms-full.txt when it needs to answer questions about Migrax.

docs.title: Changing entities
docs.text:
The everyday loop is short:

$ migrax generate
$ migrax migrate

This page covers the cases where Migrax needs a decision from you.

docs.title: Preview first
docs.text:
$ migrax plan
2 change(s) for postgresql:
  1. add column orders.notes
     ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN notes varchar(500);
  2. alter column tags.label
     ALTER TABLE tags ALTER COLUMN label TYPE varchar(100);

plan --impact adds how many rows each affected table has, read from the database, so you can spot changes that will take long on large tables.

docs.title: Renamed a field or entity?
docs.text:
To a database, a rename looks like "one column disappeared, another appeared". Dropping and re-adding would lose the data, so Migrax looks for likely renames:

  • the same name in another style, like created_at and createdAt, even when the type changed too;
  • otherwise a new column of the same type in the same table.

In a terminal it asks:

$ migrax generate
Did you rename customers.email to customers.contact_email? [y/N] y
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0004_rename_customers_email.sql:
  - rename column customers.email to contact_email

In scripts and CI, where nothing can be asked, pass the answer:

$ migrax generate --rename customers.email=contact_email
$ migrax generate --rename-table client=customer

Several column renames are separated by commas. A rename with a type change becomes a RENAME followed by an ALTER. Hibernate's foreign key names contain the table name, so a table rename also renames the table's foreign keys. From Migrax 0.17.1 on, that needs no --allow-destructive: on PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB and H2 the migration renames each key (RENAME CONSTRAINT); other databases drop it and add it again under its new name, which checks every row.

Non-interactive runs

When input isn't a terminal, Migrax prints each possible rename with the exact --rename option to use, and does not assume a rename.

docs.title: Check constraints and comments
docs.text:
generate writes the check constraints and comments your entities declare:

@Entity
@Comment("Things we sell")
@Check(name = "ck_product_price", constraints = "price >= 0")
public class Product {
  @Comment("Price in cents")
  @Check(constraints = "discount between 0 and 100")
  private int discount;
  ...
}

Migrax reads Hibernate's @Check, @Checks and @Comment (org.hibernate.annotations), and the check and comment attributes of Jakarta Persistence 3.2's @Table and @Column. A new table gets its checks inside CREATE TABLE; an existing one gets ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...).

Your condition goes into the migration exactly as you wrote it, so write it in your database's SQL. migrax verify runs the migration on a throwaway copy of that database, so a condition the database doesn't understand shows up there, before release. MySQL enforces checks from 8.0.16 on; migrax doctor warns on older servers.

A check without a name gets one from its table and condition, such as ck_product_3f2a9c1e. When you change the condition, the name changes too: the migration drops the old constraint and adds the new one. If the database already has the check under a name it chose itself (Hibernate creates unnamed checks that way), Migrax recognizes it by its condition and keeps that name. Adding a check fails when existing rows break it; fix those rows in the same migration, before the check is added.

Comments are written the way each database stores them: COMMENT ON (PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, Oracle, H2), part of the table or column definition (MySQL, MariaDB), or the MS_Description property (SQL Server). SQLite keeps no comments, so they are left out there.

With --safe on PostgreSQL and CockroachDB, a check added to an existing table goes into the second migration as NOT VALID followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, so writes keep flowing.

docs.title: Enum columns
docs.text:
Hibernate 6 and newer also writes a check for every enum column, such as status between 0 and 2, or status in ('ACTIVE','BLOCKED') for @Enumerated(STRING). Migrax leaves these out by default: with them, every new enum value needs a migration before the application can store it, and a forgotten one only shows up as failing inserts. To generate them, set migrax.enum-checks=true (or MIGRAX_ENUM_CHECKS=true).

Upgrading from Migrax 0.4

Earlier versions ignored @Check and @Comment. The first generate after upgrading writes the ones your entities already have. If you added them before with a hand-written migration, edit the generated file and remove those statements before it runs.

docs.title: Drops and narrowing changes
docs.text:
Dropping a table or column, or making a column smaller, deletes data. Migrax refuses until you confirm with --allow-destructive:

$ migrax generate
3 change(s) for mysql:
  ...
  3. drop column test_table.number_of_items  [DESTRUCTIVE]
     ALTER TABLE test_table DROP COLUMN number_of_items;
error[MXE108]: 1 destructive change(s) detected (marked [DESTRUCTIVE] above).
Review them, then run 'migrax generate --allow-destructive'. If a column or table
was renamed, pass --rename table.old=new or --rename-table old=new instead.

For a running production system, drop in two releases (expand and contract): first deploy code that no longer uses the column, then drop it in a later release.

docs.title: Naming the migration
docs.text:
The name is generated from the first changes, for example 0005_add_orders_notes_and_more.sql. Choose your own with --name; the next number is added for you:

$ migrax generate --name split_customer_name
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0005_split_customer_name.sql

docs.title: Editing generated SQL
docs.text: Generated migrations are yours: edit them before they run anywhere, for example to backfill data in the same release. Never edit a migration after it has been applied: Migrax keeps a checksum of every applied file and stops when one changes. Write a new migration instead.

docs.title: Hand-written migrations
docs.text:
$ migrax new backfill_full_names
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0006_backfill_full_names.sql

new creates the next numbered file and an empty rollback script, for changes Migrax can't derive from entities: data migrations, views, grants, partitions. --java creates a Java class instead; see Advanced migrations.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Three commands make a good CI gate:

Command Fails when Exit code migrax check an entity changed without a migration, or two migrations share a number 2 / 1 migrax lint --strict a pending migration would lock tables, fail on data, or break running instances 1 migrax verify the migrations don't produce a schema Hibernate accepts, or a rollback script fails 1

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The Migrax repository is itself a GitHub Action. It runs check, lints new migrations, posts the planned SQL as a pull request comment and uploads the HTML report as the artifact migrax-report:

.github/workflows/migrations.yml
name: Migrations
on: pull_request

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # for the comment

jobs:
  migrax:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: fsmutimeer/migrax@v0.17.1
        with:
          working-directory: .          # folder with pom.xml or build.gradle
          fail-on-lint-warnings: 'false'
Input Default Meaning working-directory . Service folder java-version 21 Java used to build Migrax and your service fail-on-lint-warnings false Fail on lint warnings, not only errors comment true Post or update a pull request comment with the results report true Write the HTML report and upload it; the comment links to it github-token ${{ github.token }} Token used to comment

Outputs: changes (entity changes without a migration) and findings (lint findings in changed migrations).

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.14.0.

Include the Migrax job in .gitlab-ci.yml. It runs in merge request pipelines and does what the GitHub Action does: check, lint of the migrations the merge request adds or changes, the HTML report (shown as Migrax report on the merge request), and a comment with the results.

.gitlab-ci.yml
include:
  - remote: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fsmutimeer/migrax/v0.17.1/ci/gitlab/migrax.gitlab-ci.yml

To change a setting, add a migrax job of your own with only the keys to replace:

.gitlab-ci.yml
migrax:
  image: gradle:8-jdk21          # the default is maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21
  variables:
    MIGRAX_DIR: services/orders  # folder with pom.xml or build.gradle

For the comment, Migrax needs a token:

  1. In the project, open Settings > Access tokens and add a token with the role Reporter and the scope api.
  2. In Settings > CI/CD > Variables, add the variable MIGRAX_COMMENT_TOKEN with that token, with Mask variable on.

Without the token the job still runs and fails on problems; only the comment is left out. Each pipeline updates the same comment instead of adding a new one.

docs.title: Bitbucket Pipelines
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.14.0.

Copy this step into bitbucket-pipelines.yml. It runs for pull requests and does the same as the GitLab job; the report is in the pipeline's Artifacts tab, where Bitbucket keeps it for 14 days.

bitbucket-pipelines.yml
image: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21   # gradle:8-jdk21 for Gradle projects

pipelines:
  pull-requests:
    '**':
      - step:
          name: Migrax
          caches:
            - maven
          script:
            - export MIGRAX_VERSION=0.17.1
            - export MIGRAX_DIR=.       # folder with pom.xml or build.gradle
            - curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o /tmp/migrax-ci.sh "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fsmutimeer/migrax/v${MIGRAX_VERSION}/ci/migrax-ci.sh"
            - sh /tmp/migrax-ci.sh
          artifacts:
            - migrax-ci/migrax-report.html

For the comment:

  1. In the repository, open Repository settings > Access tokens and create a token with the permission Pull requests: Write.
