  2. In Repository settings > Repository variables, add MIGRAX_COMMENT_TOKEN with that token, with Secured on.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Both templates run the same script, ci/migrax-ci.sh in the Migrax repository. It needs Java 17 or newer, curl, git and your build tool, so any Maven or Gradle image works. The Migrax container image has no build tool, so check can't compile the entities there.

Variable Default Meaning MIGRAX_VERSION the template's version Migrax version to download MIGRAX_DIR . Service folder MIGRAX_REPORT true Write the HTML report MIGRAX_FAIL_ON_LINT_WARNINGS false Fail on lint warnings, not only errors MIGRAX_COMMENT_TOKEN none Token for the comment; without it, no comment

The usual MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL, MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER and MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD work too: with a database, the report also shows which migrations are applied, and the drift.

docs.title: An HTML report
docs.text:
migrax report writes one page for reviewers: the schema with a diagram of the tables, entity changes that have no migration yet, every migration with its status and lint findings, and drift between the database and the snapshot.

$ migrax report --html target/migrax-report.html
Wrote target/migrax-report.html: 8 table(s), 4 migration(s), 1 pending, 3 lint finding(s), no drift.

The page is a single file that works offline; only the diagram needs the internet (it loads Mermaid from a CDN, and shows its text without it). Without a database connection, the report still has the schema, the migrations and the lint findings, and says that their status and drift were not checked.

In other CI systems, keep the file as a build artifact. In GitHub Actions without the Migrax action:

      - run: migrax report --html migrax-report.html
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: migrax-report
          path: migrax-report.html

With Maven: mvn migrax:report -Dmigrax.html=target/migrax-report.html.

docs.title: Any CI system
docs.text:
migrax check --no-input
migrax lint --strict
migrax verify          # H2, HSQLDB or Derby in memory, or Docker for other engines
migrax report --html migrax-report.html   # keep it as a build artifact

verify starts a throwaway database: in memory for H2, HSQLDB and Derby projects, or a container of your engine when Docker is available. The container runs your server's version when Migrax can reach the configured database (since Migrax 0.17.2), or else its default image; --image picks another. Without Docker, point it at an empty scratch database:

migrax verify --url jdbc:postgresql://ci-db:5432/scratch

The database user and password come from the same place as usual (environment variables or application configuration) unless you pass --user / --password.

docs.title: Machine-readable output
docs.text:
migrate, rollback, status, plan, check, lint, drift, verify, diff, doctor, baseline, repair, clean, new, merge, squash, backups and environments accept --json. Progress messages go to standard error, so standard output stays valid JSON:

$ migrax check --json    # one line, wrapped here
{"ok":false,"changes":["add column orders.notes"],"operations":[{"kind":"add_column",
"summary":"add column orders.notes","table":"orders","column":"notes",
"entity":"com.example.Order"}],"conflicts":[]}

docs.title: Comparing databases
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.14.0.

migrax diff compares the schemas of two databases of the same kind, such as staging and production, and lists what would make one match the other. Use it when a hotfix was applied by hand in one place, before a release to check that production is where staging was, or to find out why two tenants' databases behave differently.

drift compares one database with what the migrations produce. diff compares two live databases with each other, without looking at migrations or entities. To see which migrations each environment has, use migrax environments.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The source is the database whose schema you want; the target is the project's database (the one Migrax normally connects to, or --url):

$ migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop --url jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop
To make jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop match jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop:
7 change(s) for postgresql:
  1. alter column customer.name
     ALTER TABLE customer ALTER COLUMN name TYPE varchar(100);
  2. add column customer.email
     ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN email varchar(200);
  3. drop column customer.legacy_code  [DESTRUCTIVE]
     ALTER TABLE customer DROP COLUMN legacy_code;
  4. comment on customer
     COMMENT ON TABLE customer IS 'People who buy';
  5. add index idx_customer_email on customer
     CREATE INDEX idx_customer_email ON customer (email);
  6. add check orders_total_check on orders
     ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_total_check CHECK (((total >= (0)::numeric)));
  7. add foreign key orders_customer_id_fkey on orders
     ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);
To keep them, save the SQL as a migration: migrax diff <source-url> --sql

When nothing differs, it says so and exits with 0:

$ migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop --url jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop
Same schema: jdbc:postgresql://prod:5432/shop matches jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop.

Tables, columns and their types, nullability, primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, indexes, checks, comments and sequences are compared. Migrax's own tables (migrax_history and the others) are left out.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
The target uses the usual settings: the application configuration, MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL, MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER, MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD, or --url, --user and --password-file. The source has its own:

export MIGRAX_SOURCE_USER=readonly
export MIGRAX_SOURCE_PASSWORD=...        # or MIGRAX_SOURCE_PASSWORD_FILE / --source-password-file
migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop

diff only reads. A read-only user is enough on both sides. Passwords inside URLs are shown as ***.

docs.title: Turn the differences into a migration
docs.text:
--sql prints only the SQL, ready to review. To keep the changes, save it as a migration with the next free number, so every environment gets them:

migrax diff jdbc:postgresql://staging:5432/shop --sql \
  > src/main/resources/db/migration/0012_align_with_staging.sql

Read it before you commit: a column that exists only in the target is dropped, with its data. If that column was added by hand on purpose, write a migration for it instead, so the source gets it too.

docs.title: In scripts and CI
docs.text:
The exit code is 2 when the databases differ, 0 when they match. --json lists each change with its kind, a summary, its SQL, and whether it is destructive:

migrax diff "$STAGING_URL" --json | jq '.changes[] | .summary'

docs.title: All environments at a glance
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.17.0.

migrax environments asks every environment's database which migrations it has applied, so you see before a release whether staging is ahead of production, or whether someone changed a database by hand. It only reads.

Give each environment a URL in the application config:

application.properties
migrax.environments=dev,staging,production
migrax.environments.dev.url=jdbc:postgresql://dev-db:5432/shop
migrax.environments.staging.url=jdbc:postgresql://staging-db:5432/shop
migrax.environments.production.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db:5432/shop

The first line sets the order of the rows; without it they are sorted by name. Users and passwords belong in the environment, not in the file:

export MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_PRODUCTION_USER=readonly
export MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_PRODUCTION_PASSWORD=...   # or ..._PASSWORD_FILE

Every setting also works as a variable alone (MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_STAGING_URL), which is handy in CI. A read-only user is enough.

$ migrax environments
Environments for db/migrations (2 migration(s)):

  Environment  Applied  Pending  Last applied                                                 Drift
  dev          2        0        0002_add_customer_phone_create_orders.sql, 2026-10-21 20:58  none
  staging      2        0        0002_add_customer_phone_create_orders.sql, 2026-10-21 20:58  1 difference(s)
  production   1        1        0001_initial.sql, 2026-10-21 20:58                           not checked (pending)

staging: drift: customer.note: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
production: pending 0002_add_customer_phone_create_orders.sql

Here production is one migration behind, which migrax migrate there fixes, and someone added a column to staging by hand. The migrations are the ones in your current checkout: run it from the branch you are about to release.

  • Pending counts the migrations that would run there. A migration marked -- migrax:env dev counts only in dev. When an environment's name differs from the one in those lines, set migrax.environments.<name>.env.
  • Drift compares the schema with the snapshot, as migrax drift does. It is checked only where nothing is pending, because pending migrations change the schema on purpose. --no-drift skips it.
  • A database that can't be reached gets can't connect and the reason in its row; the others are still shown. All of them are asked at the same time, and each one has --timeout (30 seconds) to answer.
  • Migrations an environment has applied that are not in your checkout are listed with [!], as in migrax status: a newer branch was deployed there, or a file was deleted.

The exit code is 0 when every environment answered (pending migrations are fine), 1 when one can't be reached or a migration failed, changed or is missing there, and 2 when drift was found. --json gives the same per environment, for a dashboard or a release script:

migrax environments --json | jq '.environments[] | {name, pending}'

With several databases, each one has its own environments: migrax.databases.billing.environments.staging.url, shown with migrax environments --database billing.

docs.title: Containers and Kubernetes
docs.text:
In container platforms, migrations usually run as their own step before the new version of the application starts: a Kubernetes Job, an init container, or a deploy hook. Migrax has an official container image for this, and it runs with just the migration files; no Java project or build is needed.

Available from Migrax 0.3.0

The image is published with Migrax 0.3.0 and newer.

docs.title: The container image
docs.text:
ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1

It has Java, Migrax and these JDBC drivers: PostgreSQL (also for CockroachDB and YugabyteDB), MariaDB (also for MySQL servers), SQL Server, SQLite and H2. It runs as a non-root user, for amd64 and arm64. Migrations are read from /migrations.

$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD/src/main/resources/db/migration:/migrations:ro" \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db-password \
    -v "$PWD/db-password:/run/secrets/db-password:ro" \
    ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1 migrate
Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 1 total in /migrations.

migrate, status, rollback, repair, clean, lint, drift and doctor work in the image; doctor checks the migrations and the database connection there. generate, check and verify read your entities, so in a Java project they run where it is built (your machine or CI), not in the image. A project with a schema file can run them in the image too: mount the project at /workspace and give Migrax an empty database of its own with MIGRAX_SCRATCH_URL, because inside a container it can't start the throwaway database itself:

$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/workspace" -w /workspace \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret \
    -e MIGRAX_LOCATIONS=filesystem:db/migrations -e MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE=db/schema.sql \
    -e MIGRAX_SCRATCH_URL=jdbc:postgresql://scratch:5432/scratch \
    ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1 generate
Read db/schema.sql: 1 table(s).
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customer
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

The scratch database connects with the same user and password as your database. verify also builds the migrations on an empty database, which it can't start either: pass a second empty one with --url, for example verify --url jdbc:postgresql://verify:5432/verify.

docs.title: Your migrations in an image
docs.text:
Usually the migrations are baked into an image built with each version of the application:

FROM ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1
COPY src/main/resources/db/migration/ /migrations/
# The snapshot lets 'migrax drift' compare the database with what the migrations produce.
COPY .migrax/snapshot.json /workspace/.migrax/snapshot.json

docs.title: Other drivers
docs.text:
MySQL Connector/J (also for TiDB) and Oracle's driver aren't included, because their licenses differ from Migrax's. Add them in your image:

FROM ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1
ADD --chmod=644 https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/mysql/mysql-connector-j/9.1.0/mysql-connector-j-9.1.0.jar /opt/migrax/drivers/

Every jar in /opt/migrax/drivers (or in the folder MIGRAX_DRIVERS names) is available to Migrax. Outside the image the same works with --classpath <driver.jar> or a drivers folder next to Migrax's lib folder.

docs.title: Database logins in containers
docs.text:
Kubernetes and Docker mount secrets as files. Point Migrax at them:

Variable Contains MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL or MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL_FILE the JDBC URL MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER or MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER_FILE the user MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD or MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE the password

A *_FILE variable names a file; its content is used without the last line break. When both forms are set, the plain variable wins. --password-file <path> does the same on the command line.

docs.title: Logins with cloud identities
docs.text:
Cloud databases can accept short-lived tokens instead of passwords (AWS RDS with IAM, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database with Microsoft Entra ID). That works through the provider's JDBC plugin: put its jar in the drivers folder (or a derived image) and use the URL form its documentation gives. Migrax passes the URL and user through unchanged.

Not tested by the Migrax build

The Migrax build has no cloud accounts, so these logins are not tested by it. Check them in a test environment with migrax doctor before you rely on them.

docs.title: Running in Kubernetes
docs.text:
The manifests below are in the repository under examples/kubernetes. Each was run on a local Kubernetes cluster (kind) against PostgreSQL.

They read the database login from a Secret named shop-db with the keys url, user and password (examples/kubernetes/secret.yaml).

docs.title: A Job before the rollout (recommended)
docs.text:
Run the Job, wait for it, then roll out the application. A failed migration stops the deployment and needs a person: backoffLimit: 0 keeps Kubernetes from retrying it.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: shop-migrate
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: registry.example.com/shop-migrations:1.0
          args: ["migrate", "--lock-timeout", "2m"]
          env:
            - name: MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: shop-db, key: url}}
            - name: MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER
              valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: shop-db, key: user}}
            - name: MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE
              value: /run/secrets/shop-db/password
          volumeMounts:
            - {name: db-secret, mountPath: /run/secrets/shop-db, readOnly: true}
      volumes:
        - name: db-secret
          secret:
            secretName: shop-db
            items: [{key: password, path: password}]

$ kubectl apply -f job.yaml
$ kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/shop-migrate --timeout=5m

docs.title: With Helm or Argo CD
docs.text:
The same Job runs as a hook before each release. For Helm, add to its metadata:

  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation

For Argo CD, the annotation is argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync.

docs.title: An init container in each pod
docs.text:
Simpler to set up: every pod migrates before the application starts. Pods that start together wait for each other with --lock-timeout; the first one applies the migrations and the others find nothing to do. From the test with three replicas:

== pod/shop-7bf9684b9c-sxnq9
Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 1 total in /migrations.
== pod/shop-7bf9684b9c-5n79b
Another Migrax process holds the migration lock; waiting up to 5m...
Nothing to migrate: all 1 migration(s) are applied.

The manifest is examples/kubernetes/init-container.yaml. Give the lock timeout more time than your longest migration takes. Without --lock-timeout, the second pod fails at once with "Another Migrax process is applying migrations" and Kubernetes restarts it.

docs.title: Detecting manual changes every night
docs.text:
migrax drift exits with code 2 when the database differs from what the migrations produce, so a CronJob fails and your cluster's alerting for failed jobs tells you (examples/kubernetes/drift-cronjob.yaml):

1 difference(s) between the database and the snapshot:
  - customers.hotfix: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
Someone changed the database outside migrations. Write a migration for intended changes ('migrax new <name>'), or revert them.

docs.title: Watching the migration job
docs.text:
The metrics and traces come from the startup integrations; the image doesn't send any. A migration that runs as a Job is watched through what it leaves behind:

  • The exit code. A failed migration ends the container with exit code 1, so the Job fails and your cluster's alerting for failed Jobs tells you, as for the drift check above. In a deploy pipeline, the failed step stops the rollout.

  • One line of JSON in the logs. With --json, migrate prints its result as a single JSON line on standard output (progress messages go to standard error):

    args: ["migrate", "--json", "--lock-timeout", "2m"]

    {"ok":true,"exitCode":0,"schemas":[{"schema":null,"applied":1,"total":3}]}

    When a migration fails, ok is false and error has the error code and the message:

    {"ok":false,"exitCode":1,"error":{"code":"MXE102","message":"Migration '0004_broken.sql' failed and was not recorded as applied. ...","hint":null}}

    Log tools such as Loki, CloudWatch Logs or Datadog Logs can count these lines and alert on "ok":false, or chart applied per release.

docs.title: Startup integrations in several instances
docs.text: The Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut and Helidon integrations migrate when the application starts. When several instances start at the same time, set migrax.lock-timeout (for example 2m) so they wait for each other instead of failing.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
Entities are read into a schema model, compared with the snapshot, and the difference becomes a migration file with a rollback script; migrax migrate applies it to the database and records it in migrax_history. Entities your JPA provider's mapping (or the annotations) Schema model .migrax/snapshot.json Diff migrax generate 0002_add_customers_phone.sql + rollback script migrax migrate Database migrax_history

Schema model. Migrax builds a model of the tables your entities need. When your project has Hibernate 4 or newer, EclipseLink or OpenJPA, Migrax asks your own JPA provider for its mapping, without connecting to a database, so names, types, join tables, element collections, inheritance and sequences are exactly what your application expects. Without one of them it scans the jakarta.persistence / javax.persistence annotations instead.

Snapshot. .migrax/snapshot.json records the schema your migrations produce. generate compares the entities with the snapshot and writes only the difference. The snapshot also records the dialect and naming strategy, so the names stay stable even if your configuration changes later.

The very first generate has no snapshot, so it compares with the live database instead. When that database already has tables, it also writes them to 0001_baseline.sql and records that migration as applied there without running it, so an empty database can still be built from the migrations alone. The baseline has no rollback script: undoing it would drop every table.

Migration files. Migrations live in src/main/resources/db/migration and are numbered: 0001_initial.sql, 0002_add_customers_phone.sql, ... The name describes the change. Next to each generated migration, rollback/<same name>.sql undoes it.

History. migrax migrate records every applied migration in the migrax_history table, with a SHA-256 checksum of the file. Failed attempts are recorded in migrax_failures.

docs.title: What generate does
docs.text:
1. Compiles the project if sources changed, and asks Maven or Gradle (preferring ./mvnw / ./gradlew) for the runtime classpath. The classpath is cached in .migrax/classpath.txt and refreshed when the build file changes.
  2. Reads the entities into a schema model.
  3. Compares it with the snapshot and works out the operations: create and drop tables, add, drop, rename and alter columns, keys, indexes, unique constraints, check constraints, comments and sequences.
  4. Asks about likely renames, and refuses drops unless you pass --allow-destructive (see Changing entities).
  5. Writes the migration and its rollback script, lints the SQL, and updates the snapshot.

migrax plan shows the same SQL without writing anything.

docs.title: What migrate does
docs.text:
1. Takes a database lock, so two instances starting at the same time don't both migrate.
  2. Checks the history: an applied file that changed or disappeared stops the run.
  3. Applies pending migrations in order, each in its own transaction with its history record.
  4. Runs repeatable R__*.sql migrations that are new or changed, and the callbacks.

If a migration fails, its transaction is rolled back (where the database supports transactional DDL) and the failure is recorded. migrate then refuses to continue until you have looked at it; see Rollbacks and recovery.

docs.title: Locking
docs.text: Database Lock PostgreSQL pg_advisory_lock YugabyteDB pg_advisory_lock (2025.1 and newer), else a row in migrax_lock CockroachDB A row in migrax_lock (CockroachDB has no session locks) MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB GET_LOCK SQL Server sp_getapplock Oracle DBMS_LOCK (needs EXECUTE on DBMS_LOCK) HSQLDB, Derby A row in migrax_lock H2 Single-process database, no lock needed SQLite An operating-system lock on <database>.migrax-lock next to the database file

docs.title: Java API and JUnit tests
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.10.0.

Migrax can run from your own Java code, and its JUnit 5 extension can check in a unit test that your migrations still match your entities.

docs.title: Test that migrations match the entities
docs.text:
Add migrax-junit as a test dependency:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax-junit</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Then put @MigraxTest on a test class:

import org.migrax.junit.MigraxTest;

@MigraxTest
class BookRepositoryTest {

  @Test
  void savesBooks(DataSource dataSource) throws Exception {
    // The database already has every migration applied.
  }
}

Before the tests run, Migrax creates the test database, applies every migration from src/main/resources/db/migration and compares the result with your entities. If they differ, every test in the class fails with a list of the differences:

The migrated schema does not match the entities (Hibernate 6.6.13.Final mapping):
  - book.isbn: column is missing from the database
Generate a migration for the entity changes (migrax generate), or fix the migration that differs.

This catches an entity that changed without a new migration, and a migration that was edited by hand and no longer creates what the entities need. The test is an ordinary JUnit test, so it runs in mvn test and in your CI like every other test.

docs.title: What is compared
docs.text:
The entities are read the same way migrax generate reads them: through Hibernate, EclipseLink or OpenJPA when the project has one, otherwise from the JPA annotations. Every table, column, primary key, foreign key and check constraint the entities need must be in the database, with a matching type and nullability.

The database may contain more than the entities need: tables that no entity maps, and nullable columns that no entity maps, are fine. Other code may use them. A NOT NULL column without a default that no entity maps is reported, because inserting an entity would fail.

docs.title: Which database
docs.text:
By default the test runs on a new H2 database in memory, which needs H2 on the test classpath. This works when your migrations are written for H2.

For the database you use in production, mark a static field with @MigraxDatabase. The field can hold a DataSource or a Testcontainers JDBC container. A container that isn't running is started:

@MigraxTest
class OrderRepositoryTest {

  @MigraxDatabase
  static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17");

  @Test
  void findsOrders(DataSource dataSource) { ... }
}

You can also give a JDBC URL: @MigraxTest(url = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/test", user = "test", password = "test"). Use a database that only tests use.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning entities migrax.package, else the Maven groupId Package that holds the entities locations db/migration Migration folders on the classpath; filesystem:<path> for folders on disk javaPackage db.migration Package of JavaMigration classes validate true Compare the migrated schema with the entities rollbacks false Also test every rollback script (see below) schemas Schemas to migrate one after another env Environment: migrations marked -- migrax:env <name> run only there url, user, password The test database, when no field is marked @MigraxDatabase

The naming of tables and columns is the one the migrax command uses for your project. It is recorded in .migrax/snapshot.json.

docs.title: Test the rollback scripts too
docs.text:
With @MigraxTest(rollbacks = true), Migrax rolls each migration back with its rollback script, applies it again and checks that the schema is the same as before. A broken rollback script fails the tests and is named:

Rollback scripts: failed: 0002_add_isbn.sql fails when applied again after its rollback script ran: ...

This is the same check migrax verify runs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Test methods, constructors and @BeforeEach methods can ask for these as parameters:

Type What it is javax.sql.DataSource The migrated test database org.migrax.api.Migrax The Java API for this database (below) org.migrax.api.Migrax.MigrateResult How many migrations were applied

The database is migrated once per test class. @Nested classes share it with the class around them.

docs.title: Run Migrax from Java
docs.text:
The migrax library (org.migrax:migrax) has a Java API. Use it when your application starts some other way than the framework integrations, or in tools of your own:

import org.migrax.api.Migrax;

Migrax migrax = Migrax.configure()
    .dataSource(dataSource)
    .locations("db/migration")
    .load();

int applied = migrax.migrate().applied();
Method What it does migrate() Applies the pending migrations; returns how many, per schema status() The state of every migration (applied, pending, failed, changed, ...) without changing anything; upToDate() tells if nothing is pending or wrong rollback(steps) Rolls back the newest migrations with their rollback scripts; returns their names rollbackTo(version) Rolls back every migration after version validate() Compares the entities with the database, as described above testRollbacks() Tests every rollback script on the database. Rolling back drops data, so use a test database

The builder takes the same settings as the startup integrations:

Builder method Meaning dataSource(ds) or url(url, user, password) The database (required) locations(...) Migration folders: classpath folders, or filesystem:<path> javaPackage(name) Package of JavaMigration classes (default db.migration) javaMigrations(...) JavaMigration objects to run as well schemas(...) Schemas to migrate one after another environment(name) Environment for -- migrax:env migrations placeholder(name, value) Values for ${name} placeholders lockTimeout(duration) How long to wait while another instance migrates resume(true) Re-run a failed migration marked -- migrax:resume-safe entities(package), naming(name) For validate(): the entity package and naming classLoader(loader) Where migrations and JDBC drivers are found listener(...) Listeners for metrics and tracing (Metrics and tracing) settings(map) migrax.* settings, as in application.properties

Each method call opens its own connection and closes it again.

docs.title: Metrics and tracing
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.13.0.

When an application migrates at startup, Migrax reports what happened to the monitoring tools the application already uses: Micrometer metrics (Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog, ...) and OpenTelemetry traces (Jaeger, Tempo, ...). Dashboards and alerts then show how long migrations take, which one failed, and how long an instance waited while another one migrated.

There is nothing to set up: the startup integrations for Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE record them when the application has a MeterRegistry (Micrometer) or an OpenTelemetry bean. Without them, nothing changes.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Metric Prometheus name Tags What it measures migrax.run migrax_run_seconds outcome (success, failure), database Each migration run at startup migrax.migration migrax_migration_seconds migration (file or class name), outcome, database Each migration migrax.migrations.applied migrax_migrations_applied_total database Migrations applied migrax.migrations.failed migrax_migrations_failed_total database Migrations that failed migrax.lock.wait migrax_lock_wait_seconds database How long the migration lock took to get migrax.migrations.pending migrax_migrations_pending database Migrations that wait to run (from Migrax 0.14.0)

The tag database (from Migrax 0.15.0) is default, or the name of a further database in an application with several databases. Queries without it add the databases up.

A Prometheus alert on failed migrations, for example:

- alert: MigraxMigrationFailed
  expr: increase(migrax_migrations_failed_total[15m]) > 0

With several instances starting together and migrax.lock-timeout set, migrax_lock_wait_seconds shows how long they waited for each other.

migrax_migrations_pending is the count the health check reports. An application that migrates at startup only starts when nothing is pending, so there it stays 0; it shows what waits when a pipeline migrates (below). Migrax asks the database at most every 10 seconds; when the database can't be reached, the gauge has no value (NaN).

docs.title: When a pipeline migrates
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.14.0.

Some teams run the migrations in a deployment pipeline or have a DBA run them, and the application must never change the schema. Set migrax.migrate-at-startup=false: the application then starts without migrating and logs what waits:

Migrax: not migrating at startup (migrax.migrate-at-startup=false); 3 migration(s) pending

The health check and migrax_migrations_pending keep reporting, so a release whose migrations haven't run yet shows up: readiness is DOWN, and an alert can fire:

- alert: MigraxMigrationsPending
  expr: migrax_migrations_pending > 0
  for: 30m

migrax.enabled=false instead turns Migrax off completely, health check and metrics included.

docs.title: Traces
docs.text:
Each run is a span named migrax migrate (under the current span, when the startup has one), with one migrax migration span per migration under it:

Span Attributes migrax migrate migrax.applied (migrations applied), migrax.lock.wait_ms migrax migration migrax.migration (file or class name)

A failed migration marks both spans as errors and records the exception, so the trace shows which migration stopped the startup.

docs.title: By framework
docs.text:
Framework Metrics Traces Spring Boot Actuator's MeterRegistry The OpenTelemetry bean (Micrometer Tracing with the OpenTelemetry bridge) Quarkus quarkus-micrometer quarkus-opentelemetry Micronaut micronaut-micrometer An OpenTelemetry bean (micronaut-tracing-opentelemetry) Helidon MP, Jakarta EE A MeterRegistry CDI bean An OpenTelemetry CDI bean (MicroProfile Telemetry)

On Quarkus, the metrics of the migrations at startup reach the registry once the application has started, because Quarkus attaches its registries after the migrations run.

Turn either off with migrax.metrics.enabled=false or migrax.tracing.enabled=false.

docs.title: Your own listener
docs.text:
A MigrationListener bean of the application hears every run too: when it starts, how long the lock took, each migration applied or failed, and when it ends. Use it to send the events somewhere else, such as an audit log:

@Component   // or a CDI bean in Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE
class MigrationAudit implements MigrationListener {
  @Override
  public void migrationApplied(String version, Duration duration) {
    audit.record("migration " + version + " applied in " + duration.toMillis() + " ms");
  }
}

With the Java API, pass listeners to the builder:

Migrax.configure()
    .dataSource(dataSource)
    .listener(new MicrometerListener(meterRegistry), new OpenTelemetryListener(openTelemetry))
    .load()
    .migrate();

A listener that throws an exception is logged and never stops a migration.

docs.title: Production safety
docs.text: Migrax is built around one idea: a migration should be proven before it runs in production.

docs.title: Lint every migration
docs.text:
Every generated migration is linted as it is written, and migrax lint checks the pending ones (or --all, or the files you name). Findings explain the risk and the safer alternative:

$ migrax lint
src/main/resources/db/migration/0007_add_orders_notes_and_more.sql, statement 3: warning MX007
  ALTER TABLE test_table DROP COLUMN numberOfItems
  This deletes data, and running application instances that still use it will fail.
  Fix: Deploy code that no longer uses it first, then drop it in a later release (expand/contract: 'migrax generate --zero-downtime' does this).
1 file(s) checked, 1 finding(s).

See all lint rules. To accept a finding deliberately, put -- migrax:lint-ignore MX007 on the line before the statement.

docs.title: Non-blocking changes on PostgreSQL
docs.text: migrax generate --safe moves index and constraint creation on existing tables into a second, non-transactional migration that uses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID and VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, so writes keep flowing while they build.

docs.title: Changes while the old version still runs
docs.text: During a rolling deployment, instances of the old and the new version use the database at the same time. migrax generate --zero-downtime splits a change so that both work: see Zero-downtime changes.

docs.title: Verify before you ship
docs.text:
$ migrax verify
Applied 7 migration(s) to a fresh postgresql database.
Schema matches the entities (Hibernate 6.6.13.Final schema validation).
Rollback scripts: ok (7 rolled back and re-applied).
Verified.

verify:

  1. starts a throwaway database: in-memory H2, HSQLDB or Derby, a Docker container of your engine, or the empty database you pass with --url;
  2. applies every migration from scratch;
  3. starts your Hibernate version with schema validation against the result (without Hibernate, it compares the schema with the entities);
  4. tests every rollback script on its own, newest first: it rolls the migration back, applies it again and checks that the schema is the same as before. A script that fails or leaves something behind is named, for example Rollback scripts: failed: 0005_tag_color.sql fails when applied again after its rollback script ran: .... When older migrations have no rollback script, it checks the newest ones that do.

Run it in CI on every pull request.

docs.title: Detect manual changes
docs.text:
$ migrax drift
2 difference(s) between the database and the snapshot:
  - products.name: expected varchar(255) but the database column is shorter (varchar(100))
  - products.hotfix: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
Someone changed the database outside migrations. Write a migration for intended changes
('migrax new <name>'), or revert them.

drift reads the live database and compares it with what the migrations produce (the snapshot), or with the entities (--entities). It reports missing and extra tables and columns, keys, unique constraints, nullability, type changes and narrowed columns. It exits with code 2 when it finds drift, so it can run on a schedule.

docs.title: Drift at startup
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.16.0.

The application can run the same comparison every time it starts, so a change someone made by hand is noticed at the next deployment instead of weeks later. Turn it on in the application's configuration:

application.properties
migrax.drift.check=fail
Value When the database differs from the schema its migrations produce off (default) Nothing is checked warn The application starts and logs every difference fail The application doesn't start; the log lists every difference

The check runs right after the startup migrations, in the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations. With fail, a hand-made column stops the start like this:

Migrax: 1 difference(s) between the database and the schema its migrations produce:
  - note.manual_change: column exists in the database but not in the expected schema
Someone changed the database outside migrations. Write a migration for intended changes, or revert them.
(migrax.drift.check=fail stops the start; warn only logs.)

When it finds nothing, it logs Migrax: no drift: the database matches the schema its migrations produce. While migrations are pending (for example with migrax.migrate-at-startup=false, before the pipeline has run them) or have failed, the check is skipped: their changes would show as differences. With several databases, every database is checked, and migrax.databases.<name>.drift.check sets it for one of them.

docs.title: Put the snapshot into the application
docs.text:
The expected schema is .migrax/snapshot.json, the file generate keeps up to date and you commit. The application reads it as META-INF/migrax/snapshot.json, so the build has to copy it in:

QuarkusGradleMavenOther builds

Nothing to do: the extension copies it while the application is built, also into native executables.

Nothing to do: the Migrax Gradle plugin (id("org.migrax")) adds it to the application's resources.

Add the package-snapshot goal to the Migrax plugin; it runs while the resources are copied:

pom.xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.migrax</groupId>
  <artifactId>migrax</artifactId>
  <version>0.17.1</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals>
        <goal>package-snapshot</goal>
      </goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>

Copy .migrax/snapshot.json to META-INF/migrax/snapshot.json in the application's classpath, and .migrax/<name>/snapshot.json to META-INF/migrax/<name>/snapshot.json for each further database.

Without the file, warn logs that it can't check and fail stops the start with the same message, so a missing build step is noticed at once.

docs.title: Hibernate must not change the schema
docs.text:
When Hibernate is allowed to create or update tables at startup, the database drifts away from your migrations, and migrations later fail with "already exists". create and drop-and-create even delete all data on every start. migrax doctor finds these settings and shows the exact line to change:

  [warn]  Hibernate will change your database schema by itself
          Found:  quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy = update
                  in src/main/resources/application.properties, line 15

          Why:    Hibernate adds tables and columns itself when the application starts. ...

          Fix:    change   quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=update
                  to       quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=none
                  (or validate: Hibernate then checks the schema at startup without changing it)

docs.title: When a DBA runs the migrations
docs.text:
Where developers may not change production themselves, hand the DBA one script:

$ migrax migrate --sql > release-2026-10.sql

It is exactly what migrate would do now against that database: the pending migrations in order, each with the row Migrax records in migrax_history (so migrax status shows them as applied afterwards), transactions where the database supports them, and the end markers its tool expects (GO for sqlcmd, / after PL/SQL for sqlplus, DELIMITER for mysql). The first lines say how to run it so it stops at the first error, for example psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f release-2026-10.sql. Writing the script reads the database but changes nothing.

With --schemas tenant_a,tenant_b, the script has a section per schema that starts by switching to it (SET search_path, USE or ALTER SESSION SET CURRENT_SCHEMA), so one run of the file migrates every tenant.

A Java migration can't be written as SQL. The script stops before the first one and its last lines say what to do: run the script, then migrax migrate --to <that migration>, then write the next script with migrax migrate --sql.

docs.title: Applying a release in steps
docs.text:
To roll out several migrations one at a time (for example, run the slow index first and check the database before going on), stop after a given migration:

$ migrax migrate --to 0007
Applying migration '0007_add_order_index.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0007_add_order_index.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s) up to 0007_add_order_index.sql.
2 migration(s) after it stay pending.

--to takes the file name, its start, or the version number. Repeatable migrations (R__*.sql) wait until a migrate without --to, because they may use what later migrations add.

docs.title: A release checklist
docs.text:
• Migration generated in development and reviewed in the pull request
  • CI: check, lint --strict, verify
  • Backup taken before the production run
  • migrax migrate (or startup migration) as part of the release
  • migrax status and migrax drift afterwards

docs.title: Rolling back
docs.text:
Every generated migration has a rollback script in rollback/<same name>.sql. To undo the newest migration:

$ migrax rollback --yes
Rolling back 1 migration(s), newest first:
  0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql
Rolled back migration '0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql'.
Option Effect --steps 3 Roll back the three newest migrations --to 0004_add_index.sql Roll back everything after 0004_add_index.sql --dry-run List what would be rolled back --yes Required: confirms the change. Back up first.

The rolled-back migrations become pending again, so migrax migrate re-applies them.

Structure, not data

A rollback restores the structure: re-creating a dropped column brings the column back, not its values. The header of each rollback script says what cannot be restored:

-- Rollback for 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql. 'migrax rollback' runs it.
-- Note: deletes data written to categories since the migration ran.

To get the data back too, generate the migration with --keep-data.

docs.title: Keeping dropped data
docs.text:
$ migrax generate --allow-destructive --keep-data

With --keep-data, a migration that drops data keeps it, and its rollback script puts it back:

  • A dropped table is renamed to migrax_backup_<migration>_<table> instead. The rollback renames it back, with its rows, keys and indexes.
  • A dropped column, or a column whose type change loses data, is first copied with the table's primary key into migrax_backup_<migration>_<table>_<column>. The rollback adds the column back and fills it row by row.
  • A table without a primary key works the same way with a unique key whose columns are all NOT NULL. Without either, Migrax copies the column with all the other columns of the row and finds each row again by those values (empty values match each other). generate warns about it: rows that are the same in every other column get one value back for all of them, which only matters if they had different values in the dropped column. Columns that the same migration changes, and long text, binary and JSON columns, aren't used to match rows.
-- Rollback for 0007_drop_notes.sql. 'migrax rollback' runs it.
-- Restores the values of orders.notes from migrax_backup_0007_orders_notes.

The backup tables stay until you drop them; migrax drift and migrax generate leave them alone. List them with migrax backups, and once you are sure you won't roll a migration back, drop its backups with migrax backups --drop 0007 --yes (or --drop for all of them). Rows written after the migration ran have no backup: a restored NOT NULL column can't be filled for them, and the rollback stops there.

Hand-written migrations from migrax new get an empty rollback script for you to fill in. Java migrations roll back through JavaMigration.rollback(Connection).

migrax verify proves the rollback scripts work: it rolls every migration back on a throwaway database and applies them again (Production safety).

docs.title: When a migration fails
docs.text:
A failed migration is recorded in migrax_failures, and migrate stops until you decide what happened:

$ migrax status
  [X] 0005_fix_naming.sql                      applied 2026-10-08 11:04:45
  [!] 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql  FAILED: SQLSyntaxErrorException: Table 'categories_seq' already exists
6 applied, 1 failed.
Some migrations need attention. See 'migrax help repair'.

The message is the database's own error. Look at the database, then tell Migrax which case you are in:

The statements took effectYou restored the database

Every statement in the migration is in the database (for example, you finished it by hand):

$ migrax repair 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql --action applied --yes

You undid the partial changes, or nothing was applied; run it again:

$ migrax repair 0006_create_categories_seq_and_more.sql --action retry --yes
$ migrax migrate

Keep a record of every repair. Never edit an applied migration or delete history rows by hand.

docs.title: Migrations that are safe to re-run
docs.text: A migration that starts with -- migrax:resume-safe can be re-run after a failure with migrax migrate --resume, without a repair. Only mark migrations whose statements can run twice (for example CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, idempotent updates).

docs.title: A migration file went missing
docs.text:
status reports applied migrations whose file is gone, and migrate stops:

$ migrax migrate
error[MXE105]: Applied migration file(s) are missing from the configured migration location: 0001_initial.sql. Restore the files from version control; applied migrations must not be deleted. If you deleted them on purpose, remove them from the history with: migrax repair 0001_initial.sql --action forget --yes

Deleted by accident? Restore the file from git (git show <commit>:<path>), unchanged. This is the right fix in almost every project: other environments and new databases still need it.

Deleted on purpose, for example to start a test database over? Remove the migrations from the history:

$ migrax repair 0001_initial.sql 0002_add_email.sql --action forget --yes
Removed 0001_initial.sql from the migration history.
Removed 0002_add_email.sql from the migration history.
The database keeps the changes these migrations made. Run 'migrax status' to check the history.

The tables and columns those migrations created stay in the database; only the record goes. Migrax refuses to forget a migration whose file still exists, because migrate would run it again.

Starting over with the current database as the baseline

To make the current database the starting point, forget the deleted migrations, delete .migrax/snapshot.json and the .migrax/history folder, and run migrax generate: with no snapshot, it compares the entities with the database. It writes the current tables to 0001_baseline.sql (recorded as applied, not run) and what is really different to a second migration. Review that migration before running migrax migrate.

From then on the migrations start at the current database. On other databases that still have the old history, the baseline would try to create tables that exist, so for shared environments restore the deleted files instead.

docs.title: Starting a development database over
docs.text:
migrax clean drops every table, view and sequence in the database, the migration history included, so migrax migrate can build it again from the migrations:

$ migrax clean --dry-run
Would drop from jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop:
  table    customers
  table    migrax_history
  ...
$ migrax clean --yes
Dropped 5 table(s), 2 sequence(s) from jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop.
Run 'migrax migrate' to rebuild the schema from the migrations.
$ migrax migrate

All data is gone afterwards, so use it only on development and test databases. On servers where it must never run, set MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED=true: clean then refuses.

docs.title: Schema file from your ORM
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.17.0.

With a schema file, Migrax writes your migrations from the tables you describe in SQL. If your project already describes its tables in an ORM, you don't have to write that SQL by hand: most ORMs can print their models as CREATE TABLE statements. Export them into the schema file, and the loop is:

  1. Change a model.
  2. Export the schema file (one command).
  3. Run migrax generate, review the migration, commit it, run migrax migrate.

Tested with

Migrax 0.17.0, PostgreSQL 17 and MySQL 8.4, SQLAlchemy 2.1.5 (Python 3.13), Drizzle ORM 0.45.4 with drizzle-kit 0.31.11 (Node.js 24), GORM 1.31.2 (Go 1.25). Every output below was copied from a real run.

The settings are the ones from SQL migrations for any language, plus the schema file:

export MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret
export MIGRAX_LOCATIONS=filesystem:db/migrations
export MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE=db/schema.sql
export MIGRAX_DRIVERS=drivers

docs.title: SQLAlchemy (Python)
docs.text:
The models:

models.py
from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal

from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, Numeric, String, func
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Customer(Base):
    __tablename__ = "customer"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(150), unique=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100))
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(server_default=func.now())


class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    customer_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("customer.id"), index=True)
    total: Mapped[Decimal] = mapped_column(Numeric(12, 2))
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(20), server_default="new")

SQLAlchemy prints a table's CREATE TABLE for a given database without connecting to one. A small script writes all of them:

export_schema.py
"""Prints the tables of models.py as SQL, for migrax.schema-file."""
from sqlalchemy.dialects import postgresql
from sqlalchemy.schema import CreateIndex, CreateTable

from models import Base

dialect = postgresql.dialect()
for table in Base.metadata.sorted_tables:
    print(f"{str(CreateTable(table).compile(dialect=dialect)).strip()};\n")
    for index in sorted(table.indexes, key=lambda i: i.name):
        print(f"{CreateIndex(index).compile(dialect=dialect)};\n")

For MySQL, import mysql from sqlalchemy.dialects and use mysql.dialect().

$ python export_schema.py > db/schema.sql
$ migrax generate
Starting a throwaway postgresql database (postgres:17-alpine)...
Read db/schema.sql: 2 table(s).
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customer
  - create table orders
  - add index ix_orders_customer_id on orders
  - add foreign key orders_customer_id_fkey on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
db/migrations/0001_initial.sql
CREATE TABLE customer (id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customer_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customer_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id integer NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);

SQLAlchemy writes the id columns as SERIAL; Migrax writes them as identity columns, which hand out ids the same way. After migrax migrate, SQLAlchemy saves and loads rows as before.

Now add a field to Customer:

    phone: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(30))

Export again; migrax check sees the change, and generate writes it:

$ python export_schema.py > db/schema.sql
$ migrax check
1 change(s) in db/schema.sql have no migration:
  - add column customer.phone
Run 'migrax generate' and commit the result.
$ migrax generate
Created db/migrations/0002_add_customer_phone.sql:
  - add column customer.phone
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
db/migrations/0002_add_customer_phone.sql
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);

docs.title: Drizzle (TypeScript)
docs.text:
The schema:

schema.ts
import { bigint, index, numeric, pgTable, timestamp, varchar } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const customer = pgTable("customer", {
  id: bigint("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey().generatedByDefaultAsIdentity(),
  email: varchar("email", { length: 150 }).notNull().unique(),
  name: varchar("name", { length: 100 }).notNull(),
  createdAt: timestamp("created_at", { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
});

export const orders = pgTable("orders", {
  id: bigint("id", { mode: "number" }).primaryKey().generatedByDefaultAsIdentity(),
  customerId: bigint("customer_id", { mode: "number" }).notNull()
    .references(() => customer.id),
  total: numeric("total", { precision: 12, scale: 2 }).notNull(),
  status: varchar("status", { length: 20 }).notNull().default("new"),
}, (table) => [index("orders_customer").on(table.customerId)]);

drizzle-kit export prints the schema as SQL, without a database:

$ npx drizzle-kit export --dialect=postgresql --schema=./schema.ts > db/schema.sql
$ migrax generate
Starting a throwaway postgresql database (postgres:17-alpine)...
Read db/schema.sql: 2 table(s).
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customer
  - create table orders
  - add index orders_customer on orders
  - add foreign key orders_customer_id_customer_id_fk on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
db/migrations/0001_initial.sql
CREATE TABLE customer (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customer_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customer_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id bigint NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_customer_id_fk FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);

Drizzle names the unique constraint on email customer_email_unique; Migrax names it uk_customer_email. The constraint is the same. After migrax migrate, Drizzle inserts and reads rows as before. Adding phone: varchar("phone", { length: 30 }) to customer and exporting again gives:

db/migrations/0002_add_customer_phone.sql
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);

docs.title: Go, Rust and any other ORM
docs.text:
Some ORMs can't print their models as SQL, but all of them can create their tables, for example GORM's AutoMigrate. Let the ORM create them in a database of its own for this (not the one Migrax migrates), and copy the tables from there with pg_dump or mysqldump.

The models, in Go with GORM:

models.go
type Customer struct {
    ID        uint      `gorm:"primaryKey"`
    Email     string    `gorm:"size:150;not null;uniqueIndex"`
    Name      string    `gorm:"size:100;not null"`
    CreatedAt time.Time `gorm:"not null;default:now()"`
}

type Order struct {
    ID         uint    `gorm:"primaryKey"`
    CustomerID uint    `gorm:"not null;index"`
    Customer   Customer
    Total      float64 `gorm:"type:numeric(12,2);not null"`
    Status     string  `gorm:"size:20;not null;default:'new'"`
}

A small program runs db.AutoMigrate(&Customer{}, &Order{}) against an empty database shop_dev. Then:

$ pg_dump --schema-only --no-owner --no-privileges shop_dev > db/schema.sql
$ migrax generate
Starting a throwaway postgresql database (postgres:17-alpine)...
Read db/schema.sql: 2 table(s).
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customers
  - create table orders
  - add index idx_orders_customer_id on orders
  - add foreign key fk_orders_customer on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
db/migrations/0001_initial.sql
CREATE TABLE customers (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customers_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customers_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id bigint NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id);

After migrax migrate, GORM saves and loads customers and orders in the migrated database. Adding Phone *string with gorm:"size:30" to Customer, running AutoMigrate on shop_dev again and dumping it gives 0002_add_customers_phone.sql with ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);.

What to know about dumps:

  • Use --no-owner --no-privileges: without them, the file names the roles of your server, which the throwaway database doesn't have.
  • Migrax runs the throwaway database in your server's version, because a dump uses that version's settings. Pass --image (or set migrax.scratch-image) to choose another image.
  • The \restrict lines that newer pg_dump versions write are psql commands, not SQL: Migrax skips them. Their random key changes on every dump, but the cached model in .migrax/ still counts the file as unchanged.
  • On MySQL and MariaDB, mysqldump --no-data --skip-comments shop_dev > db/schema.sql works the same way. Unsigned ids (bigint unsigned, GORM's uint) stay unsigned in the migration.

Any ORM works the same way if it can print its models as CREATE TABLE statements or create its tables in a database you can dump. Read the migration Migrax writes before you commit it. What the file can contain lists what Migrax reads from it.

docs.title: Make it one step
docs.text:
Put the export and the check in your build or CI, so a model change without a migration is caught:

python export_schema.py > db/schema.sql   # or: npx drizzle-kit export ..., pg_dump ...
migrax check                              # exit code 2: a change has no migration yet

Commit db/schema.sql and .migrax/ with each migration: while the file is unchanged, migrax check needs no Docker (details).

docs.title: Several databases
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.15.0.

An application that uses more than one database, for example orders and billing, migrates each of them when it starts. The default database keeps the usual migrax.* settings. Each further database gets a block migrax.databases.<name>.*:

application.properties
# The default database: unchanged
migrax.locations=db/migration

# A second database
migrax.databases.billing.datasource=billingDataSource
migrax.databases.billing.locations=db/billing
migrax.databases.billing.placeholders.owner=billing_app

The default database is migrated first, then the others in alphabetical order. Each has its own migration history table, lock and checksums, in its own database.

docs.title: Settings of a database
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning datasource the database's name The data source to migrate: see By framework locations db/<name> Migration folders, separated by commas java-package db.<name> Package of Java migrations schemas none Schemas to migrate one after another placeholders.<key> none Values for ${key} in this database's migrations env migrax.env Environment for migrations marked -- migrax:env lock-timeout migrax.lock-timeout How long to wait while another instance migrates resume migrax.resume Re-run a failed resume-safe migration migrate-at-startup migrax.migrate-at-startup false: report only, as described in Metrics and tracing drift.check migrax.drift.check Compare this database with its snapshot at startup: see Drift at startup

Folders, Java migrations, schemas and placeholders belong to one database: a further database never runs the default database's migrations. The defaults db/<name> and db.<name> are kept apart from db/migration and db.migration on purpose, which is why default and migration can't be database names; nor can history and pending, the names of folders the migrax command keeps in .migrax/. Names may contain letters, digits, - and _.

docs.title: By framework
Health and metrics
docs.text:
The health checks report every database. The default database keeps its usual details (applied, pending, problems), and each further one adds its own, such as billing.pending; the check is UP only when every database is up to date. Spring Boot shows one entry per database under migrax instead.

Every metric has the tag database: default, or the name of a further database. See Metrics and tracing.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
The migrax command works on one database at a time: the default database, or the one --database names.

migrax generate --database billing
migrax migrate --database billing
migrax status --database billing

With Maven, pass -Dmigrax.database=billing (for example mvn migrax:status -Dmigrax.database=billing). In a pipeline, MIGRAX_DATABASE=billing does the same for every command.

For a further database the command reads:

What From Connection --url, then MIGRAX_DATABASES_BILLING_URL (or ..._URL_FILE), then migrax.databases.billing.url, then the framework's settings of its data source: quarkus.datasource.billing.*, datasources.billing.* (Micronaut) or javax.sql.DataSource.billing.* (Helidon). User and password the same way. Spring Boot has no standard key for a second data source, so set migrax.databases.billing.url, .user and .password Migration folders migrax.databases.billing.locations, else db/billing, under src/main/resources Entities migrax.databases.billing.package (or --package), needed by the commands that read entities, such as generate, check and plan Snapshot .migrax/billing/, next to the default database's .migrax/snapshot.json application.properties
migrax.databases.billing.datasource=billingDataSource
migrax.databases.billing.package=com.shop.billing
migrax.databases.billing.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/billing
migrax.databases.billing.user=billing

The default database leaves a further database's package out when it sits inside its own: with the entity package com.shop, the entities in com.shop.billing belong to billing only. Keep each database's entities in their own package, the same way the application's JPA setup separates them.

Each database's settings stay its own: MIGRAX_LOCATIONS, MIGRAX_SCHEMAS and the default database's placeholders never apply to billing. Its own variables start with MIGRAX_DATABASES_BILLING_, for example MIGRAX_DATABASES_BILLING_PLACEHOLDERS_OWNER. Settings for the whole application, such as MIGRAX_ENV, apply to every database unless the block sets them.

docs.title: SQL migrations for any language
docs.text:
Migrax applies SQL migrations you write yourself, in any project: Python, Node.js, Go, .NET, PHP, Ruby, or a Java application without JPA. It needs only a folder of SQL files and a database connection; it doesn't read your application's code.

What you keep: numbered migrations applied once and in order, repeatable migrations, the history table, checksums of applied files, the migration lock, rollback scripts, status, lint, repair and clean. Migrax can also write the migrations for you: keep your tables as they should be in one SQL file, and generate, check and verify work from it as they do from Java entities. See Let Migrax write the migrations.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Migrax. Either the command line tool, which needs Java 17 or newer on the machine that runs it (Installation), or the container image, which needs only Docker.
  • The JDBC driver of your database. Migrax connects through Java's database drivers, not through your application's (psycopg, pg, mysql2 and so on). See Drivers below.
  • The connection as a JDBC URL, for example jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop.

docs.title: A project layout
docs.text:
shop/
  package.json
  src/...
  db/
    migrations/
      0001_create_customer.sql
      0002_add_email.sql
      R__customer_view.sql
      rollback/
        0002_add_email.sql

The migration folder can be anywhere; tell Migrax where with --locations filesystem:<folder> (relative to the folder you run Migrax in) or MIGRAX_LOCATIONS.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A project without Java has no application configuration for Migrax to read, so set the connection with environment variables, for example in a .env file your shell or CI loads:

export MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop
export MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret
export MIGRAX_LOCATIONS=filesystem:db/migrations
export MIGRAX_DRIVERS=drivers

The same settings exist as options (--url, --user, --password, --password-file, --locations, --classpath); see Configuration.

Database JDBC URL Driver PostgreSQL jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/shop org.postgresql:postgresql MySQL jdbc:mysql://host:3306/shop com.mysql:mysql-connector-j MariaDB jdbc:mariadb://host:3306/shop org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client SQLite jdbc:sqlite:path/to/app.db org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc

Other databases: Databases.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
Download the driver's .jar from Maven Central (search.maven.org, using the name in the table above) and give it to Migrax in one of three ways:

  • put it in a folder and set MIGRAX_DRIVERS to that folder;
  • put it in the drivers folder next to the lib folder of your Migrax installation, so every project can use it;
  • pass it with --classpath path/to/driver.jar.

Without a driver, Migrax stops with error MXE106 ("No JDBC driver ... accepts URL").

The container image already has the drivers for PostgreSQL (also for CockroachDB and YugabyteDB), MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite and H2; for MySQL Connector/J and Oracle see Other drivers.

docs.title: Writing migrations
docs.text:
$ migrax new create_customer
Created db/migrations/0001_create_customer.sql and db/migrations/rollback/0001_create_customer.sql.

new creates the next numbered file and an empty rollback script. Write the SQL yourself:

db/migrations/0001_create_customer.sql
CREATE TABLE customer (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL);

You can also create the files by hand. Numbered files (0001_name.sql) and files named V1__name.sql both work, also mixed in one folder; they run in version order. Files named R__<name>.sql are repeatable: they run after the numbered ones and again whenever they change, which suits views and functions. Callbacks and placeholders work as described in Advanced migrations.

Never edit a migration after it has been applied: Migrax keeps a checksum of every applied file and stops when one changes. Write a new migration instead.

docs.title: Applying them
docs.text:
$ migrax status
Migrations in db/migrations for jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ ] 0001_create_customer.sql  pending
  [ ] 0002_add_email.sql        pending
  [ ] R__customer_view.sql      pending
3 pending.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0001_create_customer.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0001_create_customer.sql'.
Applying migration '0002_add_email.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0002_add_email.sql'.
Applying migration 'R__customer_view.sql'...
Successfully applied migration 'R__customer_view.sql'.
Applied 3 migration(s); 2 total in db/migrations.

$ migrax migrate
Nothing to migrate: all 2 migration(s) are applied.

migrax lint checks the files for risky statements before they run, and migrax migrate --dry-run shows what would run without changing the database.

With the container image, mount the folder at /migrations:

$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD/db/migrations:/migrations:ro" \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop \
    -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_USER=shop -e MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret \
    ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.1 migrate

docs.title: A database that already has tables
docs.text:
If the database was built before you started using Migrax, write migrations that describe what it already has (or one migration for all of it), then tell Migrax they are applied:

$ migrax baseline 0002 --yes
Recording 2 migration(s) as applied without running them:
  0001_create_customer.sql
  0002_add_email.sql
Recorded. Run 'migrax migrate' to apply the migrations after 0002_add_email.sql.

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0003_add_phone.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0003_add_phone.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 3 total in db/migrations.

baseline only works on a database without migration history, and --dry-run shows what it would record. Run it once per database (each environment), then use migrate as usual.

docs.title: Rolling back
docs.text:
migrax rollback --yes runs the rollback script of the newest applied migration (rollback/<same file name>); --steps n rolls back several. A migration without a rollback script can't be rolled back. Migrax checks every script first, so nothing is rolled back when one is missing:

$ migrax rollback --steps 2 --yes
error[MXE001]: No rollback script for 0001_create_customer.sql.
Write one in db/migrations/rollback/<same file name>, then run rollback again.

More in Rollbacks and recovery.

docs.title: Let Migrax write the migrations
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.17.0.

Instead of writing each migration by hand, keep one SQL file with your tables as they should be, and let migrax generate write the migration and its rollback script whenever the file changes:

db/schema.sql
-- The tables as they should be. Migrax writes the migrations.
CREATE TABLE customer (
  id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customer (id),
  total NUMERIC(12, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'
);

CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);

Tell Migrax where the file is, next to the other settings:

export MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE=db/schema.sql

(--schema-file db/schema.sql on the command line, or migrax.schema-file in a Java project's application configuration.)

Describe your tables in an ORM such as SQLAlchemy or Drizzle? Export the schema file from it: Schema file from your ORM.

To read the file, Migrax runs it on a throwaway database of the same kind and reads the tables back. For PostgreSQL, MySQL and the other server databases that is a Docker container, so Docker must be running; H2, SQLite, Derby and HSQLDB need no Docker. For PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, the container runs the same version as your database server when Migrax can reach it.

$ migrax generate
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created db/migrations/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customer
  - create table orders
  - add index orders_customer on orders
  - add foreign key orders_customer_id_fkey on orders
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.
db/migrations/0001_initial.sql
CREATE TABLE customer (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, email varchar(150) NOT NULL, name varchar(100) NOT NULL, created_at timestamp(6) with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT customer_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT uk_customer_email UNIQUE (email));
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY NOT NULL, customer_id bigint NOT NULL, total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, status varchar(20) DEFAULT 'new' NOT NULL, CONSTRAINT orders_pkey PRIMARY KEY (id), CONSTRAINT orders_total_check CHECK (((total >= (0)::numeric))));
CREATE INDEX orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (id);

Apply it with migrax migrate as usual. Commit the migration together with .migrax/: snapshot.json records the schema the migrations produce, and schema-model.json records what Migrax read from your file.

docs.title: Changing the schema
docs.text:
Edit the file, for example rename name to full_name and add a phone column:

  full_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  phone VARCHAR(30),

migrax check lists what has no migration yet, and exits with code 2:

$ migrax check
3 change(s) in db/schema.sql have no migration:
  - add column customer.full_name
  - add column customer.phone
  - drop column customer.name
Run 'migrax generate' and commit the result.

A dropped column next to a new one may be a rename. In a terminal, generate asks; in a script it stops before dropping anything and tells you how to keep the data:

$ migrax generate
Possible rename: customer.name to customer.full_name. To keep the data, rerun with --rename customer.name=full_name.
...
error[MXE108]: 1 destructive change(s) detected (marked [DESTRUCTIVE] above).
$ migrax generate --rename customer.name=full_name
Created db/migrations/0002_rename_customer_name_add_customer_phone.sql:
  - rename column customer.name to full_name
  - add column customer.phone
Rollback script written to db/migrations/rollback.
db/migrations/0002_rename_customer_name_add_customer_phone.sql
ALTER TABLE customer RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN phone varchar(30);

migrax verify applies all migrations to an empty throwaway database, compares the result with your file, and tests every rollback script:

$ migrax verify
Applied 2 migration(s) to a fresh postgresql database.
Schema matches the schema file (structural comparison).
Rollback scripts: ok (2 rolled back and re-applied).
Verified.

Everything else works as for Java entities: lint warnings, --zero-downtime, --keep-data, plan, and several databases (each with its own migrax.databases.<name>.schema-file).

docs.title: In CI without Docker
docs.text: While db/schema.sql is unchanged, Migrax reads it from the committed .migrax/schema-model.json and starts no database, so migrax check runs anywhere, including inside the container image. When someone changes the file but forgets to run generate, the saved model no longer matches and check needs Docker to read the file; without Docker it stops with error MXE115. Either way the change doesn't slip through. To read the file without Docker, give Migrax an empty database of its own with --scratch-url (or MIGRAX_SCRATCH_URL); Migrax empties it again afterwards. It connects with the same user and password as your database.

docs.title: What the file can contain
docs.text:
Tables with their columns, defaults, primary and foreign keys, unique constraints, checks, indexes and comments. Name constraints if you like. An unnamed one keeps the database's name when that name is predictable, such as PostgreSQL's orders_customer_id_fkey; random ones, such as Oracle's SYS_C... or SQL Server's FK__..., get a stable name from Migrax.

Not read from the file:

  • Views, functions, procedures and triggers. Keep them in repeatable migrations.
  • Sequences (CREATE SEQUENCE; Migrax warns). Identity columns work; for a sequence of your own, write its migration with migrax new.
  • Tables in another schema (CREATE TABLE billing.invoice; Migrax warns). Migrax reads the database's default schema.
  • ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on MySQL and MariaDB (Migrax warns). The column and its default are read; add the ON UPDATE part to the generated migration yourself.

A statement that fails on the throwaway database stops Migrax with the file name, the statement number and its line (error MXE115).

docs.title: migrax doctor
docs.text:
doctor checks the setup and says how to fix what fails. When the folder has migrations but no pom.xml, build.gradle or entity package, it skips the Java checks and checks only the migrations and the database:

$ migrax doctor
  [ok]    Java 21.0.5
  [info]  No pom.xml, build.gradle or entity package: checking migrations and the database only
  [ok]    Migrations: 3 file(s) in db/migrations
  [ok]    Database URL: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
  [ok]    Connected: PostgreSQL 16.15 (Debian 16.15-1.pgdg13+2) (driver 42.7.9)
  [ok]    Locking: supported
  [info]  Pending migrations: 0

All checks passed.

Older versions of Migrax report the build tool, the entity package and the JPA API as failed here; ignore those three lines, the migrations and database lines are the ones that matter.

docs.title: Switching from Flyway or Liquibase
docs.text: A project that already manages its database with Flyway or Liquibase can move to Migrax with one command, without running anything again on the database. migrax import reads the other tool's history and records it in Migrax's own history (migrax_history).
