docs.title: From Flyway
docs.text:
Flyway's files already live where Migrax looks for migrations (src/main/resources/db/migration), and their names work unchanged: V1__init.sql, V2__add_email.sql and repeatable R__views.sql files are ordered by their version.

$ migrax import flyway
Recorded 12 migration(s) as applied.
Next: disable Flyway (spring.flyway.enabled=false), then run 'migrax generate'; its first run uses the current database as the baseline.

What it does:

  • Every migration that Flyway applied successfully (success is true in flyway_schema_history) is recorded as applied, so migrax migrate doesn't run it again.
  • Java migrations Flyway ran are recorded by their class name.
  • A Flyway baseline (baselineVersion) is respected: files up to that version are recorded as applied too.
  • Failed Flyway migrations are not recorded; migrax migrate runs them like new files.
  • A file Flyway applied that is no longer in the folder is skipped, with a note.

If the history table has another name, pass it with --table (for example --table my_schema_history).

docs.title: From Liquibase
docs.text:
Liquibase's changelogs are XML, YAML or SQL that Migrax doesn't run. Instead, the import writes the database's current schema as one SQL migration, a baseline, and records it as applied:

$ migrax import liquibase
Wrote 0001_liquibase_baseline.sql with 9 table(s) from the current schema.
Recorded 1 migration(s) as applied.
Next: disable Liquibase (spring.liquibase.enabled=false), then run 'migrax generate'; its first run uses the current database as the baseline.

The baseline has the tables, keys, indexes and the sequences your entities use, so a new environment or migrax verify builds the whole schema from it. The database the import ran on already has all of it and never runs the file. Review its column types before you commit it; --name chooses another file name.

docs.title: Afterwards
docs.text:
1. Remove the other tool, or switch it off (spring.flyway.enabled=false, spring.liquibase.enabled=false, or your framework's setting), so that only Migrax migrates at startup.
  2. Run migrax generate. With no snapshot yet, it compares the entities with the database and writes only what is really different; usually it finds nothing and saves the snapshot.
  3. Run migrax verify to check that the migrations build the schema your entities expect.

The other tool's history tables (flyway_schema_history, DATABASECHANGELOG, DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK) stay in the database; Migrax ignores them. Drop them once you no longer need them.

The import is safe to run again: migrations already in Migrax's history are not recorded twice.

docs.title: What to commit
docs.text:
Commit Ignore (Migrax does it for you) src/main/resources/db/migration/*.sql .migrax/classpath.txt, .migrax/classpath.hash src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback/ .migrax/build.stamp and other caches .migrax/snapshot.json .migrax/history/

The snapshot is written with one table, column, index and key per line, so git can merge changes two people made to different tables.

docs.title: Two branches, same migration number
docs.text:
Alice and Bob both branch from 0007. Each generates a migration: both get 0008. After the merge, generate refuses to continue and check fails:

$ migrax check
Migrations share numbers: [[0008_add_orders_notes.sql, 0008_create_invoices.sql]].
Run 'migrax merge'.

$ migrax merge
Renamed 0008_create_invoices.sql to 0009_create_invoices.sql.
Next: run 'migrax check' (no changes expected) and 'migrax verify' to prove the merged
migrations produce the entity schema.

The migration added later moves to the next free number, together with its rollback script. merge also rebuilds a snapshot that has git conflict markers.

Migrax never renames a migration that the configured database has already applied. If both files with the same number are already applied, they are settled history: they run in file name order and are left as they are.

docs.title: Too many migration files?
docs.text:
After a while, squash old migrations into one:

$ migrax squash --to 0040_add_audit_columns.sql

The squashed file replaces 0001 to 0040. Databases that already applied those record the squashed file without running it; new databases run only the squashed file. --optimize writes just the resulting schema and drops data statements. Delete the old files once every environment has run migrate.

docs.title: Reviewing migrations
docs.text:
Treat a migration like code:

  • read the SQL in the pull request (the GitHub Action posts it as a comment);
  • check the lint findings;
  • let CI run migrax check and migrax verify.

docs.title: Zero-downtime changes
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.11.0.

During a rolling deployment, instances of the old version keep running while the new version starts. Both use the same database. A migration that renames or drops a column breaks the old instances the moment it runs, and one that adds a NOT NULL column breaks their inserts.

migrax generate --zero-downtime splits such a change into two migrations:

  • The expand migration ships with this release. Everything in it is safe for the old version: it only adds and relaxes.
  • The contract migration ships with the next release, when no old instance is left. It removes and tightens.
The expand migration ships with release N, while old and new instances run together. When every instance runs release N, migrax generate --contract writes the contract migration, which ships with release N+1. Expand migration Adds and relaxes: safe for the old version. old version new version Both run against the same database. Contract migration Removes and tightens. new version No old instance is left. Release N Release N+1 migrax generate --contract 
$ migrax generate --zero-downtime --rename customer.email=email_address
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0007_rename_customer_email_expand.sql (expand: safe while the old version runs):
  - alter column customer.email
  - add column customer.email_address
  - copy customer.email to email_address and keep both equal (trigger)
Waiting in .migrax/pending/0007_rename_customer_email_contract.sql (contract: for the next release):
  - alter column customer.email_address
  - drop column customer.email
  - remove the trigger that keeps customer.email and email_address equal
Rollback scripts written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback and .migrax/pending/rollback.
src/main/resources/db/migration/0007_rename_customer_email_expand.sql, statement 5: warning MX009
  UPDATE customer SET email_address = email
  This changes every row of the table in one transaction.
  Fix: Add a WHERE clause, or update large tables in batches.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'. When every instance runs this release, run 'migrax generate --contract' for the next one.

The expand migration on PostgreSQL:

ALTER TABLE customer ALTER COLUMN email DROP NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN email_address varchar(255);
CREATE FUNCTION migrax_sync_customer_email_address() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
    IF NEW.email_address IS NULL THEN NEW.email_address := NEW.email; END IF;
    IF NEW.email IS NULL THEN NEW.email := NEW.email_address; END IF;
  ELSIF NEW.email_address IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.email_address THEN
    NEW.email := NEW.email_address;
  ELSIF NEW.email IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.email THEN
    NEW.email_address := NEW.email;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
CREATE TRIGGER migrax_sync_customer_email_address BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE ON customer FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION migrax_sync_customer_email_address();
UPDATE customer SET email_address = email;

The contract migration removes the trigger, makes the new column NOT NULL, and drops the old column:

DROP TRIGGER migrax_sync_customer_email_address ON customer;
DROP FUNCTION migrax_sync_customer_email_address();
ALTER TABLE customer ALTER COLUMN email_address SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE customer DROP COLUMN email;

docs.title: What goes where
docs.text:
Change in the entities Expand migration (this release) Contract migration (next release) Column renamed Add the new column, copy the values, and keep both columns equal with a trigger Remove the trigger, drop the old column, set NOT NULL Table renamed Rename the table, and keep a view with the old name Drop the view Column or table dropped Make the column nullable (the new version doesn't write it) Drop it New NOT NULL column without a default Add it as nullable Set NOT NULL Column becomes NOT NULL Set NOT NULL Type gets wider (longer text, integer to bigint) Change the type Type gets narrower or changes kind Change the type New unique key, foreign key or check Add it Unique key, foreign key or check removed Drop it New table, nullable column, index or sequence Add it Index removed Drop it

When nothing has to wait for the old version, --zero-downtime writes a normal migration.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
This release. Change the entities, then run migrax generate --zero-downtime (with --allow-destructive when something is dropped). Commit the expand migration and the files in .migrax/pending/, and deploy as usual. The expand migration runs, then the new instances start while the old ones still run.

Next release. Once no instance of the old version is left, run:

$ migrax generate --contract
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0009_rename_customer_email_contract.sql.
Release them only when no instance of the version before their expand migration is left.

The contract migration gets the next number and joins the migration folder, with its rollback script. Commit it and deploy. As long as a contract migration is waiting, migrax generate reminds you of it.

Nothing else changes: migrate, the startup integrations and verify treat both migrations like any other.

docs.title: Renamed columns
docs.text:
From the expand migration on, the old version writes the old column and the new version writes the new one. A trigger copies each value to the other column, so both versions see every row. The expand migration also copies the existing values once (UPDATE customer SET email_address = email). On a large table, that update takes time and locks rows: run it in batches if you need to (lint warns about it as MX009).

On MySQL with binary logging (the default), only users with the SUPER privilege can create triggers unless log_bin_trust_function_creators is 1. Set it before the expand migration runs: SET GLOBAL log_bin_trust_function_creators = 1, or in the parameter group on Amazon RDS.

The trigger is written for PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, MySQL, MariaDB and Oracle (TiDB has no triggers). On other databases, --zero-downtime stops with an explanation; rename the column in two releases by hand, or generate without --zero-downtime during a maintenance window.

docs.title: Renamed tables
docs.text: The expand migration renames the table and creates a view with the old name. The old version reads and writes through the view. This works on PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and HSQLDB, whose simple views accept writes.

docs.title: New NOT NULL columns
docs.text:
The old version doesn't know the new column, so its rows have no value there. The column stays nullable until the contract migration, and Migrax adds a note to both migrations:

Note: customer.tier is NOT NULL in the contract migration. Rows written by the old version have no value: fill them before it runs, for example in the expand migration (UPDATE customer SET tier = ... WHERE tier IS NULL).

Give the column a default in the entity instead, and the old version's rows get it.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
Both migrations have rollback scripts. Rolling back the contract migration brings the old column back (filled from the new one, and kept equal by the trigger again). Rolling back the expand migration removes what it added.

Columns the new version doesn't write stay nullable when the expand migration is rolled back: rows written by the new version have no value for them, so NOT NULL would fail. The rollback script says so in a comment.

A widened type is narrowed again by the expand rollback, so values the new version wrote must fit the old type. Oracle narrows a number column only when it is empty (ORA-01440): set it to NULL first, or keep the wider type.

docs.title: What it can't split
docs.text:
• A changed primary key: change it in a migration of its own, without --zero-downtime.
  • --keep-data and --safe can't be combined with --zero-downtime.
  • While the expand migration is applied, the schema has the old names next to the new ones. Hibernate's schema validation accepts that. It doesn't check nullability or column lengths, so a column that becomes NOT NULL or narrower later doesn't stop the new version from starting. A type that changes kind (bigint to integer, text to a number) keeps the old type until the contract migration, which the validation may reject: change such a type in a migration of its own.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to Migrax are listed here. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and versions follow Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• --json output (and the MCP server's replies) writes characters outside ASCII as \u escapes, so an entity, table or column name like Kündé arrives intact when the output is piped on Windows. Before, Windows wrote those characters in its own code page, which is not valid UTF-8, and JSON readers such as the IntelliJ plugin got garbled names.
  • The --rename and --rename-table hints put a name in single quotes when it has characters a shell would interpret, so pasting the hint into a POSIX shell (or PowerShell) can't run part of a name as a command.

docs.title: 0.18.0-rc.1 - 2026-10-31
docs.text: First release candidate for 0.18.0, for testing: it includes everything in 0.17.2-rc.3, adds the entity class to the JSON of plan and check, and makes generate ask about the most likely rename first. It is not on Maven Central: use the CLI from the Download page or the container image ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.18.0-rc.1.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • plan --json and check --json name the entity class and the column of each change (entity, column), so an editor can point at the class that needs a migration. check --json also lists each change as an object in operations; changes stays as it was. entity is filled when the entities are read with Hibernate 5 or newer or by annotation scanning, and is null for the other readers for now, and for join, collection and secondary tables.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• When a column disappears and several new columns of the same type appear, generate now asks about the most similar one first (name -> full_name before name -> country) and, after a "no", asks about the next one. Before, it asked only about the first new column in the table, and the "Possible rename" hint printed without a terminal pointed at that one too. At most three questions are asked per column, and Migrax stops asking when the input ends (Ctrl-D).
  • The container image is built on a newer eclipse-temurin:21-jre, which fixes CVE-2026-111497 in the operating system's Brotli library (libbrotli1).

docs.title: 0.17.2-rc.3 - 2026-10-28
docs.text: Third release candidate for 0.17.2, for testing: fixes the last two findings of the security review of rc.2. It is not on Maven Central: use the CLI from the Download page or the container image ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.2-rc.3.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A password with a raw @ in a //user:password@host URL is now hidden whole, and so is the second password of a multi-host URL (//u1:p1@h1,u2:p2@h2). Before, the part after the first @ showed in doctor, status, connection errors and the other places that print the URL.
  • Hiding the password in a very long, unusual JDBC URL no longer takes seconds (26 seconds measured for a 160 KB URL, 11 seconds for a 150 KB Oracle one; now under 30 milliseconds).

docs.title: 0.17.2-rc.2 - 2026-10-28
docs.text: Second release candidate for 0.17.2, for testing: fixes from the security review of rc.1. It is not on Maven Central: use the CLI from the Download page or the container image ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.2-rc.2.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The throwaway database that verify and a schema file start in Docker is now reachable only from your own machine (port published on 127.0.0.1). Before, other machines on the same network could connect to it while it ran, with its fixed password.
  • To pick the version of its throwaway PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB database, verify connects once to the database configured for the project (URL from the environment or the application's config) when you give neither --url nor --image. It only reads the server's version, and it moves on to the version recorded in the snapshot, or the default image, when the server can't be reached.
  • When the configured database doesn't answer, verify now waits at most 10 seconds while asking it which database and version it is, instead of the driver's default (21 to 36 seconds measured on MySQL). A connect timeout in the JDBC URL is kept. Other commands still wait as long as the driver does, so a slow server is never taken for another database.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The database password was shown in plain text when the JDBC URL carried it:
  • clean printed the URL as it was, with any password in it.
  • diff, environments and the MCP server's environments tool (which sends it to the AI assistant), as well as doctor, status, init, the report HTML file, @MigraxTest and connection error messages, missed some forms: Oracle's user/password@host (also quoted), a SQL Server password in braces that contains ;, and a password containing @ in a URL with a port.

These are now shown as ***, as are MySQL's password1= to password3=, SQL Server's pwd=, keyStoreSecret= and aadSecurePrincipalSecret=, and an SQLCipher key= in a SQLite URL. Such output often ends up in CI logs and kept reports: if you used these URL forms, consider changing the password. - new and generate numbered the next migration wrongly after a migration with a number above 2147483647, such as 4294967297_x.sql: the number wrapped around, so the new file could get a small number and run before the others, and a numbered file that long made generate stop with an error. They now count on from any number, also from date-style ones such as V20261027120000__x.sql. The refusal of Java migrations numbered above 1073741823 in 0.17.2-rc.1 is gone too: such a number is simply followed. - With several databases, migrax new --java --database <name> and the CLI's Java migrations for that database used the package db.migration of the default database. They now use db.<name>, as the startup integrations and the documentation do. If you keep that database's Java migrations in db.migration, set migrax.databases.<name>.java-package. - The Java migration package (--java-package, migrax.java-package) is refused when it contains invisible characters such as control characters, which Java allows in names but which hide in folder names. - verify stopped with error[MXE000]: For input string: ... when the server version recorded in .migrax/snapshot.json was a number too large to read, for example in a hand-edited snapshot. It now ignores that version and uses the default image.

docs.title: 0.17.2-rc.1 - 2026-10-27
docs.text: Release candidate for 0.17.2, for testing: Java migration numbering, the order of column drops, verify in the server's version and the Quarkus startup metrics. It is not on Maven Central: use the CLI from the Download page or the container image ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:0.17.2-rc.1.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• verify starts its throwaway PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB container in the version of your database server when Migrax can reach it, as reading a schema file already did, so the migrations are proven on the version they will run on. Before, it always used its default image (postgres:16-alpine for PostgreSQL). --image still picks another one.
  • generate and diff now drop columns after adding and changing the table's other columns. MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle and H2 commit each schema change at once, so when a later statement of a migration failed, for example making a new column NOT NULL while it still has empty rows, the old column and its data were already gone. Now the migration stops while they are still there. The order of the summary lines changes the same way, and so can the name of the generated file.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• generate gave its file the number of a Java migration written with migrax new --java when that number was the highest one, because it counted only SQL files. Both migrations then ran in an order nobody chose (the SQL file first). Java migrations now count, and generate, check and doctor report a SQL file and a Java migration that share a number, with how to fix it: rename the one that is not applied yet. A project that already has such a pair fails check (exit code 1) until then, unless both are applied in its database.
  • migrax new --java refuses a --java-package or migrax.java-package that is not a Java package name. A value such as /tmp/x or ..x made it write the class outside the project. With a comma list of packages, the class goes into the first one.
  • Quarkus: the migrax.migrations.applied and migrax.migrations.failed counters and the migrax.run timer of the migrations at startup could stay at 0 in the application's registries (Prometheus, OTLP, ...), depending on the order in which Quarkus ran its startup steps. They now always count the startup run.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Every GitHub release lists the libraries it contains in migrax-<version>-sbom.cdx.json (CycloneDX), and each of its files has a signed record of the workflow run that built it: gh attestation verify <file> -R fsmutimeer/migrax checks it. The container image carries its own software list and build record in the registry. See Download > Check your download.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Renaming a table no longer needs --allow-destructive. Hibernate's foreign key names contain the table name, so generate --rename-table (or answering "yes" to "Did you rename table ...?") dropped the old key and added it again under its new name, and the drop was counted as a destructive change. A foreign key that comes back unchanged under a new name in the same migration is no longer destructive; one that is really removed or changed still is. It is listed as "rename foreign key ..." ("kind": "rename_foreign_key" in plan --json and diff --json). On PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB and H2 the migration renames the key (RENAME CONSTRAINT); other databases drop it and add it again, which checks every row.
  • SQLite: the rollback of a table rename lost the other changes to that table (a renamed foreign key, a changed column). SQLite makes them by rebuilding the table, and the rollback looked the table up under the name it gives back only afterwards, so the rebuild was left out without a word. It is now rebuilt under that name, and a table that can't be found stops migrax generate with an error instead.
  • Oracle: making a NUMBER column smaller (fewer decimals or fewer digits before the point, bigint to integer included) failed with ORA-01440 once the table had rows, in a migration or in the rollback of one that made it larger. Oracle allows that only on an empty column, so the change now goes through a new column: first a check that every value fits unchanged (a value with too many digits or decimals stops the migration with a message saying how many, before the column is changed, and so does an index, constraint or column grant made by hand that dropping the column would remove), then the new column is added, a trigger keeps it up to date while the application goes on writing, the values are copied and checked once more, the old column is dropped (writes fail for a moment there) and the new one gets its name, default, NOT NULL and comment. The table is rewritten and the column moves to its end; the migration account needs CREATE TRIGGER. Columns in a key, index, unique constraint or check, and identity columns, keep the plain change, which Oracle still refuses once they have values (see Reference > Limitations).

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Container image: newer JDBC drivers without known vulnerabilities. PostgreSQL 42.7.5 to 42.7.14 (could fall back to weaker authentication despite channelBinding=require, and a server could make it spend CPU on SCRAM), MariaDB 3.5.1 to 3.5.11 (could send the password in clear text to a server in the middle), SQL Server 12.8.1 to 13.6.1 (did not check some input from the server well enough). URLs with encrypt and trustServerCertificate work as before (tested on SQL Server 2022). The CLI download bundles no drivers and is not affected.
  • Container image: the base images are pinned to exact versions, so every build of a release ships the same thing, and /usr/bin/pebble, a program of the base image that Migrax never runs and that scanners report, is removed.
  • The published POMs no longer name library versions with known vulnerabilities (Micrometer, OpenTelemetry, Spring Boot). Migrax never bundled them: your application keeps its own versions, and the framework versions Migrax works with are unchanged.
  • The GitHub Action (uses: fsmutimeer/migrax@...) runs the actions it uses at exact commits instead of version tags, so a moved or compromised tag can't change what runs in your workflow.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Spring Data JDBC: projects without JPA that use Spring Data JDBC (3.0 to 4.1, Spring Boot 3.0 to 4.1) get generate, check, verify, drift and the startup migration like JPA projects. Migrax reads Spring Data JDBC's own mapping, without a database: aggregate roots are the classes with @Table and the types of repositories, and their child tables get the back-reference and key columns Spring Data JDBC names (@MappedCollection), with a foreign key to the parent. Found by itself when the project has no JPA entities, or chosen with --extractor spring-data-jdbc. Names written in @Table or @Column keep their letter case where an unquoted name would get another one (lower case on H2, Oracle, HSQLDB and Derby, capitals on PostgreSQL), as Spring Data JDBC sends them quoted. See Reference > Entity readers.
  • Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC: projects with @MappedEntity entities (Micronaut Data 4 and 5) get generate, check, verify and drift like JPA projects. Migrax reads the mapping Micronaut's annotation processor compiled, without a database, and follows Micronaut Data's rules for names, join tables, embedded values and generated ids (identity, sequences, UUIDs). Found by itself when the project has no JPA entities, or chosen with --extractor micronaut-data. Micronaut 5 projects need Migrax running on Java 25; Migrax names the Java a project needs when it can't load its classes. See Reference > Entity readers.
  • migrax environments: every environment's migrations side by side, read-only. For each migrax.environments.<name>.url (dev, staging, production, ...) it shows how many migrations are applied and pending, the last one applied and whether the schema drifted from the snapshot; -- migrax:env migrations count only where they run. All databases are asked at once with --timeout, so one that doesn't answer only marks its own row. Exit code 1 when an environment can't be reached or a migration failed, changed or is missing there, 2 on drift; --json for dashboards. Error MXE116 when none is configured. See Guides > Comparing databases.
  • Migrations from a SQL file instead of entities: with migrax.schema-file=db/schema.sql (--schema-file, MIGRAX_SCHEMA_FILE, or migrax.databases.<name>.schema-file), a project without JPA entities keeps its tables as they should be in one SQL file, and generate writes the migration and its rollback script from the changes, with rename questions, lint and --zero-downtime as for entities. plan, check, verify and doctor read the file too. Migrax reads it by applying it to a throwaway database (in memory, Docker, or an empty one given with --scratch-url) and keeps what it read in .migrax/schema-model.json, so check in CI needs no Docker while the file is unchanged. A statement that fails is named with its line (error MXE115). On PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB the throwaway database runs the server's own version, so a file written by pg_dump --schema-only or mysqldump --no-data applies as it is. See Guides > SQL migrations for any language and Guides > Schema file from your ORM (SQLAlchemy, Drizzle, and any ORM through a dump).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• migrax clean drops tables and sequences whose names keep their letter case: names with capitals on PostgreSQL, or lower-case names created in quotes on H2 and Oracle. Before, it stopped with "table does not exist".
  • The Spring Boot starter now works on Spring Boot 4. Spring Boot 4 moved the classes the starter was ordered against, so it didn't run at all: no migrations at startup, and a JPA application with ddl-auto=validate failed with a missing table. The migrax health component works with Spring Boot 4's Actuator too.
  • migrax-micronaut now works on Micronaut 4.0 to 4.9. Before, those versions skipped it without an error: no migrations at startup, and the application failed on a missing table. Micronaut 4.10 and 5 work as before.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Drift at startup: migrax.drift.check=warn or fail makes the application compare the database with the schema its migrations produce when it starts, in the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations (migrax.databases.<name>.drift.check per database). warn logs every difference, fail stops the start; the default is off. The build puts .migrax/snapshot.json into the application: the Quarkus extension (also native) and the Gradle plugin do it by themselves, Maven with the new goal migrax:package-snapshot. See Guides > Production safety > Drift at startup.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• history and pending can't be names of further databases (migrax.databases.<name>): the migrax command keeps the default database's files in .migrax/history/ and .migrax/pending/, next to each further database's .migrax/<name>/.
  • migrax-integrations and migrax-quarkus-parent are no longer published to Maven Central: they only group modules for the build, and no published artifact refers to them.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Several databases per application: a block migrax.databases.<name>.* (data source, folders, Java package, schemas, placeholders) migrates a further database at startup, in the Spring Boot, Quarkus (also native), Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations. Health checks report every database. See Guides > Several databases.
  • --database <name> on every command that works on a project (and -Dmigrax.database for the Maven goals, MIGRAX_DATABASE): the command works on that database, with its own connection, folders, entity package (migrax.databases.<name>.package) and snapshot in .migrax/<name>/. The default database no longer reads the entities of another database's package.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Every metric has the tag database (default, or the name of a further database), and spans the attribute migrax.database. Queries without the tag keep working.
  • A migration folder without a prefix (migrax.locations=db/sql, --locations db/sql) is now a classpath folder (under src/main/resources) for the migrax command and the Maven and Gradle goals too, the same as when the application migrates at startup. Before, the command looked for it in the project folder. Write filesystem:db/sql for a folder outside the resources; absolute paths are unchanged.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• migrax.migrate-at-startup=false in the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations: the application starts without migrating, for teams whose pipeline or DBA runs the migrations, and logs what is pending; the health check keeps reporting.
  • Gauge migrax.migrations.pending (migrax_migrations_pending): how many migrations wait to run, in the same integrations when the application has Micrometer. Off with migrax.metrics.enabled=false. See Guides > Metrics and tracing.
  • migrax diff <source-url>: compares the schema of another database of the same kind (for example staging) with the project's database and lists the changes that would make it match; --sql prints them as a script, --json for tools, exit code 2 when they differ. Also mvn migrax:diff. See Guides > Comparing databases.
  • GitLab CI and Bitbucket Pipelines templates: check, lint of new or changed migrations, the HTML report as an artifact, and a comment on the merge or pull request (updated on each pipeline). See Guides > Continuous integration.
  • Published on Maven Central: the library and Maven plugin org.migrax:migrax, the framework integrations, migrax-junit and the Gradle plugin org.migrax, with sources, javadoc and signatures. Builds no longer need to install Migrax from the source first.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Migrax is now licensed under the Apache License 2.0 (with a NOTICE file). Releases up to 0.13.0 keep the MIT License they were published with.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• generate no longer drops and re-adds a check constraint whose condition differs only in spacing or in parentheses around the whole condition (databases store conditions their own way, for example Derby).
  • Check conditions read from MySQL keep valid SQL quotes (MySQL reports '' as \'\'), and MySQL, MariaDB and TiDB primary keys are no longer named PRIMARY when Migrax writes them back.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Metrics and tracing of migrations at startup: Micrometer metrics (migrax.run, migrax.migration, migrax.migrations.applied/failed, migrax.lock.wait) and OpenTelemetry spans (migrax migrate with a migrax migration span each), recorded by the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon and Jakarta EE integrations when the application has a MeterRegistry or an OpenTelemetry. Turn them off with migrax.metrics.enabled=false or migrax.tracing.enabled=false. MigrationListener beans hear every run too, and the Java API takes listeners with listener(...). See Guides > Metrics and tracing.
  • Preconditions: a -- migrax:require line makes a migration check the database before it runs (table-exists, table-missing, column-exists, column-missing, or sql <query>). An unmet condition stops the run (MXE114), or with else skip records the migration without running it. status and migrate --dry-run show the conditions of pending migrations; migrate --sql checks them for the first migration and stops before later ones.
Four more databases: YugabyteDB, TiDB, HSQLDB and Apache Derby.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• YugabyteDB (2024.2 and newer), the 9th database: dialect yugabytedb, reached with the PostgreSQL driver (recognized from the server) or YugabyteDB's own driver. It writes PostgreSQL's SQL; the migration lock is PostgreSQL's advisory lock from 2025.1 on and a row in migrax_lock before. verify starts a throwaway YugabyteDB container, and --zero-downtime works as on PostgreSQL.
  • TiDB (7.5 and newer), the 10th database: dialect tidb, reached with the MySQL driver and recognized from the server. It writes MySQL's SQL; check constraints need tidb_enable_check_constraint (migrax doctor warns when it is off), --keep-data backs up with CREATE TABLE ... LIKE, and --zero-downtime can't split renames (no triggers or writable views). verify starts a throwaway TiDB container.
  • HSQLDB (HyperSQL 2.7 and newer), the 11th database: dialect hsqldb, recognized from jdbc:hsqldb: URLs. The migration lock is a row in migrax_lock, so it also holds across processes for file and server databases; verify replays the migrations in memory.
  • Apache Derby (10.16 and newer), the 12th database: dialect derby, recognized from jdbc:derby: URLs. Type changes Derby can't make in place rebuild the column, comments are left out (Derby keeps none), and verify replays the migrations in memory.
Zero-downtime changes and an HTML report.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• generate --zero-downtime splits a change so the old and the new application version can use the database at the same time: an expand migration for this release (new columns still nullable, a renamed column copied and kept equal to the old one by a trigger, a renamed table's old name kept as a view, wider types) and a contract migration for the next release (drops, NOT NULL, narrower types, new constraints). The contract migration waits in .migrax/pending/ until generate --contract adds it to the migration folder. Column renames need PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB or Oracle; table renames also work on SQL Server. See Guides > Zero-downtime changes.
  • migrax report (and mvn migrax:report) writes one HTML page for reviews and CI artifacts: the schema with a diagram, entity changes without a migration, every migration with its status and lint findings, and drift. The GitHub Action uploads it as the artifact migrax-report and links it from its pull request comment (report: false turns it off).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Lint rules MX007 (drops) and MX008 (renames) name generate --zero-downtime as the fix.
A Java API, and a JUnit 5 extension that checks migrations against the entities.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• A Java API, org.migrax.api.Migrax: Migrax.configure().dataSource(ds).load(), then migrate(), status(), rollback(steps), rollbackTo(version), validate() (do the entities match the database?) and testRollbacks(). The startup integrations run on it.
  • migrax-junit, a JUnit 5 extension: @MigraxTest migrates a test database (H2, a DataSource or a Testcontainers container) before the tests and fails them when the entities don't match the migrated schema. With rollbacks = true it also tests every rollback script. See Guides > Java API and JUnit tests.
Every rollback script tested on its own, and Oracle 23ai support.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • verify tests every rollback script on its own: it rolls the migration back, applies it again and checks that the schema is the same, and it names the script when that fails. Before, it only checked the end result, which missed a script that left something behind when an older script removed it anyway (an index on a table dropped later).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• On Oracle 23ai, boolean fields become boolean columns, as Hibernate expects there, instead of number(1,0). Migrax asks the database for its version and records it in the snapshot for commands that run without a connection. Older Oracle versions keep number(1,0).
  • verify without --url works on Oracle: the throwaway container's port was never published, so it could not connect. It now starts Oracle Free 23ai for a 23ai project and Oracle XE 21 otherwise, with its own user instead of system.
  • verify on Oracle no longer reports Hibernate's temporary tables (hte_...) as left behind after rolling everything back: schema validation doesn't create them anymore.
  • With Oracle's JDBC driver 23, a failed connection no longer prints the driver's trace (a stack trace with the PATH and Java settings) to the console; --verbose still shows it.
Hibernate 4.0 and 4.1 read through their own mapping, and installs with Homebrew and Scoop.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Hibernate 4.0 and 4.1 projects are read through Hibernate's own mapping, like 4.2 and newer, and verify has them validate the schema. Both versions are tested on every change.
  • Install with Homebrew on macOS and Linux (brew install fsmutimeer/migrax/migrax) or with Scoop on Windows (scoop bucket add migrax https://github.com/fsmutimeer/scoop-migrax, then scoop install migrax). Every stable release updates both.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The Migrax GitHub Action uses actions/setup-java@v6 and actions/github-script@v8, which run on Node 24, so workflows that use it no longer show Node 20 deprecation warnings.
The 0.7 release removes three more limitations: --schemas works on SQL Server, --keep-data keeps data of tables without a primary key, and Hibernate 4.2 and 4.3 are read through their own mapping.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• --schemas works on SQL Server. SQL Server can't switch a connection to another schema, so Migrax names the schema instead: each schema gets its own migrax_history, and in a project that sets migrax.schemas, generate writes every table as ${migrax.schema}.<table>. migrate, status, rollback, migrate --sql, clean and the startup integrations all work per schema.
  • ${migrax.schema}: a built-in placeholder for the schema a migration runs in, on every database.
  • Lint rule MX017: on SQL Server with migrax.schemas, a table without its schema in front.
  • generate --keep-data keeps dropped and narrowed columns of tables without a primary key. It finds the rows again by a unique key whose columns are NOT NULL, or else by all their other columns; generate warns in that case, because rows that are the same in every other column get one value back for all of them.
  • Hibernate 4.2 and 4.3 are read through their own mapping, like Hibernate 5 and newer, and verify has them validate the schema. Spring Boot 1's spring.jpa.hibernate.naming-strategy is read too. Older versions are still read from their annotations.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Oracle packages, package and type bodies, and anonymous blocks (BEGIN ... END;, DECLARE ... BEGIN ... END;) no longer need a line with only / after them: Migrax finds where they end, as it already did for procedures, functions and triggers.
  • PostgreSQL and CockroachDB: a migrate --sql script run with psql recorded applied_at in the server's time zone, so migrax status could show it hours before the migrations Migrax applied itself. The script now records the time in the same zone as Migrax.
  • verify: when a migration fails on the throwaway database, the error says that the migration fails on an empty database and what to check. It used to give the advice for a real database (inspect it, repair, resume), which doesn't apply there.

The 0.6 release removes most of Migrax's limitations: EclipseLink and OpenJPA are read through their own mapping like Hibernate (now from 5.0), Quarkus migrates before Hibernate and in native executables, Jakarta EE servers migrate their own data sources, and --keep-data rollbacks restore dropped data.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Quarkus: migrax-quarkus is now a Quarkus extension. It applies the migrations before Hibernate starts, so quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=validate works, and it runs in native executables. The dependency stays the same; Quarkus fetches the new migrax-quarkus-deployment artifact itself. The readiness check is added only when the application has the health extension, so the build warning about HealthCheck is gone. Migrations are listed when the application is built: set migrax.locations before the build.
  • generate --keep-data keeps the data a migration drops, and its rollback script restores it: a dropped table is renamed to a migrax_backup_* table and renamed back, and a dropped or narrowed column is copied there with the table's primary key and filled again row by row. The new migrax backups command lists the backup tables and drops them (--drop, --yes). Tested on all 8 databases.
  • OpenJPA: projects that use OpenJPA (Apache TomEE's JPA provider) are read through OpenJPA's own mapping too: its names, the indexes it puts on foreign keys, identity columns, sequences and OPENJPA_SEQUENCE_TABLE. Tested with OpenJPA 3.2 and 4.1, and on PostgreSQL and MySQL; --extractor openjpa forces it.
  • EclipseLink: projects that use EclipseLink are read through EclipseLink's own mapping, as Hibernate projects are through Hibernate's: its names, its join and collection tables, and its id strategies, including the SEQUENCE table and rows a plain @GeneratedValue needs. Before, they were read with Hibernate's rules and EclipseLink failed at runtime. Tested with EclipseLink 2.7, 3.0 and 4.0, and on PostgreSQL and MySQL. --extractor eclipselink forces it. The database reader also recognizes H2's BINARY LARGE OBJECT and CHARACTER LARGE OBJECT columns, which made the first generate change @Lob columns on H2.
  • Jakarta EE: the new migrax-jakarta-ee integration applies the migrations when the application starts on the server, to the data source persistence.xml names as the server provides it (or migrax.datasource), so the connection isn't configured twice. Tested on WildFly and Payara. Migrations and Java migrations are also found in WildFly's virtual file system.
  • Hibernate 5.0 to 5.3 are read through their own mapping and validate the schema in verify, like 5.4 and newer, instead of annotation scanning. 5.0 to 5.2 need JAXB in the project on Java 11 and newer; without it Migrax falls back as before and says what is missing. The Hibernate compatibility tests now cover 19 versions.
  • SQL Server migrations can repeat a batch with GO 5, as in SQL Server's own tools.
  • migrate --sql works with --schemas: the script has a section per schema that switches to it first. When a Java migration is pending, the script now stops before it and says how to go on, instead of refusing to write anything.
  • CockroachDB: a migration that changes a column type in a way CockroachDB can't do in place (anything but widening) turns on CockroachDB's setting for it and runs outside a transaction, as CockroachDB requires. Before, such migrations failed until edited by hand.
  • migrax doctor warns when the entities declare check constraints and the server is MySQL before 8.0.16, which accepts them without enforcing them.
  • Procedures, functions and triggers no longer need GO, DELIMITER or / lines: Migrax ends the statement with the END that closes the body's first BEGIN. Scripts with those lines work as before. New lint rule MX016 warns when a body has an unmatched BEGIN and so takes in the statements after it.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The first generate on an existing database saw a fixed-length BINARY(n) column as varbinary and wrote a change for it, for example for the binary(255) columns Hibernate 5 writes on H2. The database reader now keeps the column's real type.
  • On a database Hibernate created, an @Check without a name was added a second time by the first generate, because the database had given the existing check a name of its own. Migrax now recognizes the check by its condition and keeps the database's name.
The 0.5 release: check constraints and comments in generated migrations, stored procedures and triggers in SQL migrations, and more control over what migrate runs and where.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• generate writes check constraints and comments: Hibernate's @Check, @Checks and @Comment, and the check and comment attributes of Jakarta Persistence 3.2's @Table and @Column, on all 8 databases (SQLite keeps no comments). A changed condition drops the old check and adds the new one, and --safe adds checks on PostgreSQL and CockroachDB without blocking writes. The checks Hibernate 6+ derives from enum columns are generated only with migrax.enum-checks=true. Projects that already use these annotations get them in their next generated migration; remove any that a hand-written migration added before.
  • migrate --sql (Maven: -Dmigrax.sql=true) prints one SQL script with everything migrate would do, for a DBA to review and run with psql, mysql, sqlcmd or sqlplus: the pending migrations, the history rows Migrax records, transactions where the database has them, and each tool's end markers. Nothing changes until the script runs.
  • Migrations for some environments only: a -- migrax:env dev,test line makes a migration run only where --env, MIGRAX_ENV or migrax.env names one of them. Elsewhere status shows it as skipped ([-], state SKIPPED in --json), and health checks don't count it as pending.
  • Several migration folders: --locations, MIGRAX_LOCATIONS and migrax.locations take a comma-separated list (CLI, Maven, Gradle and the startup integrations). Files run in version order across all folders; new files go into the first one.
  • migrax baseline <migration> --yes (Maven: migrax:baseline) adopts a database whose tables already exist: it records the migrations up to the named one as applied without running them, so migrate only runs the later ones.
  • migrate --to <migration> (Maven: -Dmigrax.to=...) applies versioned migrations only up to and including the named one, for staged rollouts. The name can be the file name, its start, or the version number (--to 5). Repeatable migrations wait for the next migrate without --to.
  • Migrations can contain stored procedures, functions and triggers: a line with only GO ends a SQL Server batch, DELIMITER lines change the MySQL/MariaDB delimiter, and a line with only / ends an Oracle PL/SQL block (also usable for SQLite triggers). -- migrax:no-split sends a whole file as one statement. migrate, rollback, lint and verify all split this way.
  • Guides > Without Java entities: how to apply hand-written SQL migrations with Migrax in projects without JPA entities (Python, Node.js, other languages): drivers, connection settings, the container image and rollback scripts.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • The documentation moved to https://migrax.org/; the old address https://docs-migrax.github.io/ redirects there. The site has a new black, white and yellow look.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • migrax doctor no longer fails in projects without Java, such as the container image or a Python or Node.js project with hand-written migrations: when there is no pom.xml, build.gradle or entity package but there are migrations, it checks only the migrations and the database. Without migrations it still reports the missing build file, so a Java project opened in the wrong folder is still caught.
The 0.4 release: Migrax moves to org.migrax. Nothing else changes in how it works; see below for the one-line upgrade.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Migrax now lives under org.migrax (the project's domain is migrax.org): the Maven groupId, the Gradle plugin ID and the Java packages all change from io.migrax to org.migrax. Commands, options, configuration keys, environment variables, migration files, the snapshot and the database tables are unchanged. The migration lock has a new name too, so a 0.3 and a 0.4 instance don't wait for each other: during the upgrade, make sure only one of them runs migrations against a database at a time.

To upgrade, replace io.migrax with org.migrax in your build:

  • Maven: <groupId>org.migrax</groupId> for the plugin and the integrations.
  • Gradle: plugins { id("org.migrax") version "..." } and org.migrax:... dependencies.
  • Java migrations: import org.migrax.api.JavaMigration;.
  • Logging configuration: the logger is now org.migrax.

The 0.3 release: Migrax in containers and Kubernetes, machine-readable output, and AI assistants. It contains everything in the release candidates 0.3.0-rc.1 to 0.3.0-rc.3; the changelog lists each of their changes in detail.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• migrax mcp: a Model Context Protocol server for AI assistants (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, ...). Its tools only read; --allow-generate also lets it write migration files. It never changes a database.
  • The documentation as plain text for AI assistants: llms.txt and llms-full.txt.
  • Container image ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax (amd64 and arm64) with the common JDBC drivers, and Guides > Containers and Kubernetes with tested example manifests.
  • --lock-timeout <time>: wait for the migration lock instead of failing, for instances that start together.
  • Database secrets from files (MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE, --password-file, ...) and JDBC drivers without a project (MIGRAX_DRIVERS or the installation's drivers folder).
  • --json on every command, with failures as JSON too, and stable error codes (MXE...) listed in Reference > Errors and JSON output.
  • Health checks in the Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut and Helidon integrations.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Error lines start with error[<code>]: instead of error:.
  • Guides > Using Migrax with AI assistants: setup for Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Cursor, how to start migrax mcp through cmd on Windows for clients that can't run .cmd scripts, and why the ChatGPT app can't use a local MCP server.

docs.title: 0.3.0-rc.3 - 2026-10-10
docs.text: Third release candidate for 0.3.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.3.0-rc.2 and these changes: Migrax for AI assistants.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• migrax mcp: a Model Context Protocol server, so AI assistants such as Claude Code can call status, check, plan, lint, drift, doctor, verify and show_migration as tools. It never changes a database; --allow-generate also lets it write migration files. Guide: Guides > Using Migrax with AI assistants, with instructions to copy into a project's AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md.
  • The documentation as plain text for AI assistants: llms.txt and llms-full.txt on the docs site.

docs.title: 0.3.0-rc.2 - 2026-10-10
docs.text: Second release candidate for 0.3.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.3.0-rc.1 and these changes: machine-readable results and errors, and health checks.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• --json for migrate, rollback, repair, clean, doctor, new, squash and merge: one result object with ok and exitCode on standard output, progress on standard error. With --json, a failure is also a JSON object.
  • Stable error codes (error[MXE104]: ...), listed in Reference > Errors and JSON output.
  • Health checks in the startup integrations: a migrax health indicator for Spring Boot Actuator and Micronaut, and a readiness check for Quarkus and Helidon; UP when every migration is applied and none failed, was edited or is missing. Each is active only when the application has the framework's health module.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Error lines start with error[<code>]: instead of error:.

docs.title: 0.3.0-rc.1 - 2026-10-10
docs.text: First release candidate for 0.3.0, for testing: running Migrax in containers and Kubernetes.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Container image ghcr.io/fsmutimeer/migrax:<version> (amd64 and arm64) with Migrax and the PostgreSQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite and H2 drivers, for running migrations without a Java project. Guide: Guides > Containers and Kubernetes, with example manifests (Job, init container, Helm hook, nightly drift CronJob) tested on a local Kubernetes cluster.
  • --lock-timeout <time> (MIGRAX_LOCK_TIMEOUT, migrax.lock-timeout in the startup integrations): wait while another process holds the migration lock instead of failing, for instances that start together.
  • Database secrets from files: MIGRAX_DATABASE_PASSWORD_FILE (and _USER_FILE, _URL_FILE) and --password-file, for Kubernetes and Docker secrets.
  • JDBC drivers without a project: every jar in MIGRAX_DRIVERS or the installation's drivers folder is available, after the project's own dependencies.

The 0.2 release: two more databases, a command to start a development database over, and the fixes from 0.1.1 to 0.1.4. It contains everything in the release candidates 0.2.0-rc.1 to 0.2.0-rc.6; the changelog lists each of their changes in detail.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• CockroachDB support (cockroachdb), through the PostgreSQL driver: Migrax recognizes the server by itself, and verify starts a throwaway CockroachDB in Docker.
  • SQLite support (sqlite, SQLite 3.35 and newer): changes SQLite can't make in place rebuild the table with its rows; verify runs on a temporary SQLite file.
  • migrax clean (and mvn migrax:clean) drops every table, view and sequence so migrate can rebuild a development database; MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED=true turns it off.
  • migrax repair <migration>... --action forget --yes removes applied migrations whose files were deleted on purpose.
  • The first generate against a database that already has tables also writes those tables to 0001_baseline.sql, so an empty database can be built from the migrations.
  • Documentation for migrax import flyway|liquibase (Guides > Switching from Flyway or Liquibase), and a Download page with every release's files and SHA-256 checksums.
  • MIT license.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• migrax doctor checks locking by taking and releasing the migration lock.
  • Each database's support, including its migration lock, is one class found with java.util.ServiceLoader; the CLI is one class per command. Commands and output are unchanged.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The first generate against an existing database no longer finds changes that aren't real, on every supported database and with both ways of reading entities.
  • No JVM crash with Java 21 and Hibernate 7.3 or newer.
  • migrax import liquibase includes the entities' sequences in its baseline.

docs.title: 0.2.0-rc.6 - 2026-10-10
docs.text: Sixth release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.5 and these changes.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• CockroachDB support (cockroachdb), through the PostgreSQL driver: Migrax recognizes the server, writes CockroachDB's types, takes its migration lock as a row in migrax_lock, and verify starts a throwaway CockroachDB in Docker. Tested with the real-database suite and Hibernate's schema validation.
  • SQLite support (sqlite, SQLite 3.35 and newer): changes SQLite can't make in place, such as a column's type or a new foreign key, rebuild the table with its rows, and a rebuild that breaks a foreign key fails before it commits. verify runs on a temporary SQLite file.
  • migrax clean (and mvn migrax:clean): drops every table, view and sequence, the migration history included, so migrate can rebuild a development database. It asks first (or needs --yes), --dry-run lists what it would drop, and MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED=true turns it off.
  • Documentation for migrax import flyway|liquibase, with a guide for switching an existing project (Guides > Switching from Flyway or Liquibase).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• migrax import liquibase left the entities' sequences out of the baseline, so a database built from it failed Hibernate's validation; it now reads the database as the first generate does.
  • Hibernate's mapping of a @Lob String as varchar(255) (CockroachDB) is read as text, so long values aren't cut off.
  • Hibernate's bulk-update helper tables (HTE_<table>) are no longer seen as user tables.

docs.title: 0.2.0-rc.5 - 2026-10-10
docs.text: Fifth release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.4 and these fixes (also released for 0.1 as 0.1.4).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The first generate against a database that already has tables wrote only the differences, so an empty database couldn't be built from the migrations and migrax verify failed on the first one ("table doesn't exist"). It now also writes those tables to 0001_baseline.sql and records it as applied in that database without running it; the changes follow as 0002_.... Projects that already have migrations are not changed.
  • H2: the first generate against an existing database wanted to drop the indexes H2 creates for foreign keys (named like fk_..._INDEX_8) and refused as destructive. They are now recognized as part of the foreign key, as on MySQL and MariaDB.

docs.title: 0.2.0-rc.4 - 2026-10-09
docs.text: Fourth release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.3 and these fixes (also released for 0.1 as 0.1.3).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• More changes that weren't real in the first generate against an existing database, found by a new test that runs it on MySQL (also with Windows-style lower-case table names), MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle, reading entities both through Hibernate and by annotation scanning:
  • PostgreSQL: ids that take their value from a sequence were seen as identity columns, and the identity was dropped;
  • SQL Server: varchar(max) and varbinary(max) columns were altered to themselves;
  • MySQL: UUID columns (binary(16)) were altered to themselves; UUID columns are now kept as they are, whether stored natively or as binary;
  • numeric and decimal are treated as the same type.

docs.title: 0.2.0-rc.3 - 2026-10-09
docs.text: Third release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.2 and these changes (also released for 0.1 as 0.1.2).

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • migrax repair <migration>... --action forget --yes removes applied migrations whose files were deleted on purpose from the history; the database keeps their changes. The "files are missing" error now shows the exact command.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The first generate of a project, which compares the entities with the live database, no longer writes changes that aren't real:
  • tables whose names differ only in letter case (categories_seq in the database, categories_SEQ in the entity) on databases that fold names, such as MySQL on Windows, PostgreSQL, H2 and Oracle; this produced a CREATE and a DROP of the same table;
  • the index MySQL and MariaDB create for each foreign key, which was dropped;
  • sequences that already exist, which were created again: real sequences, and the next_val tables MySQL uses instead (sequences the entities don't use, such as those of identity columns, are never touched);
  • columns whose types the database stores the same way, such as an Instant field on MySQL (datetime(6) either way).
  • migrate with an empty migration folder now reports applied migrations whose files were deleted, instead of saying there is nothing to migrate.
  • On Windows, every command printed the path of the old class-data archive (...\migrax\cache\migrax-java21.jsa) and left the file in place: Java creates it read-only. The launcher now removes it silently.

docs.title: 0.2.0-rc.2 - 2026-10-09
docs.text: Second release candidate for 0.2.0, for testing. It contains everything in 0.2.0-rc.1 and this fix.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Migrax crashed (a JVM crash, not an error message) when reading Hibernate 7.3 or newer entities on Java 21. A Java 21 bug (JDK-8391430) breaks the class-data archive the launcher keeps to start faster, so the launcher now keeps it only on Java 25 and newer, and removes archives that earlier versions left behind.
