docs.title: Hibernate settings
docs.text: Hibernate settings in hibernate.*, spring.jpa.properties.*, jpa.default.properties.* (Micronaut), the naming-strategy keys of each framework, and persistence.xml properties are passed to Hibernate when Migrax reads the mapping. Connection and schema-generation settings are left out, because Migrax never connects Hibernate to your database while reading.

docs.title: The .migrax folder
docs.text: File Commit? Purpose snapshot.json yes Schema your migrations produce, with dialect and naming history/ yes Snapshot after each migration <name>/ yes snapshot.json, history/ and pending/ of a further database (--database <name>) classpath.txt, classpath.hash, build.stamp no Build cache; refresh with --refresh .gitignore yes Written by Migrax; ignores the caches

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
Database Dialect name Notes PostgreSQL postgresql Transactional DDL; generate --safe for non-blocking indexes and constraints CockroachDB cockroachdb Through the PostgreSQL driver; recognized from the server (details) YugabyteDB 2024.2 and newer yugabytedb PostgreSQL's SQL; DDL commits immediately (details) MySQL 8 mysql DDL commits immediately; sequences are next_val tables MariaDB mariadb Like MySQL TiDB 7.5 and newer tidb Through the MySQL driver; recognized from the server (details) SQL Server sqlserver Lock through sp_getapplock Oracle 12c and newer oracle Lock needs EXECUTE on DBMS_LOCK; booleans follow the version (details) H2 h2 For development and tests; verify uses it in memory HSQLDB (HyperSQL) 2.7 and newer hsqldb In memory, files or server; verify uses it in memory (details) Apache Derby 10.16 and newer derby Embedded or network server; verify uses it in memory (details) SQLite 3.35 and newer sqlite Changes SQLite can't make in place rebuild the table (details)

The dialect comes from the JDBC URL. When there is no database URL (for example in a CI step that only plans), pass --dialect.

docs.title: CockroachDB
docs.text:
CockroachDB speaks PostgreSQL's protocol, so the project uses the PostgreSQL driver and a jdbc:postgresql://host:26257/database URL. Migrax asks the server which database it is, and the first generate records cockroachdb in the snapshot, so later commands don't have to ask. Without a reachable database, pass --dialect cockroachdb.

What is different from PostgreSQL:

  • 32-bit integers are written as int4, because CockroachDB's integer has 64 bits.
  • @Lob values are text and bytea: CockroachDB has no large objects.
  • Indexes and unique constraints are removed with DROP INDEX table@name.
  • The migration lock is a row in the migrax_lock table, because CockroachDB has no session locks. If a Migrax process is killed while migrating, the row stays and the next migrate says how to remove it.
  • verify starts a throwaway cockroachdb/cockroach container in Docker.

CockroachDB widens a column in place (a longer VARCHAR, INT4 to INT8). Any other type change needs its experimental setting and can't run inside a transaction, so a migration with one starts with -- migrax:no-transaction and SET enable_experimental_alter_column_type_general = true. Its statements then commit one by one: if one fails, the earlier ones stay applied.

docs.title: YugabyteDB
docs.text:
YugabyteDB (its YSQL API) runs PostgreSQL's own SQL layer, so Migrax writes the same SQL as for PostgreSQL. Use the PostgreSQL driver with a jdbc:postgresql://host:5433/database URL, or YugabyteDB's own driver (jdbc:yugabytedb://). With the PostgreSQL driver, Migrax asks the server which database it is and the first generate records yugabytedb in the snapshot. Without a reachable database, pass --dialect yugabytedb.

What is different from PostgreSQL:

  • DDL commits immediately, as on MySQL: a migration that fails halfway leaves its earlier statements applied.
  • The migration lock is PostgreSQL's advisory lock where YugabyteDB has it (2025.1 and newer). On older versions it is a row in the migrax_lock table, as on CockroachDB.
  • There are no large objects, which Hibernate's PostgreSQL mapping uses for @Lob, so saving a @Lob value fails on YugabyteDB. Leave out @Lob: a byte[] field is then bytea, and a long String can be @Column(columnDefinition = "text").
  • generate --safe isn't needed: YugabyteDB builds indexes without blocking writes.
  • verify starts a throwaway yugabytedb/yugabyte container in Docker (about a minute).

Zero-downtime changes (generate --zero-downtime) work as on PostgreSQL, with triggers for renamed columns and views for renamed tables.

docs.title: TiDB
docs.text:
TiDB speaks MySQL's protocol, so the project uses the MySQL driver and a jdbc:mysql://host:4000/database URL. Migrax asks the server which database it is, and the first generate records tidb in the snapshot. Without a reachable database, pass --dialect tidb. Migrax writes the SQL it writes for MySQL, as Hibernate's MySQL dialect maps the entities for TiDB.

What is different from MySQL:

  • Check constraints (@Check, and enum checks with migrax.enum-checks) are only kept with SET GLOBAL tidb_enable_check_constraint = ON; otherwise TiDB ignores them. migrax doctor warns when the entities have checks and the setting is off.
  • --keep-data backs up dropped columns with CREATE TABLE ... LIKE and INSERT ... SELECT, because TiDB has no CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT.
  • There are no triggers and no writable views, so generate --zero-downtime can't split column or table renames on TiDB. Drops, NOT NULL and type changes split as usual.
  • There are no stored procedures.
  • verify starts a throwaway pingcap/tidb container in Docker.

docs.title: HSQLDB
docs.text:
HyperSQL is recognized from jdbc:hsqldb: URLs, in memory (jdbc:hsqldb:mem:), in files or as a server. verify replays the migrations on a new in-memory database, without Docker.

What is different from H2:

  • DDL commits immediately, as on MySQL: a migration that fails halfway leaves its earlier statements applied.
  • The migration lock is a row in the migrax_lock table, so two processes that share a file or server database don't migrate at once. If a Migrax process is killed while migrating, the row stays and the next migrate says how to remove it.
  • Sequence ids have no column default (HyperSQL has no sequence default); Hibernate takes the next value from the sequence itself.
  • Hibernate stores Instant as timestamp on HyperSQL. Projects read by annotation scanning (without a JPA provider) get timestamp with time zone for it, so prefer reading the entities through Hibernate there.
  • generate --zero-downtime keeps a renamed table's old name as a view (HyperSQL's simple views accept writes). Column renames can't be split: Migrax writes no triggers for HyperSQL.

docs.title: Derby
docs.text:
Apache Derby is recognized from jdbc:derby: URLs, embedded (jdbc:derby:memory: or a folder) or through its network server. verify replays the migrations on a new in-memory database, without Docker. Derby 10.16 runs on Java 17; 10.17 needs Java 21.

What is different:

  • Derby keeps no comments: @Comment texts are left out of the migrations.
  • Derby changes a column's type in place only to lengthen a VARCHAR, CLOB or BLOB. Any other type change rebuilds the column: a new column of the new type, the values copied, the old column dropped and the new one renamed, then NOT NULL and the indexes, keys and checks on it come back. The column moves to the end of the table. A primary key column can't be rebuilt this way.
  • Sequence ids have no column default (Derby has none); Hibernate takes the next value from the sequence itself. Decimals have at most 31 digits.
  • UUID fields are char(16) for bit data, as Hibernate stores them on Derby.
  • The migration lock is a row in the migrax_lock table, so processes that share a network server don't migrate at once.
  • Stored procedures are Java methods in Derby, so migrations can't define them in SQL.
  • With Hibernate 7, Derby's Hibernate dialect is in hibernate-community-dialects, which the project then needs (Hibernate 6 has it built in).
  • generate --zero-downtime can't split renames on Derby (no triggers or writable views).

docs.title: Oracle
docs.text:
Migrax's migration lock uses DBMS_LOCK, so the account that runs the migrations needs GRANT EXECUTE ON SYS.DBMS_LOCK TO <user>. Making a NUMBER column smaller in a table with rows uses a trigger for a moment, so it also needs CREATE TRIGGER (CREATE ANY TRIGGER when --schemas points at another schema).

Oracle 23ai has a boolean type, and Hibernate uses it there, while on older versions a boolean field is a number(1,0) column. Migrax asks the database for its version and writes what your Hibernate expects on it. The first generate records the version in the snapshot ("server": "23.26"), so commands without a database connection, such as verify in CI, write the same types. verify starts Oracle Free 23ai for a 23ai project and Oracle XE 21 otherwise, in Docker.

Moving an existing database to 23ai doesn't change its columns: number(1,0) columns stay, and new ones are boolean. If your application validates its schema with Hibernate, change the old columns in a migration of your own.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
Use the org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc driver and a jdbc:sqlite:path/to/app.db URL. With Hibernate 6 or newer, add org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-community-dialects (the same version as Hibernate): it has Hibernate's SQLite dialect, which Migrax uses to read the entity mapping.

SQLite adds, renames and drops columns, renames tables and creates indexes in place. Any other change to an existing table (a column's type, length or NOT NULL, a primary key, a foreign key, a unique or check constraint) is made by rebuilding the table, as SQLite's documentation describes: Migrax writes a migration that creates the new table, copies the rows, drops the old table, renames the new one and recreates its indexes. A rebuilt table's foreign keys are checked before the migration commits; if a row breaks one, the migration fails and nothing changes.

Good to know:

  • An identity id is declared integer: in SQLite only an integer primary key fills itself. Other whole-number columns are int or bigint; SQLite stores them all the same way.
  • SQLite has no sequences: Hibernate keeps the next value in a one-row table, which Migrax creates with its starting value.
  • The migration lock is a file next to the database (app.db.migrax-lock). While Migrax migrates, its own connection has foreign key enforcement off, because SQLite can only rebuild a table that others refer to that way; it is switched back on afterwards.
  • verify runs on a temporary SQLite file, no Docker needed. It compares the schema with Migrax's own check instead of Hibernate's validation, because Hibernate's validator rejects the integer id columns that its own SQLite dialect creates.
  • SQLite has no schemas: --schema and --schemas don't apply.
  • SQLite keeps no table or column comments, so @Comment is left out of its migrations.
  • Hibernate can't load @Lob fields through the SQLite driver; prefer plain String and byte[] fields.

The JDBC driver comes from your project's dependencies, so Migrax always uses the driver version your application uses.

docs.title: Column types
docs.text: When Hibernate is in the project, column types are whatever your Hibernate version chooses for your database. The same entity can map differently: an Instant is a timestamp(6) with time zone with Hibernate 6 on PostgreSQL and a timestamp with Hibernate 5; a boolean is bit on MySQL. Migrax records the exact type, so generate, verify and drift all agree with the application.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Each migration runs in a transaction with its history record. On PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, SQL Server, H2, Derby and SQLite, a failed migration leaves nothing behind. MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB, Oracle, YugabyteDB and HSQLDB commit DDL statements immediately, so a migration that fails halfway leaves the earlier statements applied; see Rollbacks and recovery.

Statements that cannot run in a transaction, such as PostgreSQL's CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, need -- migrax:no-transaction at the top of the migration.

docs.title: Testing against real engines
docs.text:
The Migrax build includes a suite that runs migrations and Hibernate validation against real MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB (7.5 and 8.5), PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle (XE 21 and Free 23ai), CockroachDB and YugabyteDB (2024.2 and 2026.1) containers, and on HSQLDB, Derby and SQLite:

mvn verify -Pdatabase-integration    # needs Docker

Run it with your production engine version before you rely on a new database version.

docs.title: Errors and JSON output
docs.text: Every command can report its result as JSON with --json, and every error has a stable code. Scripts, CI jobs and AI assistants can act on both without reading the text.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text:
With --json, a command prints exactly one JSON value on standard output. Progress messages ("Applying migration ...") go to standard error, so standard output stays parseable.

These commands print a result object with ok (true when the exit code is 0), exitCode and the command's own fields:

Command Fields migrate schemas: one entry per schema with schema, applied, total; with --dry-run, wouldApply (the pending migrations) rollback schemas: schema, rolledBack (or wouldRollBack with --dry-run) repair action; repaired or forgotten (the migrations) clean schemas: schema, dropped (or wouldDrop with --dry-run) with tables, views, sequences doctor checks (each with status: ok, info, warn or fail, message, fix), failures, warnings new, squash created; squash also replaces merge renamed (each with from, to), snapshotRebuilt 
$ migrax migrate --json 2>/dev/null
{"ok":true,"exitCode":0,"schemas":[{"schema":null,"applied":1,"total":1}]}

status, plan, check, drift, lint, verify and init keep the JSON shapes they had before 0.3.0; see their sections in the CLI reference.

Each change in plan --json (operations) and check --json (operations, next to the plain-text changes) names its kind, table, column (null when the change is not about one column) and entity: the class of the entity that maps the table, such as com.example.Customer. Editors and other tools use it to point at the class. entity is null for a dropped table, for tables no entity class maps directly (join, collection and secondary tables), for a schema file, and when the entities are read with Hibernate 4, EclipseLink, OpenJPA, Spring Data JDBC or Micronaut Data. A single-table hierarchy names its root class.

$ migrax check --json    # one line, wrapped here
{"ok":false,"changes":["add column orders.notes"],"operations":[{"kind":"add_column",
"summary":"add column orders.notes","table":"orders","column":"notes",
"entity":"com.example.Order"}],"conflicts":[]}

docs.title: When a command fails
docs.text:
With --json, a failure is also one JSON object on standard output, with the exit code 1:

{"ok":false,"exitCode":1,"error":{"code":"MXE104","message":"Checksum changed for applied migration 0001_initial.sql","hint":"..."}}

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Error (see the error code) 2 Changes or drift found (check, drift)

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text:
Errors print as error[MXE104]: <message> followed by a hint. A code never changes its meaning; new situations get new codes.

Code Meaning What to do MXE000 Unexpected error Run again with --verbose and report it with the output MXE001 Wrong command, option or input Read the hint; migrax help <command> lists the options MXE101 Another process holds the migration lock Wait, or use --lock-timeout so instances wait for each other MXE102 A migration failed Fix the migration; on databases without transactional DDL, check what was applied, then repair MXE103 A failed migration must be repaired first Inspect the database, then migrax repair <migration> --action applied (or retry) MXE104 An applied migration file was changed Restore the file; write a new migration for new changes MXE105 An applied migration file is missing Restore it, or migrax repair <migration> --action forget --yes if you deleted it on purpose MXE106 No JDBC driver for the database URL Add the driver to the project, --classpath, or the drivers folder MXE107 Cannot connect to the database Check the URL, network, user and password MXE108 Destructive changes need confirmation Review them; --allow-destructive, or --rename for renames MXE109 Migrations share numbers migrax merge renumbers them MXE110 No entities found Pass --package; migrax doctor shows what Migrax found MXE111 Docker is needed for verify Start Docker, or pass --url with an empty scratch database MXE112 clean is disabled MIGRAX_CLEAN_DISABLED is set; clean only development databases MXE113 No database URL configured Set it in the application config, MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL, or --url MXE114 A migration's precondition is not met Change the database so the -- migrax:require line holds, or end the line with else skip MXE115 The schema file can't be read Fix the statement the message names, start Docker, or pass --scratch-url with an empty database MXE116 No environments configured Give each environment a URL: migrax.environments.<name>.url or MIGRAX_ENVIRONMENTS_<NAME>_URL

docs.title: Entity readers
docs.text: With Hibernate 4 or newer in your project, Migrax asks your Hibernate version itself for the mapping, without connecting to a database. The generated schema is therefore exactly what your application expects: names, types, join tables, element collections, inheritance and sequences.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Every version below is tested on each change to Migrax. A fixture project with identity and sequence ids, enums, embedded types, element collections (sets, ordered lists, embeddables), one-to-many, many-to-one and many-to-many relationships, single-table inheritance and @Version is generated, migrated and verified. That same Hibernate version then validates the schema, and the rollback scripts are tested.

Hibernate Entities Typical frameworks Status 7.0 – 7.4 jakarta.persistence Spring Boot 4, recent Quarkus 3 releases, Micronaut 5 Supported 6.3 – 6.6 jakarta.persistence Spring Boot 3.2 to 3.5, Quarkus 3, Micronaut 4, Helidon 4 Supported 6.0 – 6.2 jakarta.persistence Spring Boot 3.0 and 3.1, early Quarkus 3 releases Supported 5.3 – 5.6 javax.persistence Spring Boot 2.1 to 2.7 Supported 5.0 – 5.2 javax.persistence Spring Boot 1.4 to 2.0 Supported (needs JAXB, see below) 4.0 – 4.3 javax.persistence Spring Boot 1.0 to 1.3, JBoss AS 7, JBoss EAP 6, WildFly 8 and 9 Supported before 4.0 javax.persistence older applications Annotation scanning only

Tested patch versions: 4.0.1, 4.1.12, 4.2.21, 4.3.11, 5.0.12, 5.1.17, 5.2.18, 5.3.36, 5.4.33, 5.5.9, 5.6.15, 6.0.2, 6.1.7, 6.2.52, 6.3.2, 6.4.10, 6.5.3, 6.6.58, 7.0.10, 7.1.36, 7.2.25, 7.3.13 and 7.4.12.

Hibernate 5.0 to 5.2 need JAXB

These versions use JAXB, which Java 11 and newer no longer include. Migrax runs on Java 17, so add it to your project as your application on Java 11 or newer needs anyway: javax.xml.bind:jaxb-api and org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-runtime (2.3.x). Without it, Migrax reads your entities from their annotations and verify compares the schema itself, and both say that JAXB is missing.

Hibernate 4

The migrations follow Hibernate 4's own rules: its names (Hibernate 4 keeps names as written, such as createdAt, unless the application sets a naming strategy) and its id generators: a plain @GeneratedValue is an identity column on H2, MySQL, MariaDB and SQL Server and the shared hibernate_sequence on PostgreSQL and Oracle, and sequences count up by 1 unless hibernate.id.new_generator_mappings is on. Spring Boot 1's spring.jpa.hibernate.naming-strategy is read like hibernate.ejb.naming_strategy. Hibernate 4.0 to 4.2 implement JPA 2.0, so @Table(indexes = ...) needs 4.3. Hibernate 4.0 and 4.1 have no sequences on SQL Server (their newest SQL Server dialect is for 2008), so entities there use identity columns, as the application itself needs.

docs.title: EclipseLink
docs.text:
When your project uses EclipseLink instead of Hibernate, Migrax asks your EclipseLink for its mapping, again without connecting to a database. The migrations then have the names EclipseLink uses (its default names such as ID and Customer_SCORES, written in lower case except where the database's table names are case-sensitive, as on MySQL), and what its id strategies need:

  • GenerationType.IDENTITY: an identity column.
  • GenerationType.SEQUENCE: a database sequence, started the way EclipseLink expects; on databases without sequences (MySQL), an identity column, as EclipseLink uses there.
  • A plain @GeneratedValue (or TABLE): EclipseLink's SEQUENCE table and its row for each generator.

Tested versions: 2.7.15 (javax.persistence), 3.0.4 and 4.0.4 (jakarta.persistence). The same fixture project is generated, migrated and verified, and then EclipseLink itself saves and reads every kind of entity against the migrated database. EclipseLink has no schema validation, so verify compares the schema with the mapping itself.

docs.title: OpenJPA
docs.text:
Projects that use OpenJPA (the JPA provider of Apache TomEE) are read through your OpenJPA's own mapping, also without a database. The migrations get OpenJPA's names (the class and field names as written, such as Tag and createdAt, in lower case except where the database's table names are case-sensitive), the indexes OpenJPA puts on foreign keys, and its id strategies: identity columns, database sequences, and OPENJPA_SEQUENCE_TABLE for a plain @GeneratedValue (OpenJPA adds its row itself).

Tested versions: 3.2.2 (javax.persistence) and 4.1.1 (jakarta.persistence), with OpenJPA saving and reading every kind of entity against the migrated database, as for EclipseLink. OpenJPA has no sequences on MySQL and MariaDB: use GenerationType.IDENTITY there.

docs.title: Spring Data JDBC
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.17.0.

Projects that use Spring Data JDBC instead of JPA are read through your Spring Data JDBC's own mapping, without a database. Migrax finds the aggregate roots under the entity package: the classes with @Table (org.springframework.data.relational.core.mapping.Table) and the types of your repositories, so a class without annotations counts once a repository uses it. The migrations get the tables Spring Data JDBC reads and writes:

  • Names from Spring Data JDBC's naming (createdAt becomes created_at), or as written in @Table, @Column and @MappedCollection(idColumn, keyColumn).
  • A child entity (a Set, List, Map or single property of another entity) gets its own table with the back-reference column to its parent, the key column for a List index or a Map key, and a foreign key to the parent. A reference to another aggregate (AggregateReference) is a plain column, without a foreign key, because the two are saved and deleted on their own.
  • Embedded values (@Embedded) become columns of the same table, with their prefix.
  • A Long or Integer id is an identity column, as Spring Data JDBC lets the database create it; @Sequence (Spring Data JDBC 3.5 and newer) creates the sequence instead.
  • Enums are stored by name, byte[] as binary data. Only ids and primitive types (int, boolean) are NOT NULL: Spring Data JDBC has no annotation that says a column can't be empty.

Spring Data JDBC puts every name in quotes, and a quoted name keeps its letter case. So where an unquoted name would get another case, Migrax quotes the name too: a name you write in lower case, such as @Table("customers"), on H2, Oracle, HSQLDB and Derby (CREATE TABLE "customers"), and a name with capitals, such as @Column("Nick"), on PostgreSQL. Names Spring Data JDBC derives itself, and every name on MySQL and SQL Server, are written as usual.

Spring Data JDBC is used when the entity package has no JPA entities; with --extractor spring-data-jdbc it is used in any case. migrax doctor shows the version it found. The Spring Boot starter applies the migrations at startup without JPA too.

Tested versions: Spring Data JDBC 3.0, 3.2, 3.5 and 4.1 (Spring Boot 3.0.13, 3.2.12, 3.5.16 and 4.1.1), on H2 and PostgreSQL. A fixture with every kind of aggregate is generated, migrated and verified, and then Spring Data JDBC itself saves, loads, updates and deletes it against the migrated database; after a new field, the second migration is checked the same way.

Not read: a collection of simple values (List<String>), which Spring Data JDBC stores as a database array (Migrax warns and leaves the column out), and a naming strategy or quoting setting your application changes in its own beans: write such names in the annotations.

docs.title: Micronaut Data
docs.text:
New in Migrax 0.17.0.

Projects that use Micronaut Data JDBC or R2DBC (@MappedEntity) are read through the mapping your Micronaut Data's annotation processor compiled into the classes, without a database or a running application. The migrations follow Micronaut Data's own rules:

  • Names from the entity's naming strategy (fullName becomes full_name), or as written in @MappedEntity, @MappedProperty and @JoinTable. Micronaut Data puts names in quotes, so on PostgreSQL a name with capitals (@MappedEntity("Publisher")) is created in quotes too.
  • NOT NULL for every property that isn't @Nullable, as Micronaut Data expects.
  • A many-to-one or one-to-one reference becomes its _id column with a foreign key. A many-to-many relation (or a one-to-many without mappedBy) gets its join table, without foreign keys: Micronaut Data deletes an entity without its join table rows, so a foreign key there would make deletes fail.
  • Generated ids as Micronaut Data makes them: an identity column, a sequence (GeneratedValue.Type.SEQUENCE, named <table>_seq or ref, and every generated id on Oracle), or a UUID the database fills in (on MySQL, MariaDB and TiDB Micronaut Data sends the UUID itself). UUIDs are varchar(36) on MySQL, MariaDB, TiDB and Oracle, as Micronaut Data stores them there.
  • Embedded values (@Embeddable) become columns of the same table, named as your version names them (Micronaut Data 5 leaves out the prefix).
  • @MappedProperty(definition = ...) is used as written; @Size(max) and JPA's @Column(length, precision, scale) set sizes.

Micronaut Data is used when the entity package has @MappedEntity classes and no JPA entities; with --extractor micronaut-data it is used in any case. Entities written with JPA annotations (micronaut-data-hibernate-jpa) are read as JPA entities, as before.

Tested versions: Micronaut Data 4.0, 4.14 and 5.2 (Micronaut 4.0.6, 4.10.22 and 5.2.3), on H2 and PostgreSQL. A fixture with every kind of entity is generated, migrated and verified, and then Micronaut Data itself saves, loads, updates and deletes it against the migrated database; after a new field, the second migration is checked the same way.

Not read: array properties (String[], PostgreSQL arrays) and other types without a @MappedProperty(definition): Migrax warns and leaves the column out. Micronaut 5 projects need Migrax running on Java 25.

docs.title: Without Hibernate, EclipseLink or OpenJPA, or before Hibernate 4
docs.text: Migrax then scans the JPA annotations and applies Hibernate 6's rules. That covers the common mappings, but types and sequence names can differ from older Hibernate versions (they use one shared hibernate_sequence, for example). migrax doctor warns when this applies. Check generated migrations carefully and run migrax verify.

docs.title: Choosing the reader
docs.text:
--extractor Behavior auto (default) Spring Data JDBC's or Micronaut Data's mapping when the package has no JPA entities, else Hibernate's mapping when possible, else EclipseLink's or OpenJPA's, else annotation scanning hibernate Hibernate's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used eclipselink EclipseLink's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used openjpa OpenJPA's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used spring-data-jdbc Spring Data JDBC's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used micronaut-data Micronaut Data's mapping only; fails with the reason if it can't be used annotations Annotation scanning only

migrax doctor shows which reader is used. migrax inspect prints the schema it read.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: What Migrax doesn't do yet, and what to do instead.

docs.title: Reading your entities
docs.text:
Hibernate older than 4.0. Migrax reads these projects from their annotations, using the rules of current Hibernate versions. Most mappings come out the same, but older versions differ in places: they share one hibernate_sequence between entities, for example. migrax doctor tells you when this applies. Review the generated migrations and run migrax verify before you release them. See Entity readers.

JPA providers other than Hibernate, EclipseLink and OpenJPA, such as DataNucleus, are read the same way, with Hibernate's naming rules. If your provider names tables or columns differently, set the names in your entities (@Table, @Column) or check the generated migrations.

docs.title: Reading a schema file
docs.text:
Sequences, tables in another schema, and MySQL's ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP in a schema file are not read; Migrax warns when the file has them. Identity columns work. Write migrations for sequences and other schemas yourself (migrax new), and add ON UPDATE to the generated migration.

Views, functions, procedures and triggers belong in repeatable migrations, not in the schema file.

docs.title: Projects without Java
docs.text:
Migrax itself runs on Java 17 or newer. Projects in other languages don't need Java on their machines: use the container image. They still get generated migrations: describe the schema in a schema file, or export it from your ORM (Schema file from your ORM), and migrax generate writes the migrations and their rollback scripts from it.

Migrating at startup works in Java applications (Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, Helidon, Jakarta EE). Elsewhere, run migrax migrate before the application starts, for example as a step of the deployment or an init container.

docs.title: Moving data
docs.text: Migrax changes the structure, not the values. It adds, renames, changes and drops columns and tables, and keeps the values of renamed ones, but it can't know how values should change shape, such as splitting full_name into first_name and last_name. Write that step yourself, in Java or SQL, between two generated migrations: Moving data between columns.

docs.title: Changing columns
docs.text: Oracle: a smaller NUMBER column in a key, index, unique constraint or check. Oracle makes a NUMBER column smaller (fewer decimals or fewer digits before the point) only while the column is empty. For other columns Migrax moves the values through a new column, which rewrites the table; a trigger keeps the new column up to date while the application goes on writing, and writes fail for a moment only while the old column is dropped. Dropping a column in a key, index, unique constraint or check would drop those too, so there the migration stops with ORA-01440 once the table has rows, and changes nothing. The same goes for identity columns. An index, constraint or column grant that only the database has (made by hand), or a function-based index on the table, stops the move with a message before anything is changed. Keep the larger type, or write the change yourself (migrax new): drop the key, index or constraint, add a column with the new type, copy the values into it, drop the old column, give the new one its name, and create the key, index or constraint again.

docs.title: Rolling back
docs.text: A rollback brings back the structure, not the data, unless the migration was generated with --keep-data. Rolling back a migration that dropped a column re-creates the column, but its values are gone; with --keep-data they come back from a backup table. See Keeping dropped data.

docs.title: Lint rules
docs.text:
Migrax lints every migration it generates, and migrax lint checks pending migrations (or --all, or named files). Each finding explains the risk and a safer alternative.

Severity: errors make lint exit with 1. Warnings do too with --strict. Info findings are advice.

To accept a finding on purpose, add a directive on the line before the statement:

-- migrax:lint-ignore MX007
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN legacy_code;
Code Severity Database Finds Safer alternative MX001 warning PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX on an existing table without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes until it finishes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own -- migrax:no-transaction migration (generate --safe does this) MX002 warning all NOT NULL column without a default on an existing table fails when the table has rows Add a DEFAULT, or add it nullable, backfill, then make it NOT NULL MX003 warning all Column type change can rewrite or lock the table, and fails or truncates when the type gets narrower Test on a production-size copy; for large tables add a new column, backfill, switch, drop MX004 warning PostgreSQL SET NOT NULL scans the table under an exclusive lock CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT later MX005 warning PostgreSQL Adding a foreign key checks every row while blocking writes to both tables Add it NOT VALID, validate in a later migration (generate --safe) MX006 warning PostgreSQL Adding a unique constraint builds its index while blocking writes CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX (generate --safe) MX007 warning all Dropping a table or column deletes data and breaks instances still using it Deploy code that no longer uses it, then drop in a later release (generate --zero-downtime) MX008 warning all Renaming breaks instances still running the old code Rename in steps (add, write both, switch reads, remove; generate --zero-downtime) or use a maintenance window MX009 warning all UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE changes every row in one transaction Add a WHERE, or update large tables in batches MX010 warning all TRUNCATE deletes all rows and cannot be undone by a rollback script Make sure it is intended and backed up MX011 warning PostgreSQL A volatile default rewrites every row under an exclusive lock Add the column without a default, set the default separately, backfill in batches MX012 error PostgreSQL A statement that cannot run inside a transaction (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM, ...) Add -- migrax:no-transaction to the migration MX013 warning PostgreSQL Adding a primary key builds an index while blocking writes CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX MX014 warning PostgreSQL Adding a check constraint scans the table under an exclusive lock Add it NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT later MX015 info SQL Server, Oracle Index builds lock the table unless they run online WITH (ONLINE = ON) (SQL Server Enterprise) or ONLINE (Oracle Enterprise) MX016 warning all A procedure, function, trigger, package or block whose body has an unmatched BEGIN, so it takes in the statements after it Give every BEGIN its END, or end the body with GO, a DELIMITER line or a / line MX017 warning SQL Server with migrax.schemas A table without its schema in front lands in the login's default schema, not in each tenant's Write ${migrax.schema}.<table> (several schemas) MX000 error all The migration could not be parsed Fix the SQL

docs.title: Naming strategies
docs.text:
Hibernate turns entity and field names into table and column names, and each framework configures that differently. Migrax must use exactly the same rules, or the generated tables won't be the ones your application looks for.

Strategy Used by homepageURL fullName Join table for Product.tags spring Spring Boot homepageurl full_name product_tags jpa Quarkus, Helidon, Jakarta EE, plain Hibernate, Micronaut without Micronaut Data homepageURL fullName Product_Tag micronaut Micronaut Data homepage_url full_name product_tag jpa-snake Hibernate with only a snake_case physical strategy homepageurl full_name product_tag

Names you give explicitly with @Table(name = ...) or @Column(name = ...) pass through the same physical rule: Spring Boot and Micronaut Data turn them into snake_case too.

docs.title: How Migrax chooses
docs.text:
1. An explicit setting: --naming, MIGRAX_NAMING or migrax.naming.
  2. The naming recorded in .migrax/snapshot.json by the first generate. This keeps names stable even if the configuration changes later, for example when the database URL moves into environment variables.
  3. A naming strategy configured for Hibernate, such as spring.jpa.hibernate.naming.physical-strategy or hibernate.physical_naming_strategy.
  4. The framework's default, detected from the build file and configuration.

migrax init and migrax doctor show the result. When the snapshot's naming differs from what your framework uses, doctor warns and explains how to switch.

Changing the naming of an existing project

Switching naming renames every affected column. Set migrax.naming, run migrax generate, and accept the renames it proposes, so the data is kept.

docs.title: Sequences
docs.text:
Generated ids (@GeneratedValue with AUTO or SEQUENCE and no named generator) use:

Hibernate Sequence 6 and 7 <entity>_SEQ per entity, allocation size 50 6 and 7 with Micronaut Data one hibernate_sequence 5.x one hibernate_sequence, allocation size 1

On MySQL, which has no sequences, Hibernate uses a one-row next_val table of the same name, and so does Migrax.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with migrax doctor: it checks Java, the build, the entities, the database connection and risky settings, and says how to fix each problem. In a folder with migrations but no pom.xml, build.gradle or entity package (the container image, or a project in another language), it checks only the migrations and the database. Add --verbose to any command for debug output and stack traces.

migrax is not recognized

The terminal was opened before Migrax was installed. Open a new terminal; for the terminal inside VS Code or IntelliJ IDEA, restart the editor. See Installation.

No database URL found

Migrax looks for the URL in your framework's usual setting; the error names the right key for your framework. Set it there, or use MIGRAX_DATABASE_URL / --url. See Configuration.

Hibernate could not read the entity mapping; scanning JPA annotations instead

Migrax fell back to annotation scanning. Run with --extractor hibernate to see the exact error. Common causes: entities using javax.persistence with Hibernate 6+ (or jakarta with Hibernate 5), a Hibernate version older than 4.0, or Hibernate 5.0 to 5.2 without JAXB (the message says so; see Entity readers).

A migration fails with 'already exists'

Something created the table before the migration ran, usually Hibernate with ddl-auto=update or schema-management.strategy=update. Set it to none, restore the database to the state before the migration, then migrax repair <migration> --action retry --yes and migrax migrate.

Generated SQL renames or drops every column

The naming strategy doesn't match the one your tables were created with. Check the Naming: line of migrax doctor, and set migrax.naming to the strategy the tables use. See Naming strategies.

migrate stops: a migration changed or is missing

Applied migrations must not change. Restore the original file from git, and put the change in a new migration (migrax new).

--no-build cannot find the JDBC driver

--no-build reuses the dependencies resolved by the last build. Run one command without it first (or with --refresh).

verify cannot start a database

For engines other than H2, verify needs Docker. Without Docker, pass an empty scratch database: migrax verify --url <jdbc-url>.
